en: [1] The Section on Impurity (Āśaucakāṇḍa).

Now, for the purpose of defining the *ekoddiṣṭa* and other types of *śrāddha* rites to be performed at the beginning of the period of impurity and so forth, the section on impurity (*āśaucaprakaraṇa*) is commenced. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:

During a period of ritual impurity, one should suspend giving gifts, receiving them, performing fire-oblations, Vedic study, and rites for the ancestors, with the exception of the offering of funeral cakes for the deceased.

The term *āśauca* (impurity) should be understood as that state of impurity arising from the birth or death of a *sapiṇḍa* relative, which is characterized by unfitness for religious acts such as giving gifts (*dāna*) and so forth, or which consists of a specific form of sin. This alone is taught to be the meaning of the word *āśauca*. We shall later confirm this through the agreement with the text of Bhaṭṭācārya, which is not far off. The meaning is that while such impurity exists, one should not perform ancestral rites (*pitṛkarma*) other than the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) that benefit the deceased, nor should one engage in giving or receiving gifts, and so on. By the exclusion (*paryudāsa*) "excluding the rice-ball offerings for the deceased," it is shown that the *śrāddha* intended to benefit the deceased must be performed even while impurity persists. Dakṣa states that the duration of this impurity is not for a long time.
Immediate purification, as well as one day, three days,
four days, six, ten, twelve days, a fortnight, and likewise a month.
"Likewise, there is another [period] ending at death; however, there are ten fortnights in the case of birth-impurity (sūtaka).

[2] The phrase "ten fortnights" is not for the purpose of restriction, because more than ten fortnights are also seen in the Smṛtis. ... But in the case of a short time, three [days] apply to the highest [caste].
For a Kshatriya, however, it is four nights; for a Vaishya, it is five days indeed.
But for a Śūdra, this purification is proclaimed to take eight days.

Thus, even the period of five days and so forth has been recorded. This is the meaning: in the case of a miscarriage occurring within a short time—that is, before the completion of the fourth month of gestation—there is no impurity (*āśauca*) according to the specific month; rather, for the highest caste, the Brāhmaṇa, three days are the cause of purification for the mother; for the *Rājanya* or Kṣatriya caste, four nights are the cause of purification for the mother; for the Vaiśya caste, five days are the cause of purification for the mother; and for the Śūdra caste, purification of the mother occurs after eight days in the case of a miscarriage. (For a Brāhmaṇī woman, three nights; for a Kṣatriyā, four nights; for a Vaiśyā, five nights; and for a Śūdrā, eight nights are the causes of purification. Regarding the meaning of the word *śuddhi*, one should look to what Bhaṭṭācārya stated: "Purification (*śuddhi*) is either the destruction of sin (*pāpakṣaya*) or fitness for religious duty (*dharmayogyatva*). The destruction of sin refers to the elimination of a particular sin arising in those connected to the birth or death of a *sapiṇḍa* relative. Fitness for religious duty means being fit for the performance of religious acts such as giving gifts (*dāna*). Thus, the meaning of the word *śuddhi* has been explained in two ways by Bhaṭṭācārya according to different views. It should be understood that, conversely, the term *āśauca* (impurity), according to different views, denotes the particular sin caused by birth or death and the unfitness for performing religious acts such as giving gifts. In the case of a miscarriage occurring shortly [after conception], the impurity belongs to the mother alone, not to the father or other *sapiṇḍa* relatives. And so it was stated immediately thereafter by that very same author.
"In the case of a miscarriage, there shall be a three-night period for the mother, during which the sapinda relatives must avoid impure acts. [3]

The phrase “for three nights” refers to those of the Brāhmaṇa caste, since for Kṣatriyas and others, periods of four nights and so forth have been prescribed. As for that which was stated by Sumantu: “In the case of a miscarriage, the days [of impurity] are equal to the months of gestation, and there is immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca),” that refers to the fourth month. This is a regulated option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*). Thus is the meaning: in the event of a miscarriage in the fourth month, the mother’s impurity lasts four nights, while for a male *sapiṇḍa*, there is immediate purification upon bathing. Accordingly, Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha states: “In the case of a miscarriage, the days are equal to the months for women; for a man, it is merely bathing; however, in the case of a slightly hardened miscarriage, it is three nights. This is clearly intended for a miscarriage occurring in the fourth month, because a slightly hardened miscarriage is impossible in other months. The essential meaning of this statement is: in the event of a miscarriage in the fourth month—whether due to softness or slight hardness—the mother’s impurity lasts three nights; for a male *sapiṇḍa*, if the miscarriage is soft, there is immediate purification, but if it is hard, the impurity lasts three nights. Because of the mention of the “man” (*puruṣa*), there is no impurity here for female *sapiṇḍas*; rather, by virtue of the singular number, the father’s impurity lasts three nights. As for that which was stated by Marīci as lasting three nights for both male and female *sapiṇḍas* in common:

Regarding the statement, "In the case of a miscarriage, [the impurity lasts] for three days for the mother according to her months [of pregnancy], and for the father and others for three days," and that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "In the event of a miscarriage, the sapindas have an impurity of three nights"—these refer to the subject of a miscarriage occurring in the fifth or sixth month, because a miscarriage is impossible at other stages of the month. The intended meaning is as follows: in the event of a miscarriage in the fifth month, the impurity for the mother is five nights; in the sixth month, it is six nights; but for the father and other sapindas, it is three nights even throughout both of those months. As for what was stated by Yama:
"In the case of a son whose teeth have not yet emerged, or a child, or likewise in the case of a miscarriage..."
For all sapindas, however, the period of impurity lasts for one day and night.
Thus, that [rule] refers to a qualified *sapiṇḍa* or to one who is not present. As for what was stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) applies to the *sapiṇḍas* when there is a miscarriage of the fetus."

This refers to the case of a soft (mṛdu) miscarriage occurring within the fourth month; for it is precisely in that context that Sumantu and Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha prescribe immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) for a male *sapiṇḍa*. Thus, it should be understood that the term "fall" (*pāta*) is used figuratively for a miscarriage by virtue of its quality of emerging from the mother’s womb. This is because, if it were taken in its primary sense, it would result in a contradiction with the previously cited statements. The period of impurity (*āśauca*) of four nights and so forth mentioned for the three months beginning with the fourth applies equally to all four castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas, since no specific distinction is recorded. Furthermore, Manu has placed this in conjunction with the general purification of a menstruating woman (*rajasvalā*) in order to indicate that the rules regarding impurity apply to all four castes alike.

"In a miscarriage, a woman is purified by nights equal to the months [of pregnancy]; when the menstrual flow has ceased, every menstruating woman is purified by bathing. Here, "every" means women of all castes (*sarvavarṇa*). Regarding miscarriages occurring in the seventh month and onwards, one should refer to what is stated in other *smṛtis*.
"Up to the fourth [month] there may be a flow; a miscarriage occurs in the fifth and sixth.
Beyond that, in the case of a full-term birth, there shall be *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) for ten days.

Here, the prefix *ā* indicates inclusion. The phrase "for ten days" (*daśāham*) applies specifically to the case of a Brāhmaṇī woman, not to women of other castes. Thus it is stated in the *Ādipurāṇa*:

[5] "When a miscarriage occurs within six months, their purification is held to be by days equal in number to the months. This means that from the fourth month onwards. By the phrase "as stated for one's own caste," this is what is meant: ten days of impurity for a Brāhmaṇī, twelve days for a Kṣatriyā, fifteen days for a Vaiśyā, and one month for a Śūdrā. As for that which was stated by Pracetas:
A woman who has given birth becomes pure after ten days for all castes;
however, during her menstrual period, this rule regarding women across all castes does not apply separately.

The meaning is that the rule of impurity lasting three nights upon the appearance of menses for women applies without distinction to all social classes (*varṇa*). In this context, the statement that "for all classes, a woman in childbirth becomes pure after ten days" refers to the impurity characterized by a lack of ritual fitness caused by the discharge of blood at the time of delivery; this is because it is mentioned in conjunction with the impurity of a menstruating woman. Beyond that [period], the impurity prescribed for their own respective castes applies to them.

The aforementioned statement refers to the common impurity (*āśauca*) shared by all *sapinda* relatives, such as parents and others, because it is stated to be "that which is prescribed for one's own caste. As for the statement by Paiṭhīnasi: "One may cause a woman who has given birth to a son to perform rites after twenty nights, and one who has given birth to a daughter after a month," that statement intends to refer to the impurity characterized by unfitness for duties such as giving gifts; thus, there is no contradiction with what was stated previously. Here, "rites" (*karmāṇi*) refers to those intended for transcendental results (*adṛṣṭārtha*), such as sacrifices and gifts. "After twenty nights have passed" means that once twenty days have elapsed starting from the day of birth, she becomes fit for acts such as giving gifts.
"A woman who has given birth becomes pure after ten days for all castes"—in this [verse], the word "all" must be restricted to castes other than the Śūdra. And so says Parāśara:
"A woman who has given birth, if she belongs to the twice-born castes, becomes pure after ten days."
"When the thirteenth day has arrived, the Śūdra woman becomes pure; of this there is no doubt."

Thus, regarding a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*): there is a state of impurity (*aprāyatya*) caused by the discharge of blood, which lasts for ten nights among the twice-born and others, and serves as the basis for avoiding them from a distance of three *yugas* (nine cubits) and so forth; furthermore, there is a form of impurity consisting of unfitness (*agha*), which causes untouchability and the like, lasting for ten, twelve, or fifteen days according to one's own caste; and finally, there is that characterized by disqualification from religious duties such as giving gifts, which among the twice-born lasts for twenty nights after the birth of a son and for one month after the birth of a daughter—this is how it should be understood. As for that which is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
If nine months have passed, there is always purity upon birth,
whether that person is dead or still living, after a number of days equal to the number of months.

Thus, "below nine months" means starting from the seventh month; this is the remainder [of the sense]. This refers to *sapiṇḍa* relatives other than the woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*), because if it applied to all *sapiṇḍa* relatives including the *sūtikā*, it would result in a contradiction with the previously cited statements. And so, as for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: "For the *sapiṇḍas* of a Brāhmaṇa, there is impurity (*āśauca*) lasting ten days on account of birth or death; twelve days for a Kṣatriya; fifteen days for a Vaiśya; and one month for a Śūdra"—this statement of Viṣṇu applies [to those cases], whereas in the ninth or tenth month, due to the powerful winds of labor...
He is drawn out like an arrow with a fever from a mechanical device through a small opening.

Thus, this should be understood as referring to the subject of delivery in the ninth or tenth month as stated by Yājñavalkya. As for that which was stated by Paiṭhīnasi: "Upon a birth, the sapinda relatives are pure; however, there is *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) for the mother and father.
The *sūtaka* belongs to the mother alone; having performed ablutions, the father becomes pure."

Thus, this is its meaning: upon the birth of a *sapiṇḍa*, those *sapiṇḍas* other than the father and mother are pure; for although the impurity characterized by the disqualification from religious duties (*dharma*) caused by the birth of a *sapiṇḍa* exists, they are fit for touch because that impurity does not exist in their case. Consequently, there occurs for the mother and father the state of *sūtaka*, characterized by untouchability, due to the possibility of such contact. And the reason for that possibility is that the mother and father are the cause of pain to the living being being born. This causality is, in the case of the father, indirect through his role as progenitor, while in the case of the mother, it is direct through her exertion conducive to the emergence of the fetus from the womb. Therefore, because of its gravity, *sūtaka*—which cannot be removed by mere bathing—belongs to the mother alone and not to the father. Thus, even in the absence of waiting for a specific period for the sake of purification, the father becomes pure by mere bathing and, through the destruction of the impurity (*agha*), becomes fit for touch. Accordingly, another *Smṛti* states: "In the case of birth, this same [impurity] belongs to the mother and father; the untouchability belongs to the mother alone, and not to other relatives. Similarly, immediately after death, the impurity characterized by unfitness for religious acts belongs only to the mother and father prior to the cutting of the umbilical cord, and not to other *sapiṇḍas* who lack the agency of causing pain to the living being being born. Even between the two, the impurity which causes untouchability and cannot be removed by mere bathing belongs to the mother alone; this is the meaning. By this, the claim that in the case of birth there is no production of sin (*pāpa*), and therefore the impurity is only characterized by unfitness for religious duties and not of the nature of *agha*, is refuted. Now, [one might object: an impurity characterized by both untouchability and unfitness for religious duties is possible only for those who are eligible for rites like the *Agnihotra* but are unmarried, since for them there is an absence of untouchability. Therefore, the cause of birth is indeed twofold. As for the statement of Aṅgiras: [The text continues with the citation of Aṅgiras.]

"Prior to the bath, one is untouchable at birth; there is a loss of ritual acts and impurity"—this should be understood as referring to the father. If, after the bath, the father touches the woman who has given birth, then those two who touch her remain untouchable even after his bath. And so Parāśara says:
"If a twice-born man desires contact with his wife when she has given birth..."
"But if that Brahmin is a knower of the six Vedāṅgas, there shall be no impurity for him. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that he desires contact with his wife—that is, he engages in contact characterized by physical touch—and for that twice-born man (*dvija*), there shall arise a state of untouchability (*aspṛśyatva*) caused by touching a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*). Although one should have said "the husband," the use of the term "twice-born" is intended to indicate that this same rule applies equally to any twice-born man who touches a *sūtikā*, even if he is not her husband. For this very reason, Sumantu states: "The impurity (*sūtaka*) belongs only to the mother and to those who touch her, but not to others. This refers to the state of impurity (*sūtaka*) characterized by unfitness for religious rites, which arises from the flow of blood at the time of childbirth. The meaning is that for a person who touches that *sūtikā*, there occurs the impurity characterized by untouchability, but not for other people who do not touch her. Vasiṣṭha also [states]: [Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence regarding Vasiṣṭha.]
"There is no impurity during childbirth for men, provided they do not come into contact [with the woman];
in that case, it is the *rajas* (menstrual blood) that should be known as impure, and that does not exist in a man. Thus [it is said].
Parāśara, however, declares an impurity of the same form [as that of women].
"But during childbirth, if the householder does not cause a mixture [of castes],
the mother is purified after ten days, while the father becomes pure by immersing himself [in water].
Thus says Atri as well.
"From contact arises the defect regarding death and birth pertaining to another;
by avoiding that [contact], immediate purification is ordained even for the father.
Here, "death and birth pertaining to another" means death and birth related to someone else. This is also stated in the Ādipurāṇa:

"But in the case of birth-impurity (sūtaka), once the father has seen the face of the newborn, he becomes pure at that very moment by performing a bath along with his clothes. Thus says Saṃvarta as well.
When a son is born, bathing with one's clothes on is prescribed for the father;
the mother becomes pure after ten days, while the father may touch [others] immediately upon bathing.

The meaning is that it does not entail any fault. The meaning is that the mother becomes pure, that is, fit for physical contact. As for what was stated by Bodhāyana: "At birth, there is impurity for ten days for both the mother and the father; some say it is for the mother alone"—this impurity is characterized by a lack of ritual fitness (*asamavāya*). In this regard, the statement "for ten days for both the mother and the father" is presented as a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), as is understood from the use of the word "only" (*tāvat*) in the phrase "some say it is for the mother alone. Therefore, this very position—"for the mother alone"—is the correct view (*samyakpakṣa*), and thus there is no contradiction with what was stated previously. As for what was said by Aṅgiras:

"In the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), contact with anyone except the woman who has given birth does not cause impurity"—this refers to cases other than those involving an uncle (*pitṛvya*) who has not bathed. As for that which was stated by the same author:
"No impurity is declared for *sapiṇḍas* who perform the rites during a birth."

Thus, the meaning of this is as follows: for those who perform rituals—namely, those who perform sacrifices and other rites for the sake of pleasing the deities known as the *janmadā* (givers of birth)—there is no impurity (*āśauca*), characterized by unfitness for ritual action, among their paternal ancestors and other *sapiṇḍas* on the days when the performance of sacrifices and other rites to the *janmadā* deities occurs; that [impurity] pertains only to the time of the actual performance. And so says Vyāsa:
"The deities named *janmadā* reside in the lying-in chamber;
for the purpose of sacrifice to them, purification is prescribed at birth."
The mention of "sacrifice" (*yāga*) is intended as an illustration for acts such as worship (*pūjā*). For this very reason, it was stated by that same author:
"On the first day, the sixth, and the tenth—on these three days at all times, one should not observe impurity (*sūtaka*) upon the birth of a son."

It is intended that *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) is characterized by unfitness for religious duties (*dharma*), because it is designated as the occasion for sacrifice (*yāga*). There is an absence of impurity regarding the occasion for sacrifice on either the first or the tenth day. As for the time for the sacrifice:
"On the sixth day, one should cause the sacrifice and the gift-offering to be performed for the birth-givers.

The meaning is that, for the sake of the sacrifice, purification is proclaimed therein. Furthermore, even on the tenth day, the injunction for the sacrifice is specifically at night. And so says Mārkaṇḍeya:
Likewise, the sixth night must be guarded with special care;
a vigil should be kept at night, as well as offerings for the "givers of birth.
Men should hold weapons in their hands, and women should engage in dance and song.
"They should perform a night vigil on the tenth day, even during a period of birth-impurity. [11] Thus it is said.

On the first day, that is, at the time of performing the birth-rites (*jātakarma*) and other ceremonies for the occasion of a birth, [one may accept gifts] throughout the entire first day—not merely on the first day. Thus Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "When a boy is born, as long as the umbilical cord has not been severed, there is no fault even in accepting molasses, sesame, gold, clothing, upper garments, cows, or grain; some say this applies to that very day. This means that on the day of a boy's birth, there is no fault in giving, receiving, and so forth, as long as the umbilical cord remains unsevered. Some maintain that this refers specifically to that day. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says: "That day is not defiled, because it is the cause of the birth of the ancestors."

The day on which the birth of the son occurs does not become defiled; that is to say, it does not incur the state of being unfit for gifts and worship due to the occasion of the birth. This is because, on that day, the birth of the ancestors—the father and others—takes place in the form of a son. As for what was stated by Jaimini:
"As long as the umbilical cord is not severed, so long one does not incur *sūtaka*;
once the cord is severed, thereafter *sūtaka* is prescribed."

Thus, this is its meaning: the impurity (*āśauca*) consisting of *agha* for all *sapinda* relatives, caused by the severance of the umbilical cord, occurs only after the possibility of the cause of impurity has arisen, and not prior to it.

Now, one might object that impurity in the form of *agha* (sin/defilement) does not apply to those other than the *sapinda* relatives and paternal uncles, because there is no cause for it; anticipating this, Hārīta states the reason: "Because they are overcome by the deceased, they inquire: 'By what means is the impurity of the corpse removed when a birth occurs during a period of prosperity? Since their time has not been cut off, and because of the great continuity of the lineage, the impurity belongs to the family. However, for those who share the same water (*samānodaka*), the impurity caused by a birth should be understood as lasting three nights;
for those who share the same water, purification from a birth is held to occur after three nights.
This is because of such a traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*). Regarding the three-day period of impurity (*āśauca*) for the *sapiṇḍas*, such as the father and others, even at birth, Bṛhan-Manu says:
"If one who was born alive dies, or if there is stillbirth (*sūtaka*), the full period of *sūtaka* applies to the mother, while for the father and others it lasts for three nights."

The meaning is this: if a newborn infant dies before the cutting of the umbilical cord, then there is a ten-day period of impurity (*āśauca*) for the mother, while for all *sapiṇḍas*, including the father and others, it is three nights. As stated in the words of Bṛhat-Pracetas: "If a child should die after having lived for even a moment, the purification of the mother is after ten days, but for those born of the same lineage (*gotra*), it is immediate."

Thus, that [rule] refers to one who performs the *agnihotra* under discussion, because of the traditional teaching of Śaṅkha: "Impurity for that time [occurs] due to bathing and ritual touching for the sake of the *agnihotra*. As for what was stated by Hārīta: "Whether a child is born and then dies, or dies at birth, there is ten-day [impurity] for the *sapiṇḍas*"—the word "birth-impurity" (*sūtaka*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Here, the ten days mentioned regarding a child born and then dead should be understood as occurring after the cutting of the umbilical cord of the newborn infant; otherwise, a mutual contradiction would arise, as this would have the same scope as the statement of Bṛhan-Manu. Regarding the case of a child dying at birth, Pāraskara also has prescribed ten days of birth-impurity.

"If there should be a miscarriage in the womb, there shall be impurity (*sūtaka*) for ten days"—the word "of the *sapiṇḍas*" is to be supplied as the remainder. In both cases, the mention of "ten days" is intended to indicate the period prescribed for one's own caste. As for that which says:
"Where a son is born dead, or if one who was born dead is revived..."
The birth-impurity (sūtaka) shall belong to the mother alone; for the father and others, it lasts for three nights.

Thus, this [rule] refers to fathers and others who are endowed with good conduct and Vedic study; furthermore, even for such fathers and others, the three-night impurity (*sūtaka*) occasioned by death or birth need not be observed in the Kali age.
Thus concludes the determination of impurity due to childbirth in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the determination of impurity due to death.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"I shall proclaim the purification of the deceased as well as the purification of objects, for all four castes, duly and in their proper order. Now,

if it is argued that the meaning "of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras" is already established by the word "varṇānām," and thus the word "caturṇām" (of the four) is redundant, it is replied:
When a fellow religious student has passed away, a fast of one day is prescribed;
for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, the fast lasts for a night with its two surrounding days (pakṣiṇī).

In such statements as these, those rules regarding impurity (*āśauca*) for which no specific caste (*varṇa*) is mentioned are intended to apply not merely to the first caste (the Brāhmaṇa), but to all castes; it is for the purpose of making this known that the word "of the four" (*caturṇām*) is used. And this very point has been stated by the author of the *Bhāṣyārthasaṃgraha*:
"In the case of non-sapinda relatives who are Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), when the teacher has passed away, likewise when a king has passed away, and during the menstrual periods of women..."
[14] Likewise, in the case of childless women, maternal uncles, and kinsmen—
in such instances as these, the period of impurity is equal for all four castes.
Since [the rule] would have been established by the mere mention of "of the castes," the specific mention of "four" is for the sake of clarity.

Thus, in accordance with the stated order, the purification regarding the deceased (*preta-śuddhi*) is first described. Regarding this, Paiṅgya states: "If the deceased is in the womb, the mother's [impurity lasts] ten days. The phrase "impurity due to a deceased person" (*pretāśauca*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. Concerning those *sapiṇḍas* other than the mother in this matter, Bṛhad-Viṣṇu has said: "In the case of one born dead, there is immediate purification for the family. However, regarding one who dies after being born, Vyāghra says:
"If one dies after being born, immediate purification is ordained for the *sapiṇḍas*."
"By ten days alone [is purification for] the husband and wife, and likewise for uterine siblings.
Regarding the phrase "by ten days," this refers to the case of a child who dies on the day of birth. He (the same author) also speaks regarding the case of a child who dies after the day of birth:
"If the rite of first exit (*niṣkramaṇa*) is performed for a newborn infant within ten days..."
"Śātātapa declared that for the parents, purification occurs through the birth-impurity itself. Thus [it is said].

The mention of "the parents" is intended as an illustration for the uterine brothers. "Niṣkramaṇa" means death. The meaning is that by the *sūtaka* itself—that is, by the remaining days of the birth-impurity—the purification of the parents and the uterine brothers from the impurity caused by the child's death occurs. Thus, the meaning is that the death-impurity of the parents and others for a child who has died within ten days is purified by those very days of *sūtaka*. As for the statement of Paiṅgi: "When the name is given to both and to the uterine brothers," the phrase "when the name is given" (*kṛte nāmani*) is intended as an illustration for the tenth day, which is the day of the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). The sense is this: when a newborn child dies on the day of birth, there is ten-day impurity for the mother, the father, and the uterine brothers; but when the name is given—meaning when the tenth day, the day of the naming ceremony, has passed—there is one day and night of impurity for those same individuals. And so says Śaṅkha.
"Within ten days, for a child who has passed away, purification shall occur simultaneously with the purification from birth;
beyond ten days, it shall take one day.

Within ten days—that is, during the interval of ten days—if a child has passed away, there shall be purification for the mother and father, as well as for uterine brothers, through the same purification that follows birth, even if death occurs after the birth-impurity has begun. And beyond these [ten days], for them, it shall take one day. As for that which was stated by Yama:
If a child dies sometime within ten days, one should not observe the impurity for the dead; rather, purification occurs through the impurity of birth.

Thus, this is the meaning: during the period of *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth) that has first commenced, the impurity caused by the death of an infant (*śiśumaraṇāśauca*) need not be observed by the mother and others after the *sūtaka* has passed; for both parents are purified by the *sūtyāśauca* itself—which pertains specifically to the duration of the birth-impurity—even more so than by the impurity of a corpse (*śāvāśauca*), and the uterine brothers are likewise purified. As for what was stated by Āpastamba: "In the case of *sūtaka*, the impurity lasts until the rising from the confinement bed (*utthāna*); if that same child dies, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*), and no water libation is offered here," the meaning of this is as follows: when a child dies in the midst of the *sūtaka* that had begun upon its birth, the impurity for the mother and others lasts until the *utthāna*, just as the *sūtaka* is prescribed to last until the tenth day or until the rising of the woman who gave birth. Thus, the impurity for the death of the infant also lasts for that same duration for the mother and others, because they are purified by the end of the *sūtyāśauca*. In that regard, for the mother and others, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) like that of other *sapiṇḍas*; and "no water is offered here" means no water is offered for the deceased. By the phrase "impurity until the rising," he shows that even if the infant dies on the tenth day while still within the *sūtaka*, the impurity ends on that very day, and that the specific rules mentioned in such texts as "if the remainder of the day [is left], [purification is] by two days; if at dawn, by three" do not apply here. As for the statement in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*, "Birth-impurity does not purify [one from] corpse-impurity," that refers to a case where another *sūtaka* occurs separated by two or three days; otherwise, it would contradict the singular statements regarding the subject matter of the previously mentioned impurities. As for what was stated by Bṛhan-Manu... [text continues].
If a child dies within ten days, its relatives shall not observe the impurity of death (śāvāśauca); instead, the impurity of birth (sūtyāśauca) is prescribed.

Thus, the meaning of this is as follows: if a child dies within ten days, the kinsmen—even paternal uncles and others—should not observe the impurity caused by death (*śāvāśauca*) for a long duration, as they do in the case of a mother and so forth; rather, it must be immediate. However, the impurity caused by birth (*sūtyāśauca*) is ordained for paternal uncles and other kinsmen as well, lasting for a long period such as ten days, according to what is prescribed for their own caste, just as it is for a mother and others. As for that which was stated by Śāṭyāyana: "But if a child passes away before the end of ten days, there shall be purification immediately; there is neither impurity nor birth-impurity (*sūtaka*)."

Thus, this refers to maternal uncles and other such relatives. Consequently, the meaning is as follows: for maternal uncles and other kinsmen, there is no impurity caused by birth (sūtaka) or death (śāva) here that must be removed by the passage of time; rather, the lack of purity resulting from consuming their food, or the impurity of birth and so forth, perishes through mere bathing—just like the lack of purity caused by physical contact.
Thus ends the section on impurity resulting from the death of an infant occurring during the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the section on impurity resulting from the death of an infant occurring after the period of birth-impurity.
In this regard, Śaṅkha says:
"If a child dies within ten days [of birth], purification occurs simultaneously with the birth itself;
after ten days but before the *caula* ceremony, it lasts for one day."
"Thereafter it shall be for three nights; prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass, it shall be [for one night]. Thus [it is said].

"Below the *caula* ceremony"—that is, prior to the *caula* prescribed for the first year, which amounts to saying "prior to the eruption of teeth. Thus, the meaning is as follows: during the period when the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) continues within the ten-day interval, if a child dies, there is purification from the impurity of death along with the impurity of birth. After the ten days—meaning after the cessation of the birth-impurity—but before the eruption of teeth, if a child dies, the impurity lasts for one day and night; after the eruption of teeth but before the tying of the girdle (*mauñjībandhana*), it lasts for three nights. In this context, the statement "there shall be purification together with [the end of] birth" refers specifically to the mother and father.
"Purity for the parents shall come through the birth-impurity itself," so said Śātātapa;

this is because of the force of that previously cited statement as well. And thus, by virtue of its association with this, the rule "one day after ten days" should be understood as applying when the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) takes place on the tenth day, since the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* states: "The naming ceremony occurs when ten nights have passed from birth, or after a hundred nights, or after a year. Therefore, just as the naming ceremony may take place at the time of ten nights and so forth, [the impurity lasts for one day]:
"Until the naming ceremony, purity is immediate; until the eruption of teeth, it is one day."
It is taught that for the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā), [the period of impurity] lasts three days, and likewise until the initiation (vratā) for the rite of growth (vṛddhi).

Thus, the "immediate purification" (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) mentioned in another *Smṛti* should be understood as applying from after the ten days until the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). This is the meaning of that other *Smṛti*: after the cessation of the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) but before the naming ceremony, purification is immediate; before the eruption of teeth, it is by one day and night; after the eruption of teeth but before the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*) prescribed for the third year, it is by three nights; and beyond that, but before the investiture with the sacred girdle (*mauñjibandhana*), purification is by those same three nights accompanied by the cremation rite (*agnisaṃskāra*) and the offering of water (*udakadāna*). For this very reason, the author of the *Saṃgraha* [states]:
Regarding the stages of naming, the eruption of teeth, the tonsure, and the initiation ceremony,
the periods of impurity are respectively immediate, one day, three days, and thereafter [ten days] for those who maintain the sacred fires and perform water-libations regularly.
As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha:
"Immediate purification is prescribed for a child who has not yet cut its teeth;
likewise, purification occurs after one day and night for a child whose tonsure ceremony (caula) has not been performed."
"Regarding one for whom the *caula* ceremony has not been performed," the meaning is "prior to the time of the *cūḍā* ceremony. Furthermore, as stated by Yājñavalkya:
"Until the eruption of teeth, purification is immediate; until the *caula*, it is declared to be overnight;
until the initiation (*vratādeśa*), it is three nights; and beyond that, ten nights."

Thus, the meaning is as follows: for one who has passed away after birth and beginning with the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) but prior to the eruption of teeth, the impurity (*āśauca*) of relatives lasts for a day; from the eruption of teeth until before the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*), it lasts for a day and night; and from the tonsure until the initiation (*upanayana*), the impurity lasts for three nights. These two statements refer to cases other than those involving the mother, the father, or a uterine brother. Regarding this subject, Aṅgiras states: "In the case of a child whose teeth have not yet emerged, purification is ordained to be immediate. This is the scope he declares.

"Indeed, for one who is born after [the parents], there shall be impurity [only] until the relatives have performed their bath with their clothes on outside [the house]. Here, "born after" (*anujāta*) means a child younger than one whose teeth have appeared; that is to say, one whose teeth have not yet emerged. Furthermore, there exist many other statements in this section that appear to contradict the statements already presented; the resolution of those contradictions will be discussed in the section to follow.

Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, [the topics concerning] impurity resulting from the death of a child while one is in a state of birth-impurity (sūtaka) have been addressed. Now follow the topics concerning the funeral rites for the body and the impurity resulting from the death of a child;
regarding this, the Ādipurāṇa states:
In the case of women, however, an embryo that has fallen, or one born dead,
or one who dies before the teeth have emerged, or likewise after six months have passed;
"Having adorned him with garments and ornaments, he should be cast [into the fire] like a piece of wood; having slowly dug into the earth, purification is prescribed immediately. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that a woman’s fetus which has miscarried; one who was born but died at that very moment; and one who, having not yet cut its teeth, dies after six months—these should be adorned with many garments and garlands, the ground should be dug, and they should be placed in a pit like a piece of wood. This implies that immediate purification (*sadyaḥ-śauca*) applies to all except the mother, the father, and uterine brothers. Regarding the mother and others, however, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) previously stated in the relevant section should be applied. As for the case of one whose teeth have already emerged, it has been stated in the *Ādi-purāṇa* itself:

"Having abandoned one who has died after teeth have emerged, one should observe impurity for only one day. This refers to the case of one who has been abandoned after the eruption of teeth. The meaning is that, having deposited the body in the forest according to the previously stated rule, one should observe impurity for one day. Furthermore, this one-day period of impurity applies to cases other than those involving the mother and so forth; regarding the mother and others, the three-day impurity mentioned in the preceding section should be understood to apply. As it is stated in the Ādi Purāṇa: "And having buried one who has died before two years have passed in the ground..."

"However, for the relatives, there shall be impurity (āśauca) for three nights in all cases. This is the meaning of the first statement: that a child who has teethed but died before completing two years of age should be placed in a pit in the earth according to the previously mentioned procedure and then covered over. The meaning of the second statement is that for the relatives, such as the mother and others, there shall be a period of impurity lasting three nights in the aforementioned circumstances. Yama states the specific rule regarding the burial of a child less than two years old:
"One should bury a deceased child under two years of age in the ground after anointing it with clarified butter."
"Singing the Yamagāthā while recollecting the Yamasūkta.

Regarding the *gāthās*, these are the three verses beginning with "He who [is the lord] of this world that is within the belly" (*yo 'sya kauṣṭhyajagataḥ*). The *Yamasūkta* consists of six verses beginning with "Having departed" (*pareyuvāṃsam*). Manu also says:
"Relatives should place a deceased child less than two years old outside [the village]."
Having adorned [the body], one should place it on pure ground, except for the collection of the bones.

"No cremation with fire should be performed for him, nor should the water-libation rite be performed. Having abandoned him in the forest like a log, they should observe impurity for exactly three days. (21) The meaning is as follows: leaving behind that ground where the previous collection of bones was made, and having dug a pit in another clean spot of ground, the relatives (*bāndhavāḥ*) should place the body of the deceased there and cover it over with bricks, clods of earth, stones, and so forth. The use of the plural "relatives" is intended to indicate that the following of the corpse by kinsmen may or may not take place here. If the plural were intended to express a restrictive rule (*niyamaparam*), [the meaning would differ].

Otherwise, there would result a contradiction with the statement of Yājñavalkya: "One should bury a deceased child less than two years old, but no water [libation] thereafter. Therefore, the intended meaning is that the burial should be performed by one, two, or three people. Regarding the statement of Yājñavalkya, "one should not perform the water libation," it is explained in his commentary (*bhāṣya*) that this does not prohibit the bath taken for the sake of purification after the digging, but rather prohibits the offering of water to the deceased. This has also been stated by Yājñavalkya regarding the death of a two-year-old child.
Having followed [the corpse] as far as the cremation ground, the other [survivors], surrounded by their kinsmen,
[should perform the rites] with the worldly fire while reciting the Yama-sūkta and the Gāthās.
"He is to be burned... thus [it is said].

The other, who is one who has died at two full years of age, is to be followed by his kinsmen as far as the cremation ground (*ā śmaśānāt*); that is to say, he is to be carried there and cremated with a common fire (*laukikāgni*) by those very kinsmen while they mutter the *Yamasūkta* and the *Yamagāthā*. Here, by the force of the restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) "he is to be followed," it is understood that the following must necessarily be performed by the kinsmen. From the designation "the other" (*itara*), it is understood that for one less than two years of age, there is no such mandatory rule. Furthermore, it is understood that burial (*nikhanana*) occurs only before the completion of two years. And the "common fire" is to be taken as an unprepared fire, distinct from the fire of a *caṇḍāla*. [22]
The fire of a Caṇḍāla, the fire of impurity, the fire of one in birth-impurity,
the fire of an outcaste, and the fire of a funeral pyre are never fit for being taken up by the learned.

This is because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) of Devala. By stating "with the worldly fire" (*laukikāgninā*) in this statement, he shows that there is a fire distinct from the fire produced by the *araṇi* sticks (the churning fire), intended for the purpose of *homa* in the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the birth ceremony (*jātakarma*). For this very reason, Devasvāmin stated: "The production of fire from the *araṇi* sticks is for the purpose of the *homa* in the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*) and others; even when that [churning fire] exists, it is improper to set aside the alternative of using the fire already present. Now, an objection may be raised: "The fire-rite (*agnisaṃskāra*) prescribed by Yājñavalkya for a child who has completed two years is not mandatory (*nitya*), since Manu, having introduced the topic with 'Relatives should place a deceased child under two years outside,' states 'No fire-rite should be performed for him' (*nāsya kāryo 'gnisaṃskāraḥ*). This suggests that the pronoun "his" (*asya*) refers to the child under two years, and thus your interpretation is incorrect. To this we reply: Having prescribed burial as if it were mandatory for the case of a child under two years, it would be improper to prescribe an alternative method—such as discarding the body like a log—in that same context without using a word like "or" (*vā*). Therefore, because the pronoun "his" (*asya*) is in close proximity to "under two years," it is logical that it refers only to the child who has completed two years, which is the subject immediately preceding it. Thus, there is no room for the objection. Furthermore, if a prohibition of the fire-rite were being made for a child who has completed two years, then upon the inquiry "How then is the body to be treated? the rule for discarding it like a log in the forest becomes necessary. This is not the case for a child under two years, because even if the fire-rite is prohibited there, the previously mentioned form of burial still remains available. Therefore, it must be explained exactly as stated. Regarding the rule "They should observe impurity for three days" (*kṣapeyus tryaham eva tu*), although it is not specifically mentioned here, nevertheless, since that same author [Yājñavalkya] stated that for children who have undergone the tonsure ceremony, impurity lasts for one night, and that for those up to three years of age, the sapinda relatives have an impurity of one day and night, the three-day impurity applies specifically to the mother, father, and uterine brothers, so as not to contradict that. This is because the three-day impurity for those from the appearance of teeth up to three years of age has been established as pertaining to the mother, father, and uterine brothers. By saying "No fire-rite should be performed for him, nor should the water-libation rite be performed," he shows that the water-libation rite follows the fire-rite. Consequently, it should be understood that the performance or the cessation of both the fire-rite and the water-libation rite occurs together. And therefore: [The text continues with the following: ...and thus, the rule for the three-night impurity, though not explicitly stated here, is applied to the mother, father, and uterine brothers, because the three-day impurity for those from the appearance of teeth up to three years of age has been established as pertaining to the mother, father, and uterine brothers. By saying "No fire-rite should be performed for him, nor should the water-libation rite be performed," he shows that the water-libation rite follows the fire-rite. Consequently, it should be understood that the performance or the cessation of both the fire-rite and the water-libation rite occurs together. And therefore, [the text concludes].

"Ritual water-offerings (udakakriyā) should not be performed by relatives for one who has not reached three years of age. From this other statement of Manu, which prohibits the ritual water-offering, it should be understood that the cremation rite (agnisaṃskāra) is also prohibited. Furthermore, this prohibition regarding the cremation rite and the offering of water applies only prior to the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa); after that, it is obligatory. Alternatively, one may perform it once the child has teethed, or even when the naming ceremony has been completed.

This is because of the statement made by that very author: "From the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) until the eruption of teeth, and thereafter until the end of the third year, the relatives shall perform neither the fire-consecration (*agnisaṃskāra*) nor the offering of water (*udakadāna*). The meaning is as follows: from birth until the end of the second year, there is either burial (*vikhanana*) without the rite of water-offering, or burial accompanied by the fire-consecration; from the completion of the third year until the end of the second year, there is either abandonment in the forest like a log without water-offering, or abandonment accompanied by the fire-consecration. This is the summarized meaning to be understood here. By stating "not for one under three years," he shows that the prohibition of fire-consecration and water-offering does not apply from the time the third year is incomplete until the tying of the girdle (*mauñjibandhana*). Therefore, it should be understood that even in the death of one who has completed three years but whose *caula* (tonsure) has not been performed, the fire-consecration is mandatory and the water-rite is obligatory. For this very reason, Aṅgiras says:
"Even if one who has not yet had the tonsure ceremony dies after having teethed, having cremated him there, one should observe the impurity for a maiden for three days. Thus it is said.

"Jātadanta" means one whose teeth have appeared, that is to say, one who has completed three years of age. Having cremated the deceased for whom the *cūḍā* ceremony was performed, and having performed the water-libation rites for him alone, even a *sapiṇḍa* other than the mother and father should observe impurity (*āśauca*) for three days; this is the meaning. By using the phrase "even though," he shows that for one under three years of age who has had the *cūḍā* performed, cremation, the offering of water, and three nights of impurity are mandatory, but not for one for whom the *cūḍā* was not performed. And this has been shown by Lokākṣi: "One should perform the water-libation silently, and likewise the funeral rite (*saṃskāra*) silently."

"For all those whose *cūḍā* ceremony has been performed, even in other cases, there are two [rites] at will. This refers to the *saṃskāra*, namely the cremation (*agni-saṃskāra*). "In other cases as well" means that even for one whose *cūḍā* has not been performed, from the time of naming until the completion of the second year, one may—at will—that is, with the desire for the spiritual welfare of the deceased—perform the two rites consisting of cremation and the offering of water. Once the cremation has been performed, because of the rule regarding the offering of water, the rule of three nights of impurity applies to the *sapiṇḍa* relatives, such as the mother and others. And so says Parāśara:
"When one who has teethed, one who has not yet teethed, or one whose *cūḍā* has been performed, passes away..."
"The cremation of those [deceased children] shall cause impurity for three nights.

(25) This means that for those whose teeth have not yet emerged but who have been subjected to cremation, all their *sapiṇḍa* relatives—even those other than the mother and so forth—shall remain impure for three nights. In the *Ādipurāṇa*, it is stated that even when cremation is performed for one whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākaraṇa*) has not been completed, there is a three-night period of impurity for those other than the father and so forth. "But where a deceased child under two years of age is cremated..."
But those who, overcome by excessive delusion, practice according to the customs of their country—
"In that case, the period of impurity for the kinsmen lasts for three nights. Thus it is said.

"Practicing the customs of the region" means practicing the local customs of one's own country. "Delusion" (*moha*) means affection (*sneha*). As for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "The water-rites and purification [are required] from the second year onwards; some say from the eruption of teeth"—the meaning of this is as follows: the rite of offering water preceded by the cremation (*agni-saṃskāra*), performed with the desire for the welfare of the deceased, as well as the three-day period of impurity (*āśauca*) for all *sapiṇḍa* relatives, should be understood to apply from the second year up to the third year, or from the eruption of teeth up to the third year. The phrase "some say from the eruption of teeth" is intended to indicate another opinion, since Manu states, "or when the naming has been performed," thereby indicating that the offering of water and so forth begins from the time of the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). From the eruption of teeth onwards, the impurity belongs to the parents alone; prior to the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*), the impurity belongs to the parents alone—the remainder of the sense being that a three-day impurity must be observed by the parents alone.
Until the naming ceremony, purification is immediate; for one day until the eruption of teeth;
and three days for the tonsure ceremony, so it is said.

Thus, because another *smṛti* text prescribes a three-night period of impurity regarding the mother and father from the time of the eruption of teeth until the performance of the *cūḍā* ceremony, the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "only by the mother and father" is intended to exclude the three-night impurity for other *sapiṇḍas*, not to exclude impurity altogether. For if that were the case, it would contradict the rule: "Until the eruption of teeth, it is immediate; until the *caula*, it is prescribed as one night."

Otherwise, there would be an unavoidable contradiction with such statements as those establishing the impurity (*āśauca*) for *sapiṇḍa* relatives. By this very reasoning, the statement of Pāraskara—"In the case of a child who has died before reaching two years of age, the impurity belongs to the mother and father"—is explained. For this very reason, he himself stated immediately thereafter: "Having not cremated the body, they bury it for one night or three nights. In that context, the option of three nights refers to the mother and father; however, the option of one night should be understood as referring to *sapiṇḍa* relatives other than them. By the phrase "having not cremated the body, they bury it," it is shown that in this particular case, burial takes the place of cremation. As for what was stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita: "When a child has passed away—whether he be less than two years old, or one who has no teeth and has not yet cut them—there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*)," the grammatical connection is: "When a child less than two years old has passed away, there is immediate purification. This refers to the performance of the Agnihotra and other rites under discussion, based on the Smṛti of Śaṅkha: "For the sake of the Agnihotra, through bathing and touching water, there is purification for that duration. Therefore, even for Śaṅkha, there is no contradiction with the previously cited statements such as "Until the tonsure (*caula*), it is remembered as lasting one night. As for what was stated by Kāśyapa: "For children whose teeth have not yet appeared, purification occurs after three nights"; and what was stated by Vaivasvata: "In the case of a child, whether teeth have appeared or not, the impurity lasts three nights; Gautama says it is immediate purification"; and also what was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "When a child less than two years old has died, or in the case of a miscarriage, the impurity for *sapiṇḍas* is three nights; Gautama says it is immediate purification"—in these cases, the "three nights" refers to the subject of cremation (*agnisaṃskāra*). "Immediate purification" refers specifically to the absence of cremation, pertaining to the performance of the Agnihotra under discussion. As for what was stated by Paiṭhīnasi: "For those whose tonsure has not been performed, it is three nights"—that too refers to the subject of cremation. Or, in the absence of cremation, it refers to the mother and father. As for what was stated by Yama:
A child who has not yet reached two years of age attains the state of a preta,
as does a son whose teeth have not yet emerged, a young infant, or likewise one who has miscarried from the womb.
Whether the hair-tuft has been cut or the deceased has gone to another country,
there is one day and night of impurity for all the sapinda relatives.

Thus, these four statements are connected with the phrase "impurity lasts for a day and a night" (*ahorātram aśaucakam*) in all three cases. The meaning of the first statement is as follows: when a child who has teethed but is less than two years old dies, there is only burial; in that case, the impurity for *sapiṇḍas* other than the father and so forth lasts for a day and a night. The meaning of the second statement is as follows: when a son whose teeth have not yet emerged dies after the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) and burial has been performed, the impurity for the mother and father lasts for a day and a night. From the use of the term "son" (*tanaya*), it is understood here that [the impurity applies] to the mother and father. Regarding the miscarriage mentioned in the third statement, the impurity lasts for one night.

In order to avoid contradicting the statement of Marīci—that "in the case of a mother’s death it is as [many days] as the month [of pregnancy], and for the father and others it is three days"—it should be understood that this refers to the *sapiṇḍa* relatives of a virtuous father and so forth. It is explicit in that very same text that the fourth statement concerns a child who has undergone the *cūḍā* ceremony and died in a foreign land; therefore, even this does not contradict other scriptural passages. As for what was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"The impurity (*āśauca*) due to a death is prescribed as either three nights or ten nights."
[28] For a child less than two years old, the period of impurity (sūtaka) belongs to both parents; however, for one who has died, it belongs to the mother alone.

Thus, the meaning is "of both parents. Consequently, when one dies before reaching two years of age, it is stated that there is a ten-night period of impurity (*śāvāśauca*) for the parents. However, because this would result in a contradiction with the many previously cited texts prescribing a three-night period of impurity, it must be connected specifically with the phrase "there is a three-night period of impurity" in order to avoid that conflict; it is not intended to be connected with the phrase "there is a ten-night period of impurity. Therefore, there is no contradiction between this statement and the previously mentioned texts. As for the statement from another *Smṛti*: "When one dies before two years of age, [impurity] belongs only to the parents, not to others," its meaning is as follows: when burial is performed for one who has died before two years of age, there is a three-night impurity only for the parents and not for other *sapiṇḍas*, since for them a single night is prescribed. Thus, everything is faultless.

Thus, the rule for impurity (āśauca) determined by age and stage of life is common to all castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, because it is prescribed for both parents without reference to specific castes. The meaning is that whatever immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) and so forth is ordained for an age such as six months and so on, that applies equally to all Brāhmaṇas. Although there are other statements by Ṛśyaśṛṅga concerning impurity based on age and stage of life which prescribe long periods of impurity for Kṣatriyas and others, nevertheless, they have not been recorded here because—according to the maxim "from an abundance of ritual action comes an abundance of fruit"—there is no corresponding abundance of purification here, and because practitioners would show disregard [for them].
Thus ends the section on the impurity regarding the funeral rites for the bodies of deceased infants in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the sections concerning the impurity regarding the birth of children to women.

It has been stated without distinction that in the case of miscarriage or the death of a child, male or female, there is impurity for the duration of a *śāva* (funeral) period. Now, some statements concerning the subject of impurity due to the death of a female offspring are recorded. Regarding this, Āpastamba says:
"In the case of an immature girl, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is ordained.
The remainder [of the sense] is that this applies even after the eruption of teeth. And thus:
In the case of a child who has not yet cut its teeth, purification is prescribed after three days;
however, for a child whose tonsure ceremony (cūḍā) has not been performed, purification occurs after one day and night.

In this context, it should be understood that the prescription of impurity for one day and night (*ahorātra*) in the event of the death of a child after the eruption of teeth refers to boys other than girls. However, Manu has prescribed this specifically for non-girls:
"For males whose tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has not been performed, impurity is declared to last for one night.
The term *nṛṇām* means "of males" (*puṃsām*).

"But for those whose *cūḍā* ceremony has been performed, purification is held to occur after three nights"—this statement of Manu also refers exclusively to non-maidens (*akanyā*), because of the connection with the word "of men" (*nṛṇām*). If it is asked how there can be impurity upon the death of a maiden who has had her *cūḍā* performed, Āpastamba states: "They attain purification in one day [upon the death] of one whose *cūḍā* has been performed. This means that if a maiden who has had her *cūḍā* performed dies before marriage, the impurity lasts for a day and night;
however, if an unmarried maiden dies, the impurity lasts for one night.
The period of impurity for kinsmen, such as the father and others, has thus been proclaimed.

Thus, according to the recollection of Mārkaṇḍeya. In this context, the construction is not "of the father and other relatives" (*pitrādīnāṃ bāndhavānām*); for if impurity (*āśauca*) lasting a day and night were prescribed for all relatives beginning with the father, it would result in a contradiction with other Smṛtis. Therefore, to avoid that, the construction should be understood by supplying the words: "for the father and others, in this matter, there is an impurity of three nights as proclaimed in another Smṛti. The use of the plural form "of the father and others" (*pitrādīnām*) is intended to indicate that even for uterine brothers, because of the excellence of their proximity to the father, the impurity is not that of a mere relative (*bandhu*), but rather exactly like that of the father. This was stated by Yama:
"When both parents have passed away, what indeed should be the period of impurity for women?
You, O Yama, have declared that purification occurs after three nights."

The syntactical connection here is: "In the event of the death of women who have not undergone the *cūḍā* ceremony, how does the impurity (*āśauca*) of the parents come to be? There arises a doubt: is the impurity for the relatives (*bandhu*) one night, or is it greater than that due to an excess of proximity? The meaning is that this uncertainty is resolved by the rule that purification for the parents occurs after exactly three nights; thus, there is no further deliberation required. It should be understood that the term "parents" (*pitr̥*) in the phrase "of the parents" includes the father’s kin and others. Likewise, wherever the term "parents" is used, it should be recognized as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for siblings and other paternal relations. Kārṣṇājini also states the specific distinction regarding the impurity of paternal uncles and other paternal relatives.

For women who have been given away or not yet given away, and for those who have been consecrated or not yet consecrated, the impurity for the mother and father shall last three nights; for others, it shall be according to the rule.

The phrase “among those who have not been given away” implies “among those whose teeth have not yet appeared,” because Śaṅkha has stated that for parents and others there is one night of impurity (*ekarātra-aśauca*) when the teeth have not appeared. For women whose teeth have appeared, the impurity of parents and others should be understood to be exactly like that for a male offspring. The meaning of the phrase “for others according to the rule” is as follows: for others—namely paternal uncles and so forth—the purification for unmarried girls is immediate (*sadyaḥśauca*) prior to the performance of the *cūḍā* ceremony; it is one day (*ekāha*) prior to their being given away in marriage; and for those betrothed (*vāgdattā*), purification is after three days (*tryaha*) prior to the actual wedding, in accordance with other such rules. “*Prattā*” means one to whom the giving has begun, that is to say, one who has been betrothed (*vāgdattā*). “*Saṃskṛtā*” means one who has been consecrated by the sacramental rite of marriage (*vivāha-saṃskāra*).

That woman who was previously promised in marriage but has not yet been formally given away is called "unconsecrated" (asaṃskṛtā); for her, it is traditionally held that the impurity lasts three nights for both parties.

Thus, according to the *Marīci-smṛti*: "In the case of both [families], namely the husband's and the father's, relatives (bāndhava) become pure after three days; however, those who share the same ancestry (sanābhaya) become pure in the very time prescribed [for their specific caste]. Thus says Manu.

The meaning is as follows: upon the death of women who have been betrothed but not yet formally married by the rite of *vivāha*, the kinsmen on the husband’s side—who had attained the status of relatives at the time of the betrothal—become pure after three nights (*trirātra*). As for the *sanābhayas* (blood relations), namely the *sapiṇḍas* extending up to three generations who are closely related to the maiden, they become pure according to the same three-night rule stated here. This interpretation is established precisely by the force of the scriptural statement: “For unmarried women, the *sapiṇḍa* relationship extends to three generations. However, in the *Padma Purāṇa*, the impurity regarding the death of a maiden is explained in detail.
If a girl dies anywhere from birth until the end of the tonsure ceremony (caula),
there shall always be immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) for all castes.
Therefore, up until the giving of the bride in marriage, it lasts for exactly one day;
beyond that, once the marriage has commenced, the settled rule is that it lasts for three nights.
[32] "And when the verbal betrothal has been performed, for three days both [the father and the bridegroom] are [impure];
thereafter, for those who have been given away, it belongs to the husband alone.
In the case of death or birth, the period of impurity shall be that prescribed for one's own caste. Thus [it is said].

The meaning of the passage beginning with "up to the giving of the word [of betrothal]" (*vāgdānaparyantam*) is as follows: "From that"—meaning from that *caula* ceremony—until the giving of the word of betrothal, in the event of the girl's death, there is impurity (*āśauca*) for one day, that is, for a full day and night (*ahorātra*). Beyond that, after the betrothal has occurred, even in the case of a postponement of the marriage, the settled rule is that there is indeed a three-night period of impurity while she is still in the state of betrothal. Once the betrothal has been performed, there is a three-night period on both sides (the bride's and the groom's families). After the marriage, in the case of the death or the birth of a child of those who have been properly given away and wedded, there shall be only the ten-day impurity prescribed for their own caste for the husband's side alone. Regarding the rule "three nights when [the marriage] has commenced," Śaṅkha states an exception for a girl who has already seen her menses.
"If a woman sees her menses while still uninitiated in her father's house, there is never any cessation of impurity when she dies. Thus it is said.

Some have explained that [the impurity] does not subside at any time prior to the period of ten days and so forth prescribed for its own class. Just as there is a postponement of the marriage, there should be a postponement of the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*) and the betrothal (*vāgdāna*); by parity of reasoning, the determination should be made that until the tonsure there is immediate purification, and until the betrothal there is purification after one day. Regarding the appearance of menses in a girl who has neither been tonsured nor betrothed, one should refer to the statement beginning with "The woman who [remains] in her father's house... If she dies thereafter, Mārkaṇḍeya states that the impurity ceases on the paternal side: "But for a maiden, marriage is declared to be the equivalent of the completion of her vows."
"For those who have been married, the period of impurity is prescribed on the paternal side. [33] Thus it is said.

Regarding an exception to this rule, Viṣṇu states: "In the case of women consecrated by the sacrament of marriage, there is no impurity on the paternal side; however, if her birth or death should occur in the father’s house, then there shall be one night or three nights [of impurity]. The meaning of the phrase "if her birth or death" and so forth is as follows: for paternal relatives such as uncles and others, there is impurity for one night in the event of the birth of a child residing in the womb of women consecrated by marriage occurring in the father’s house, and for three nights in the event of her death—respectively, one night for birth and three nights for death. Accordingly, Śaṅkha, following the word "relatives," says: "Likewise, for three days [is the impurity] when girls who have been given away die in the house. The meaning is that when married women die in the father’s house, paternal relatives such as uncles and others shall observe impurity for three days. Alternatively, Viṣṇu’s statement may be explained according to the following arrangement: for relatives, there is one night of impurity in the event of birth or death, while for the father and others, there are three days.
If a girl who has been given away dies or gives birth while still in her father’s house,
her kinsmen are purified by a single day, but her father is purified by three days.

Thus, because it is stated with such a specific restriction in the *Brahma Purāṇa*, the mention of the father (*janaka*) is intended to indicate the mother and the uterine brothers as well. Accordingly, when a birth occurs in the father’s house, there is one night of impurity (*āśauca*) for those on the father’s side; in the case of a death, it is three nights or one night. When a birth or a death occurs elsewhere than in the father’s house, there is no impurity for the father’s side. However, in the case of a birth or a death occurring in their own home, there is three nights of impurity for both parents; even if the death occurs in another house, it is three nights, but in the case of a birth, there is no impurity for either of them due to the absence of a cause—this is how it should be understood. As for what was stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita: “If a maiden dies after the verbal betrothal has been made but before the marriage has been performed, there is three nights of impurity on both sides, i.e., on both the husband’s and the father’s sides. Once she is married, there is cessation from the *gotra* (lineage), the *piṇḍa* (ancestral offerings), and the *āśauca* (impurity). [34] Here, by the word *āśauca*, the offering of water (*udakadāna*) which is to be performed during the state of impurity is indicated. Therefore, the meaning is this: when a married daughter dies in her father’s house, there is one day of impurity for her paternal uncles and other relatives, and there is cessation from the *piṇḍa* and water-offerings from the father’s *gotra*. Thus, there is no contradiction with what was stated previously. Paiṭhīnasi states the reason for the cessation of *piṇḍa* and *āśauca* from the father’s *gotra*: “A maiden, once given away, becomes another’s. This means that a married daughter belongs only to the *gotra* of her husband.

"Upon the offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), the lineage (*gotra*), and the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), she attains oneness with her husband"—so says the Smṛti. Therefore, the meaning is that the offering of the funeral cake and water for a married woman must be performed by [her son] using her husband’s *gotra*. For this very reason, Mārkaṇḍeya states:
"In the Brāhma and other forms of marriage, whatever maiden has been wedded..."
The rites of offering rice-balls and water for her must be performed by [the husband] using his own family name.
"In the cases of the Āsura and other [inferior] forms of marriage, [the bride's name is given] according to dharma by means of the father's gotra."

"By the father's lineage" means by the maiden’s father’s lineage. For a married woman, the rites of offering rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water (*udaka*) must be performed by the husband’s kin. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "For those who have been given away [in marriage], the others should perform [the rites], and those women [should perform them] for them. The meaning is that the husband’s kin should perform the funeral rites (*aurdhvadaihika*) for married women, and upon the death of those husband’s kin, those married women should perform them. It has been established in the *Śrāddhakāṇḍa* that this refers to cases where there is an absence of more proximate heirs, such as sons and so forth.
Thus ends the section on impurity regarding female offspring in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, other statements concerning impurity due to death (*śāvāśauca*) are also recorded.
Regarding this, Aṅgiras states:
"Henceforth, we shall describe in due order the attainment of the [four] castes, as well as the impurity on account of death (śāva-āśauca), exactly as it has been observed by the wise."

The meaning is: "Henceforth, we shall describe the impurity (*āśauca*) caused by the death of one who has been initiated (*upanīta*)," because the impurity caused by the death of one who has not been initiated has already been stated previously. For this very reason, it was said: "Three nights [of impurity] until the instruction of the vows (*vratādeśa*), and ten nights thereafter. The "instruction of the vows" is the initiation (*upanayana*). The meaning is that after that—whether death occurs in childhood, youth, or old age—the impurity lasts for ten nights. Regarding this matter, Manu also says:
"A period of impurity (āśauca) lasting ten days is prescribed for sapindas in the case of a death. Here, "among sapindas" means among the sapindas of a Brahmin; for it is said:
"A Brahmin becomes pure after ten days, a Kshatriya after twelve days..."

"A Vaiśya is purified in fifteen days, and a Śūdra in a month," because it has been stated by that very [author]. The meaning is that for Sapiṇḍas who are Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, impurity due to birth or death (śāvāśauca) is prescribed for ten days, twelve days, fifteen days, and one month, respectively. As for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya: "Impurity due to birth or death is held to last three nights or ten nights."
Thus, there is no contradiction, as the three-night period therein refers to those who are *samānodaka* (sapindas up to the seventh degree). Bṛhaspati says the very same thing:
"Sapindas become pure after ten days following a death or a birth;
kinsmen (*sakulya*) become pure after three nights, and those born of the same lineage (*gotraja*) become pure by bathing."

What, then, is the distinction among those who are *sapiṇḍas* and so forth? It is said: that specific lineage from which a particular descent has proceeded is designated as the "archetypal ancestor" (*kūṭastha*). Counting from him as the starting point within his lineages, sons, grandsons, and others up to the seventh person—provided they have not entered another *gotra*—are to be understood as *sapiṇḍas* to one another. Thus, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The *sapiṇḍa* relationship for all [members] is based on *gotra* and extends to seven generations."

The *sapiṇḍas* extend from the *kūṭastha* (the common ancestor) down to the seventh generation. This means that for all those born in the lineage of the *kūṭastha*, there exists the qualifying condition of being of a single *gotra*. Likewise, it should not be understood that there is mutual *sapiṇḍatā* among daughters' sons and grandsons born in the lineages of the *kūṭastha*'s male and female descendants due to a difference in *gotra*. This seven-generation *sapiṇḍatā* is the same for all castes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas; however, *sapiṇḍatā* ceases in the seventh person among those of the same caste, but in the fourth person among those of different castes.

Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Parāśara: "Among those of the same caste as the *kūṭastha* (the common ancestor), the status of being a *sapiṇḍa* ceases beyond the seventh degree; among those of a different caste, it ceases beyond the third generation. So says Śātātapa: "The *sapiṇḍa* relationship is prescribed for sons, for *sapiṇḍas*, and for unmarried women, extending to three generations on the paternal side."

Sapiṇḍa-relationship ceases after seven generations. Beyond that, they are *samānodaka* (distant kinsmen). Bṛhaspati has stated that those who are *samānodaka* are indeed *sakulya* (lineage members). Those from whom the status of *samānodaka* has ceased are *gotraja* (members of the same lineage); however, the status of *samānodaka* may persist up to the fourteenth generation.
According to some, this status lasts as long as the memory of birth and name remains; beyond that, one is said to belong merely to the same *gotra*.

Thus, because of the recollection of [the deceased as] a tiger (*vyāghra-smaraṇāt*). "Birth" (*janman*) and "name" (*nāman*) constitute "birth-and-name" (*janmanāmanī*); according to some, the status of being a *samānodaka* (distant relative) lasts as long as there is recollection of those two.
