Beyond this, however, the status of being a *samānodaka* ceases, according to the opinion of some. And it has been stated directly by Manu: "But the *sapiṇḍa* relationship ceases with the seventh person;
the status of being a *samānodaka*, however, [ceases] when the birth and the name are no longer known. (MDh 5.60)

The "non-communication of birth" means the removal of the memory that "this person is born of our lineage"; the "non-communication of name" means the removal of the memory that "he belongs to the family of Devadatta. Thus, the meaning is that even upon the removal of the memory of either the birth or the name, the status of being a *samānodaka* (one who shares the same water libation) ceases. Accordingly, it is stated in another Smṛti: "The cessation of the status of being a *samānodaka* occurs upon the non-communication [of these];
it also ceases when either the birth or the name is not known."

Thus, even when there is no recollection [of the deceased], for those among whom the status of *samānodaka* (sapinda) has not ceased, they are kinsmen of the same lineage (*gotraja*) and attain purification through bathing. For those who, despite the non-recollection of birth or name, possess the status of being of the same lineage (*sagotra*) because they have passed beyond fourteen generations, their purification occurs by mere bathing alone; for it is recorded in the Smṛti: "For *samānodakas*, purification lasts three days; for *gotrajas*, one day."

This is because the statement of Jābāli refers specifically to those born of such a *gotra*. By the rule "for *samānodaka* relatives, three days," it is not restricted that the three-day period applies only to *samānodaka* relatives, for we observe traditional legal texts (*smṛti*) indicating this also applies to those who are not *samānodaka*. Thus says the *Smṛti*:
"One shall be impure for three days in the case of a maternal grandfather, a teacher (*ācārya*), and a *śrotriya*.
Here, "maternal grandfather" (*mātāmaha*) means the father of one's mother; "teacher" (*ācārya*)...
But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the secret doctrines (Upanishads), him they call an Ācārya.

Thus, he possesses the characteristics already described. A *śrotriya* is one who has studied a single branch [of the Veda], according to the traditional teaching of Baudhāyana: "Having studied one branch, one becomes a *śrotriya*. The meaning of the passage is as follows: when the maternal grandfather, the teacher, or a *śrotriya* have died, the daughter's son (*dauhitra*), even if not himself a *śrotriya*, as well as their respective pupils and the neighboring twice-born (*dvija*), shall remain impure for three days. Impurity lasts for three days specifically in the case of a *śrotriya* and in the case of a neighboring *dvija* alone; for it will be stated later that for those who are not neighbors but reside in the same village, the period is one night. For this very reason, Manu has specified a particular qualification regarding the *śrotriya*.
"But upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who has completed his studies, one shall remain impure for three nights. Thus [it is said].

One who has received initiation (*upasaṃpanna*) is one who is close by, that is to say, a neighbor. Āśvalāyana also prescribes three nights [of impurity] for a teacher (*guru*) endowed with the characteristics of a teacher: "And for a teacher who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, there is three nights. A father is a *sapiṇḍa* teacher; any other who possesses the aforementioned characteristics is an [ordinary] teacher, because he is designated as such immediately thereafter by that same author in the words, "for other teachers. Therefore, in this case as well, it should be understood that for a student initiated by another, there is three nights of impurity upon the death of a teacher who is not a *sapiṇḍa*. And these three nights are to be observed when the cremation and other rites are performed by another. As Manu says:

"But a disciple, performing the *pitṛmedha* for his deceased guru, becomes pure after ten nights along with those who eat the food of the deceased"—that is, those who subsist on the property of the deceased, namely the *sapiṇḍas* belonging to the family of the deceased. The meaning is that the disciple who performs the *pitṛmedha* becomes pure after ten nights together with them. And thus, since the ten-night period of impurity is occasioned by the performance of the *pitṛmedha*, it should be understood that even in the case of a daughter's son (*dauhitr*) and others, the ten-night period applies if they perform the *pitṛmedha*. Pracetas also says:

"In the case of the death of a maternal aunt or a maternal uncle, a mother-in-law or a father-in-law, a preceptor, an officiating priest, or a patron for whom one sacrifices, one becomes pure after three nights. Thus it is said.

In order to avoid contradicting the rules for impurity (*āśauca*) prescribed for female relatives (*pakṣiṇī*) to be mentioned later regarding maternal aunts and others, a certain qualification must be assumed. In that regard, when the parents are absent or incapacitated, or when a maternal aunt or a maternal uncle is present, or when a sister’s son is present, or when the mother-in-law and father-in-law, or the son-in-law and the supporter [of the bride], or a teacher who has performed the initiation (*upanayana*) and other rites, or an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), or a sacrificial recipient (*yājya*) descended from the lineage of the sacrificer’s family, or one descended from the lineage of a Kṣatriya family dies, the relative on the opposite side, such as a nephew (*bhāgineya*), becomes pure after three nights. Vṛddha-Manu also says:
"But what should be the case for married women when both parents have passed away?
Purification occurs after three nights; so said the venerable Yama."

The meaning is that upon the death of both parents, or the death of either the father or the mother, there is purification after three nights for daughters who have been consecrated by the marriage sacrament. Regarding the death of a daughter’s son (*dauhitra*), the same author says:

"When a daughter’s son or a sister’s son has died, a *pakṣiṇī* [period of impurity] should be observed; but if he has been consecrated [by marriage], the period shall be three nights—such is the established law. [40]

In the case of a daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) or a sister’s son (*bhaginīsuta*) who has been consecrated by the *upanayana* sacrament, there is three nights (*trirātra*) of impurity for the maternal grandfather and grandmother, and for the mother’s sister and the maternal uncle. Regarding one consecrated by the *upanayana*, the term “bird-night” (*pakṣiṇī*) applies; the meaning is that the maternal grandfather and others should pass a night flanked by the preceding and following days. Here, although this discussion concerns the impurity resulting from the death of one who has undergone *upanayana*, it should be understood that the rule is stated to apply even to one who has not undergone it, as otherwise there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Bodhāyana also says: “One should observe three nights, a day and a night, and one day [of impurity] in the case of a pupil (*śiṣya*), a fellow-student (*satīrthya*), or a co-student (*sahādhyāyin*). These are three statements. The meaning of the first statement is: when a pupil initiated by another dies, the teacher (*ācārya*) shall observe three nights of impurity. The meaning of the second statement is: among fellow-students who have completed their studies and share the same teacher, upon the death of any one of them, the other fellow-student shall observe a day and a night. The meaning of the third statement is: among co-students who share the same teacher and study together, upon the death of one of them, the other co-student shall observe one day of impurity. Hārīta also says:

"In the case of wives who have had previous husbands, and in the case of adopted sons, the impurity lasts for three nights for the maternal grandfather, but for one day for those within the sapinda relationship. Thus [it is said].

A *parapūrvā* is one who has had another husband previously—that is, a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman). A *kṛtaka* son is one born through causes other than [natural] birth, such as an adopted son (*datta*) and so forth. The meaning of the sentence is as follows: upon the death of a wife who was previously married to another when her maternal grandfather and others have died, there is a three-night period of impurity for both the former and the latter husbands. Upon the death of a *kṛtaka* son, there is a three-night period for him by whom that son was produced through causes other than [natural] birth. Furthermore, for those *sapiṇḍas* of both the former and latter husbands who possess such a *kṛtaka* son, the period of impurity is one day and night. It should be understood that here, in the context of discussing the impurity of *sapiṇḍas* and daughters' sons (*dauhitras*), the impurity of the *sapiṇḍas* of a *punarbhū* is also stated. However, Śaṅkha states that even for a wanton woman (*svairiṇī*) and a *punarbhū*, the impurity lasts for three nights.

"In the case of non-aurasa sons, wives who have gone to another, and one's own wives who have had a previous husband, purification is held to occur after three nights. Regarding "non-aurasa sons," this refers to those such as the *kṣetraja* (son of the wife) and *dattaka* (adopted son); regarding "wives who have gone to another," this refers to unchaste women (*svairiṇī*) who have resorted to another husband without a formal remarriage; and regarding "one's own wives who have had a previous husband" (*parapūrvāḥ*), this refers to *punarbhūs* (remarried women) who have not transgressed their caste. Viṣṇu states that in the case mentioned by Śaṅkha, there is a three-night period even for the birth [of such children].
"And when non-legitimate sons have been born or have died,
and when wives who previously had other husbands have given birth or have died"—
in this [verse], the word "by three nights," heard in the preceding statement as "when the maternal grandfather has passed away, by three nights," is to be supplied here. Aṅgiras also says:
"If anyone who is not a sapinda dies in someone's house by any means whatsoever, his impurity should also be known to last for three nights; there is no doubt in this matter. Thus [it is said].

This refers to the death occurring in the primary residence (*pradhānagṛha*). However, regarding death in a non-primary residence (*apradhānagṛha*), Viṣṇu says: "Even when one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* dies in one's own house, there is impurity for one night. Regarding the death of those related by birth (*yonisaṃbandha*) who are not *sapiṇḍas*, Gautama says: "There is impurity for three days (*pakṣiṇī*) upon the death of one related by birth who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, and likewise for a fellow student (*sahādhyāyin*). The term "not a *sapiṇḍa*" is used to exclude paternal uncles and others who are indeed *yonisaṃbandhas*. Therefore, the meaning is this: those related by birth who are not *sapiṇḍas*—such as a maternal uncle, a maternal aunt, a sister, a nephew, a paternal aunt, her sons, and so forth—the relative who stands in opposition to them (the *pratiyogin*), such as the nephew and so on, shall observe impurity for three days (*pakṣiṇī*) upon their death. As for the term "fellow student," its meaning is this: if one has studied for a long period, such as twelve years, under the same teacher in the same school of scripture (*gurukula*), then upon the death of that person, the other fellow student shall observe impurity for three days. Manu also says:
"Upon the death of a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, there is impurity for one night.

This means that upon the death of a maternal uncle who has provided little assistance, a pupil who has studied the Veda with its auxiliary limbs as taught by another, an officiating priest who performs his duties from the time of the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires) throughout life, or a kinsman such as a sister's son and others upon the death of their own father, mother, or maternal uncle, one becomes impure for one night. Kinsmen (*bāndhava*) are defined in another Smṛti:
"The sons of one's father's sisters and the sons of one's mother's sisters [are kinsmen]."
One's own maternal uncles' sons should also be known as one's own kinsmen.
The sons of one's father’s paternal aunt, the sons of one's father’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's father’s maternal uncle are to be known as paternal kinsmen (pitṛbāndhava).
The sons of one's mother’s paternal aunt, the sons of one's mother’s maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's mother’s maternal uncle are to be known as maternal relatives (mātṛbāndhava).
Vṛddha-Manu also says:
"Upon the death of one's mother-in-law, sister, maternal aunt, maternal uncle, father’s sister, or mother’s sister, one should pass the night in the state of *pakṣiṇī*."

"In the case of a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a friend, or a teacher, as well as the wives of teachers, there is impurity for a *pakṣiṇī* night; likewise if one's maternal grandmother has died. [43] Thus it is said.

The meaning of the preceding verse is that one should spend three nights with parents who have provided little assistance; with a sister who acts for the benefit of her mother; with a maternal aunt (*mātulānī*), that is, the wife of a maternal uncle, who has provided little assistance; with a maternal uncle (*mātula*) himself; and with a paternal or maternal aunt (*pitṛṣvasṛ* and *mātṛṣvasṛ*) who have provided little assistance. In the second verse, however, the mention of "maternal uncle" is for the purpose of qualifying the father-in-law (*śvaśura*). The meaning is: when a maternal uncle gives his daughter to his nephew and thus becomes his father-in-law, he is referred to as "father-in-law. [One should also spend three nights] with a friend accepted according to the rules of friendship, and with a teacher who instructs in the scriptures.
One should know that person as a teacher in this world by virtue of that service of learning, whoever benefits one with their learning, whether it be little or much.

This is because the term *guru* is traditionally applied even to one who provides instruction in the scriptures. As for what was stated by Jābāli, after saying, "For those born of the same lineage, a day [of impurity] is prescribed," he further said:
"Likewise toward a maternal relative, a teacher, a friend, and a regional ruler.
Here, "maternal relative" (*mātṛbandhu*) refers to a maternal uncle (*mātula*). As for what was stated by Yājñavalkya:
It has been stated: "In the case of unmarried girls, however, [the penance is] for one year; in the case of a young girl who has not yet had the tonsure ceremony, [it is] for six months.
And:
"Also in the case of a teacher's resident pupil, a fellow student of the Veda, a maternal uncle, and a Śrotriya."
In the case of sons not born of one's own loins, and of wives who have not attained their due status.

Thus, regarding that which was stated by Viṣṇu: "Purification occurs after one night in the case of the wife of a teacher (*ācārya*), a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), a maternal uncle (*mātula*), a father-in-law (*śvaśura*), a mother-in-law (*śvaśrū*), a fellow student (*sahādhyāyin*), and a pupil (*śiṣya*)," it should be understood that the word *guru* mentioned by Jābāli and the word *guru* mentioned by Yājñavalkya have the same meaning as the word *upādhyāya* mentioned by Viṣṇu. For this very reason, Āśvalāyana, having stated, "In the case of a *guru* who is not a *sapinda*, there is a three-night [impurity]," further stated, "In the case of other teachers (*ācāryas*), there is one day. The meaning of "other teachers" is those other than the *ācārya* defined by such passages as, "He who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda... The one-night rule for a maternal uncle refers to a maternal uncle who has provided no assistance. The one-night rule for a son refers to a son accepted in some manner or another. The one-night rule for a pupil refers to a pupil of another teacher. The one-night rule for a *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas) refers to a *śrotriya* of the same village, according to the Smṛti of Āśvalāyana: "One day [of impurity] for a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) and for a *śrotriya* of the same village. The one-night rule regarding non-aurasa sons and wives married to others refers to cases where those non-aurasa sons and others are not present. The prescription of one night for both parents-in-law refers to parents-in-law who have provided no assistance to the son-in-law. The one-night rule for a fellow student refers to a fellow student with whom one studied for a period of time other than twelve years; otherwise, there would be a contradiction between Jābāli’s statement and the previously cited statements prescribing a three-night period. As for that which was stated by Manu...

"When the king has died, for one who resides within his domain, [there is impurity] as long as there is light"—meaning "sajyotis" (with light) refers to that which exists together with light: if death occurs during the day, the period of impurity lasts as long as the sun is visible; if at night, it lasts as long as the stars are visible. This rule applies to the ruler of a small territory, whereas for the ruler of a great province (*mahāmaṇḍala*), a single night's rule is prescribed. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Manu states that there is no study as long as there is light when the ruler of one's own country dies: "When the lord of a village, the head of a family, a learned *śrotriya*, or an ascetic [has died...]"
"When the disciple has met his death, [the teacher remains] pure until the appearance of the stars.
Here, *kulapati* means the head of the community. This refers to cases where no learned *śrotriya* or similar authority is present. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"But when a sister has passed away, and likewise when a brother has passed away..."
When a friend, a son-in-law, a grandson, or a sister’s son has died.
In the case of a brother-in-law or his son, one becomes pure immediately by bathing.

Thus, when a sister who has undergone the marriage sacrament dies, the uterine brother becomes pure immediately by bathing; the meaning is that he does not become pure after three nights like his mother or father. And when a uterine brother who has undergone the initiation (upanayana) sacrament dies, the sister becomes pure immediately by bathing. When a friend—one devoid of long-term attachment—or a son-in-law dies, both parents become pure immediately by bathing. When a brother-in-law (syālaka), that is, a wife’s brother, or his son dies, one becomes pure immediately by bathing. Regarding the daughter’s son (dauhitra) and the sister’s son, the immediate purification applies to cases where the daughter’s son and others are not present; therefore, there is no contradiction with the previously stated three-night period for the daughter’s son and others. It has been stated that the impurity for those related by water (samānodaka) and so forth is the same for all three castes; this is because, unlike the impurity for sapinda relatives, no specific mention or particular traditional rule (smaraṇa) is recorded here, and because a general indicator must be stated. For instance, at the beginning of the section on impurity:
Impurity [due to death] lasts for ten days among those who are not sapindas, as well as for a learned teacher (shrotriya) or a preceptor (guru) who has passed away while abroad;
likewise, it lasts for three days for women during their menstrual period.
Likewise, among childless women, maternal uncles, and paternal relatives—
in these and similar cases, there is an equal duration of impurity for all four castes.
"Since the term 'of the castes' (*varṇānām*) alone would have sufficed, the mention of 'four' (*caturṇām*) is for the sake of clarity.
Thus, [the rule applies] to those who are childless or whose offspring have perished through miscarriage and the like."
Thus ends the section on other matters concerning impurity due to death (*śāvāśauca*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows [the discussion of] sapindas and others who reside in a distant location or exist at a different time.
The statements concerning the impurity resulting from birth and death are recorded here; Manu says:
"That rule for impurity due to a corpse which has been proclaimed applies only when one is in close proximity."
In his absence, that procedure should be known to be performed by the relatives and kinsmen.

*Saṃbandhinaḥ* refers to those related by marriage, meaning *samānodakas* (those connected through water-libations). *Bāndhavāḥ* refers to close relatives, meaning *sapiṇḍas* (those sharing the same funeral cake). *Kalpaḥ* means rule or injunction. The meaning of the sentence is as follows: the rule for impurity due to death (*śāvāśauca*)—which is to be understood from such scriptural statements as "Impurity on account of death is ordained for ten days among *sapiṇḍas*, but after three days for those who offer water"—is to be observed by relatives and kinsmen when a death occurs among *sapiṇḍas* and others. Furthermore, this aforementioned rule for impurity due to death is to be observed by relatives and kinsmen in the case of a death occurring in a distant land. The mention of "impurity due to death" (*śāvāśauca*) is intended to indicate impurity due to birth (*janmāśauca*) as well.
For those who desire complete purity, the same rule applies even in the case of birth;
however, for those related by the offering of water (ekodaka), purification is held to occur after three nights following a birth.

By this statement, the rule regarding birth-impurity for *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas* that has been proclaimed should be understood as applying to a birth occurring in a proximate location. Regarding a birth occurring in a non-proximate location, the rule to be stated hereafter is to be understood. First, then, he [the author] shows the specific rule for the death of a *sapiṇḍa* in a non-proximate location: "But he who hears of one deceased who was staying in a foreign land within ten days [of the death], shall remain impure only for the remainder of those ten nights. Thus.

*Vigata* means deceased. *Videśastha* means residing in a distant land. [47] *Anirdaśam* means not having passed ten days; this is intended as an illustration for periods such as twelve days and so forth. The meaning of the sentence is as follows: if one hears of a *sapiṇḍa* who has died in a distant land while still within the period of impurity prescribed for his own caste, he shall remain impure for exactly as much time as remains of his own period of impurity. This same rule applies equally to a birth occurring in a distant land. And so says Bṛhaspati:

"Upon hearing that a relative has died in another country, or that a son has been born, one becomes pure after the remaining days of the ten-day period, provided the ten days have not yet elapsed. Here, "died in another country" means deceased in a distant location; "the birth of a son" refers to the birth of a relative's offspring or one's own child. Śaṅkha also says:
"Having heard that a virtuous person has gone to another country or likewise died, one shall remain impure for only as long as remains of the ten-day period. Thus it is said.

"A son born in another land" refers to one who has gone to a distant region—that is, the birth of a virtuous child not present in one's own vicinity. Regarding death occurring in a distant land, Pāraskara states: "In the case of one who has died while abroad, those who have offered water for him shall remain [in impurity] for the remainder of the period, starting from the time they hear of it. "Having offered water" means having given water to the deceased. This is intended as an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for sleeping on the ground and other such practices that must be observed during the state of impurity following death. Regarding the death of a *samānodaka* (a sapinda relative) who is in a distant land, Manu says: "But when a child, or one residing in another country, or one who belongs to a separate funeral ball (*pṛthakpiṇḍa*) has passed away..."

"Having immersed oneself in water while still wearing one's clothes, one becomes pure immediately. Here, "separate from the *piṇḍa*" (*pṛthakpiṇḍa*) means one who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, that is to say, a *samānodaka*. "Residing in another country" (*deśāntarastha*) means residing in a place where one is not present. By the fact of residing in another country, the child (*bāla*) is qualified as being a non-*sapiṇḍa*. The meaning of the sentence is as follows: when a child or a *samānodaka* residing in a distant land has died, one becomes pure at that very moment, immediately upon hearing the news of the death, by bathing with one's clothes on. In this same way, there is purification even in the case of the birth of a *samānodaka*. And so says Bṛhaspati:
Impurity regarding death is fully proclaimed to apply when [the event] occurs in one's presence;
if someone dies or is born in a distant land, immediate purity is declared.

Here too, the mention of *śāvāśauca* (impurity due to death) is intended to illustrate *sūtaka* (impurity due to birth). For this very reason, the rule for impurity to be stated later regarding absence is indicated here. Thus, the immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) prescribed for *samānodakas* (agnates) in cases of death or birth is to be understood as applying when they are present and there is no specific period such as three nights prescribed for their presence. When that [specific period] exists, one should also understand the purification by the remainder of it, because the statement of Śaṅkha—"whatever remains of the ten nights"—is intended to indicate the specific periods of impurity for birth and death among *samānodakas* who are present, and because of the traditional teaching of Yājñavalkya: "In the case of one who has gone abroad, there shall be the remainder of the time. Devala speaks when the news of a birth occurring in a distant land is heard after the ten days have passed: [Devala: ... [text omitted] ... Therefore, the following should be understood: when the news of a birth occurs while the ten-day period is still current, the purification is by the remainder of those ten days; when the news is heard after the ten days have elapsed, the purification is by the remainder of the specific period prescribed for the *samānodakas*; and when the news is heard after that specific period has also passed, the purification is immediate (*sadyaḥśauca*). This is because the term "remainder" (*śeṣa*) in the rule "whatever remains of the ten nights" is used to denote the remainder of the specific period prescribed for the *samānodakas*. Furthermore, the rule "in the case of one who has gone abroad, there shall be the remainder of the time" establishes that the purification is by the remainder of the specific period prescribed for the *samānodakas*. Consequently, the following should be understood: when the news of a birth occurs within the ten days, the purification is by the remainder of those ten days; when it occurs after the ten days but before the specific period of the *samānodakas* has ended, the purification is by the remainder of that specific period; and when it occurs after that specific period has ended, the purification is immediate. "There is not even the slightest impurity regarding days that have already passed.
This means that with respect to days that have elapsed, there is not even the slightest impurity resulting from childbirth. Furthermore, as for what was stated by Manu:
"Having heard of the death of a relative or the birth of a son after ten days have passed..."
"A person becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes.

By the phrase "and the birth of a son," it is understood—according to the principle that the word "son" implies a kinsman's son—that this refers to a relative. This is because the word "son" (*putra*) denotes a specific type of connection. Thus, the meaning of the sentence is as follows: upon hearing of the death of a kinsman or the birth of a kinsman's offspring after the ten-day period has elapsed, the purification for one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* occurs at the very moment of hearing the news through bathing with one's clothes on. However, regarding those residing nearby who possess the required qualities, the impurity lasts for one day: "A Brahmin who is endowed with the sacred fires and the Vedas is purified in one day."
For one who is inferior or even more inferior, the periods are three days and likewise four days.

Thus it has been stated by Candra and others; when that period of impurity (*āśauca*) has passed, one should observe what was previously mentioned in such statements as, "the death of a relative after ten days" (*nirdaśaṃ jñātimaraṇam*). In the phrase "the death of a relative after ten days," just as there is purification upon hearing news of birth or death on the first, third, or fourth day despite the term "ten days" (*daśāha*), so too here there is purification according to specific intervals of time. The mention of "ten nights" (*daśarātra*) in the statement "whatever remains of the ten nights" is intended to indicate other intervening periods that take the place of the ten-night period. For this very reason, it was stated by the author of the *Saṃgraha*:

"Whatever period has been ordained for a particular caste by virtue of its qualities, having heard [of a death] within that interval, at the beginning, or at the end, one becomes purified by the remainder of that period. Thus it is said. Regarding those Brahmins who are devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), after the lapse of the ten-night period of impurity (*śāvāśauca*) prescribed for them, Jābāli speaks concerning the hearing of news of the death of a *sapiṇḍa* in a nearby location:
"In the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), for each respective [birth], there shall be three nights of impurity;

but when a year has passed, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is ordained. Although the word *sūtaka* primarily refers to the impurity of childbirth, it nevertheless applies here to death-impurity (*mṛtaka*) due to the commonality of being a state of ritual uncleanliness (*aprāyatya*). This is because, in the context of births, it is impossible to prescribe three nights of impurity for *sapiṇḍa* relatives whose period of impurity has already elapsed. This has also been stated by Manu:
"But when ten days have passed, one shall be impure for three nights;
however, when a year has elapsed, one becomes pure immediately. Thus it is said.

Therefore, from that statement, the phrase spoken by the ancient author—"but if one should hear [of a death] while staying in a foreign land"—is here understood to carry over. Consequently, the meaning is this: if one should hear of a *sapiṇḍa* relative who has died while residing in a distant place, after the period of impurity prescribed for one's own caste but before the first year has elapsed, that person shall remain impure for three nights. However, if the period of impurity has passed—that is, if the first year has elapsed—and one should then hear of it, one becomes pure by means of a bath. And so says Śaṅkha: "But when ten nights have passed, one shall be impure for three nights."
"Likewise, when a year has passed, one becomes pure simply by bathing.

Regarding this matter, Gautama also says: "And having heard [of the death], after the tenth day. Here, the phrase "if one hears" from the present context is drawn forward by the word *ca* ("and"). Some connect the term *pakṣiṇī* (a period of two days with an intervening night), which occurs in the subsequent sūtra, to this point; however, that is incorrect, because it would render the word *ca* redundant and would contradict the numerous statements previously cited. [As it is said: "But when the period of impurity has passed, if one hears that a kinsman has died..."
In that case, there shall be impurity for three nights if [the death occurs] within one year.

Furthermore, this would result in a contradiction with the statement of Devala. The meaning is as follows: when one's own days of impurity have passed, if a *sapiṇḍa* who died in a distant location is heard of within the first year, there shall be three nights (*trirātra*) of impurity. Regarding the hearing of a death even after the first year, that same author says: "If he is heard of by his own people as dead after the first year, there shall be only one day..."

If one who died in a distant land is heard of by the sapindas after the first year has passed, then their period of impurity lasts for one day; this applies to the case of a sapinda within five generations.
However, if a full year has elapsed, immediate purification (sadyah-śauca) is prescribed.

Thus, the immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) mentioned by Jābāli refers to the case of *sapiṇḍas* beginning with the fifth degree. This alone is the proper arrangement of the subject matter here. For instance, among those prior to the fifth degree, there is *sāpiṇḍya* because three are the recipients (*devatā*) of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and the other is directly connected to the act of offering the rice-balls as the agent; whereas among the fifth and subsequent degrees, there is *sāpiṇḍya* through the connection to the act of offering rice-balls as the recipient of the smearings obtained from the hand of the offerer. And thus, where there is direct *sāpiṇḍya*, there is one night’s impurity; where it is through a lineage, there is immediate purification. In this way, there is no contradiction with the previously mentioned rules prescribing immediate purification. Therefore, the three-night period mentioned for before a year, and the immediate purification and one-night period mentioned thereafter, should be understood as applying to cases where the deceased is in close proximity, provided they do not meet the definition of being in a foreign land (*deśāntara*). Regarding the case of death in a foreign land defined by its specific characteristics, Vasiṣṭha says: "If one hears that someone has died in a foreign land after ten days have passed, the impurity lasts for one night. This applies after the first year. For this very reason, Viṣṇu and Vasiṣṭha state: "But when the [initial] impurity period has elapsed—at the end of a year, by one night; beyond that, by a bath. And so, as for what was stated by Paiṭhīnasi: [52]
"Upon hearing of the death of one who has died in another country—whether a eunuch, a forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*), or an ascetic (*yati*)—there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*).

This [text] must be connected with the supplied phrase "having heard of the death in another country after the first year has passed. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the previously cited statements of Viṣṇu and others. When the question arises as to what the definition of "another country" (*deśāntara*) is, Vṛddha-Manu says:
"Where there is the interval between two great rivers, or where a mountain acts as a barrier, or where speech becomes divided—that is called another country (*deśāntara*).

This is the meaning: the space between two great rivers, or where a mountain stands as a separator between two regions, or where a difference in languages such as Apabhraṃśa and others exists—that is designated as another country. When it is asked what these great rivers are, the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa* states: "The Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Tuṅgabhadrā, and Kāverī—these are the great rivers. [Also] in the *Vāmana Purāṇa*:
The Godāvarī, Bhīmarathī, Kṛṣṇaveṇī, Sarasvatī,
Tuṅgabhadrā, Suprayogā, Siṃhā, Kāverī, and Revatī.
The Dugdhodā, Nalinī, Revā, Niśitā, and Kalabhasvanā—
these great rivers, though vast themselves, have issued forth from the foot of the Sahya mountain.

The meaning of the phrase “even the great rivers” is as follows: any other extensive rivers besides those specifically enumerated are also considered great rivers. In this way, it should be understood that the space between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā—the southern region relative to the Yamunā and the northern region relative to the Gaṅgā—constitutes a distinct territory (*deśāntara*). Likewise, it should be known that the spaces between the Godāvarī and other great rivers also constitute distinct territories when compared to the regions situated beyond them. It must not be argued that the southern and northern banks of a great river constitute distinct territories in relation to one another, for they are merely adjacent. As stated by Bṛhan-Manu:
Where there is indeed a division of rivers within a short distance,
that is declared by the Self-Existent One himself to be another country.

The names of countries refer to Aṅga, Vaṅga, Kaliṅga, and so forth. "Distinction of rivers" refers to specific river regions, extending as far as the great rivers (*mahānadī*). The mention of the distinction of rivers is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the previously mentioned mountains and other features. The meaning of the sentence is as follows: where there are other names such as Aṅga and Vaṅga, or great rivers and the like, in close proximity—even though they possess the characteristics of different countries—Svayambhū has declared them to be "different countries" (*deśāntara*) on account of their commonality and other factors. Thus, even for one who is extremely near, if he qualifies as being in a "different country," then according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha, "when the deceased is in a different country," etc., a single night's impurity cannot apply here; for [otherwise] it would be contradictory that three nights apply when not near, while one night applies when near. Therefore, with regard to the varying degrees of separation caused by death, that which was stated by Devala— [Devala: "If a person dies in a distant land, one should observe the impurity for ten days. If he dies in a neighboring region, one should observe it for five days. If he dies in a nearby village, one should observe it for three nights. If he dies within the same village, one should observe it for one night. ...is what should be followed. Thus, the rule of one night applies to those situated within the same village, while the rule of three nights applies to those situated nearby. For this reason, the statement of Śātātapa—that "if one dies in a foreign land, one should observe the impurity for ten days"—is intended for those who have gone abroad for the purpose of trade or similar pursuits. However, in the case of those who have gone abroad for the sake of pilgrimage or the like, the rule of one night applies even to those situated in a foreign land, because they are not separated by death. This is the established conclusion. Furthermore, the rule of three nights applies to those situated nearby, while the rule of one night applies to those situated within the same village. Up to three fortnights, there shall be a three-night impurity; likewise, up to six months, it is a "pakṣiṇī" [impurity]; but for a period prior to nine months, it is one day; beyond that, one is purified by bathing alone.

Thus, that [definition of] "another country" (deśāntara) is to be understood as referring to a different location nearby. In this regard, the determination should be understood according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). The phrase "up to three fortnights" implies "beyond the period of impurity prescribed for one's own caste, such as ten nights and so forth. Bṛhaspati, however, defines another country by a specific number of *yojana*s:
"Some say another country extends for sixty *yojana*s;
others say forty, and others likewise thirty."

In this view, however, the three-night impurity for a nearby location mentioned by Jābāli and others should be understood to apply to a region within thirty *yojanas*. Where there is an intervening obstacle such as a great river even within those thirty *yojanas*, then for a different nearby location, that which is stated in the text—"there shall be a three-night [impurity] until three fortnights have passed"—should be observed. Regarding the case of one deceased beyond thirty *yojanas*, even when no intervening obstacle such as a great river exists, it should be understood that immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) alone applies here, as stated by Vasiṣṭha in the passage beginning "when the deceased is in another country," and also by Viṣṇu: "until one year has passed; after that, beyond that, by bathing. Thus, the aforementioned impurity for a deceased person who has passed away applies to *sapindas* other than the mother and father. But regarding the mother and father, in both the immediate vicinity and a nearby location, the impurity lasts ten nights. And so says Paiṭhīnasi:
"If both parents should die, even if the son is far away, from the moment he hears of it, he shall be in a state of impurity (sūtaka) for ten days starting from that day. Thus [it is said].

By the term "one situated at a distance" (*dūrastha*), both one residing in one's own vicinity and one residing in another distant land are meant here. By the word "also" (*api*), it should be understood that one residing in a nearby foreign land is also included. "One would become a *sūtakin*" means one would become subject to impurity due to death (*maraṇāśaucī*). Regarding this, something has been stated by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*): in the phrase "having heard," the words "after that" (*tata ūrdhvam*) are to be supplied as an ellipsis. Consequently, if news is heard within the ten-day period, even for a son, purification occurs through the remainder of that very period, just as in the case of other *sapiṇḍas*. As for what was stated by Dakṣa:
"But upon the death of a great guru, even if a year has passed, the funeral rites must be performed according to the rule by one wearing wet clothes. Thus it is said.

"Wearing wet clothes" means being accompanied by wet clothes. "Even when a year has passed" means after a very long period of time. "The rite for the deceased" (pretakārya) is intended here as the offering of water and funeral cakes (piṇḍa) prescribed for the days of impurity (āśauca). That very same rite must be understood as applying to the son who performs the secondary consecration (saṃskāra), even if he is currently incapable of performing the primary consecration, provided that he has undertaken the rules of impurity because he was capable at the time [of the initial death]. As for the statement by Yājñavalkya that there is immediate purity (sadyaḥśauca) consisting of the offering of water but devoid of the rites for the deceased once a year has passed—"Having offered water to the deceased when a year is complete, one becomes pure"—that refers to *sapiṇḍa* relatives other than the son. In the phrase "upon the fall of a great guru" (mahāgurunipāte), the term "great guru" refers to both the father and the mother, and not to the father alone.
According to the Dharma, there are two gurus for a man in this world: his father and his mother.
Of these two, the father is a guru, but the mother is remembered as the greater guru.
Thus, because of the remembrance of the mother’s extraordinary dignity, Dakṣa himself has made an exception for the mother in another statement prescribing a three-night period of impurity:
"When a father's wife has passed away— even if a year has elapsed— the best of the twice-born shall remain impure for three nights, with the exception of his own mother."
Another Smṛti states:
"But if, after ten days have passed, the householder later becomes aware [of the birth], his impurity lasts for three nights; it does not belong to anyone else regarding that object."
On this point, Vyāghra says:
"Since age is equal for all, even when it has passed [the time for initiation], the rite of initiation must be performed;
however, the penalty arising from the lapse of time applies to that very act."

That which is prescribed as immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) and so forth regarding age—consisting of six months and so on—is equal and without distinction for all castes, such as the Brāhmaṇas. However, when one dies in the vicinity of an initiated person (*upanīta*), there is impurity (*āśauca*) lasting ten, fifteen, or thirty days for the Brāhmaṇa and other castes; it is specifically upon the death of an initiated person that this "transgressed" impurity applies, not upon the death of one who is uninitiated. As for what is stated in the *Smṛtyarthasāra* regarding the inequality of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes—namely, that after ten days have passed since the death of parents, even if they were in a distant land, a son who hears of it more than a year later should observe impurity for ten days and so forth according to his caste—that is questionable, because it contradicts the statement of Vyāghra: "In [the case of] age, it is equal for all. Furthermore, as for what was said by that same author concerning the subject of parents—wherein equality is asserted even in other contexts, stating: "The same applies to husband and wife toward each other, and likewise for all castes mentioned, as well as for stepmothers of lower castes"—that too is questionable, because no such specific instruction regarding women, men, and so forth is seen in the works of renowned authors such as Prajñākara, Varadarāja, and others.
Thus ends the section on impurity due to birth and death among *sapiṇḍas* and others residing in distant places or times in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the sections concerning the concurrence of multiple impurities.
Regarding this, Devala says: "But when impurities occur simultaneously, purification should be understood as being determined by the more serious one."

The term *aghānām* (of impurities) refers to a general inclusion; it encompasses the periods of impurity (*āśauca*) prescribed for miscarriages, abortions, and births, those periods of impurity due to death based on age-stages, and those periods of impurity due to death occurring after the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). The meaning is that when two such impurities (*aghānām āśaucānām*) coincide simultaneously, purification is to be understood as occurring through the more serious (*garīyas*) of the two. An impurity that must be removed over a long duration is "more serious," while one that must be removed over a short duration is "less serious. By this principle, the third [period] is more serious than the first and second, and it should be understood that among the fourth and subsequent periods, each succeeding one is more serious than each preceding one. However, since it is impossible for a subsequent impurity to be more serious than a prior one merely by virtue of its longer duration when both belong to the same family—namely, birth and death impurities—the author has stated the following in response to the inquiry: "Which of these two is more serious?"
But in the conjunction of death and birth, death would be the more significant. Thus it is said.

By this, it is stated by implication that there is no mutual relationship of gravity or lightness between birth and death impurities (*janana-maraṇa-āśauca*) when they are equal in duration. But how is the impurity of death more serious than the impurity of birth? It is said: in the first section, impurity was established as consisting of specific sins (*pāpa-viśeṣa*). And it is established in the *Daṇḍadharmaśāstra* that gravity and lightness occur according to the magnitude or smallness of those specific sins. Thus, here too, because the cause is greater, the impurity of death must be understood as being heavy by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*), whereas because the cause is smaller, the impurity of birth is understood to be light by its very nature. When it is asked: "How is the cause of the impurity of death greater, and how is the cause of the impurity of birth smaller? Hārīta says: "Because of being overwhelmed by the deceased, the impurity of the corpse (*śāvāśauca*) belongs to the family; because of the connection with prosperity upon birth, fools deliberate, 'By whom? [The impurity of birth belongs to the individual]. Because of the severance of the family lineage and because of the abundance of suffering, the impurity of the family occurs. The meaning of this is as follows: because of the abundance of contact with the deceased—the cause of the impurity of death—the impurity of the corpse, which is the family's sin (*agha*), becomes great for the family. Regarding the cutting of the umbilical cord, which produces an abundance of suffering for the infant, there is a sense of agency for the family through some form of consent, based on the maxim: "What is not prohibited is permitted for the sake of the child. Thus, the impurity of birth is the family's sin. Since the impurity consisting of sin arises specifically from the consent to the cutting of the umbilical cord, it does not occur immediately after birth—unlike the impurity characterized by disqualification from ritual acts (*karmānadhikāra*)—but rather only after the cutting of the umbilical cord. And so says Jaimini.

"As long as the umbilical cord is not severed, so long does one not incur birth-impurity (*sūtaka*); once the cord is severed, thereafter birth-impurity is ordained. Because of the greater weight [of the latter], when there is a coincidence of impurity due to death (*śāva*) and impurity due to birth (*sūtyā*) occurring at the same time, the purification from the birth-impurity sometimes takes place first, because it lasts for a longer duration than the impurity due to death. For this very reason, Aṅgiras says:
If a death occurs during a period of birth-impurity, or if a birth occurs during a period of death-impurity,
then one should perform purification with respect to the death-impurity, and not the birth-impurity.

This very point is also stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "When birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) occurs while death-impurity (*śāva*) has already arisen, the birth is purified by the death; birth-impurity does not purify death-impurity. [59]

The meaning is that even if impurity due to death (*śāvāśauca*) arises during the period of impurity due to birth (*sūtyāśauca*), the birth-impurity does not purify the death-impurity. Therefore, in this case, purification from the death-impurity occurs only at its own [prescribed] time. Thus said Aṅgiras: "If death should occur after a birth within the ten-day period, the relatives must observe the impurity for the deceased in that regard."

The meaning is this: when a death-impurity (maraṇāśauca) occurs during the period of birth-impurity (jananāśauca) that is of equal duration, then the relatives must observe the impurity caused by contact with the deceased, beginning from the day of death, until its own prescribed time has elapsed. However, when there is a coincidence of two impurities of equal duration, Śaṅkha states that although both are equal, priority should be given to the more serious one: "In the case of a collision of equal impurities, one should conclude [the observance] according to the first."

The meaning is that when two periods of impurity (*āśauca*) of equal duration—whether by birth or by time—occur together, one should complete the second period of impurity at the very same time as the conclusion of the first. Viṣṇu also states: "If another birth occurs during the midst of an impurity caused by a birth, there is purification upon the cessation of the previous impurity; likewise if a death of a relative occurs during the midst of an impurity caused by a death. The meaning is that once the remainder of the period of the first impurity has elapsed, purification occurs even from the subsequent [impurity]. As Manu says: "If a death or a birth should occur again within the ten-day period..."
"A Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that [period] has not yet passed ten days.

By this turn of phrase, it is stated that purification from a subsequent period of impurity occurs precisely by means of the remainder of the preceding period of impurity. This has been clearly stated by Yājñavalkya:
"In the event of a birth or death occurring in the interval, one is purified by the remaining days."

The meaning is that an intervening period of impurity (*āśauca*)—whether of equal duration or longer than the remaining days of a prior impurity—is purified by those remaining days. However, where an intervening impurity is of longer duration than the prior one, purification does not occur through the remaining days of the prior impurity; because the prior impurity is brief and thus lighter, purification occurs in its own short duration alone. Thus says Śaṅkha: "An [impurity] of unequal duration is [purified] by the second, according to the word of Dharmarāja."

The second period of impurity (*āśauca*), being of a longer duration than the first period of impurity, is not equal to it; that is to say, it passes away by means of the second period of impurity. Yama also says: "One should conclude a period of impurity involving an increase in defilement (*aghavṛddhi*) by the latter [period];
for example, if one should enter a ten-day period while a three-day period has already commenced."
"If, however, impurity should recur, one becomes pure upon its completion. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is that one should conclude the second period of impurity (*āśauca*) by means of the latter, which has increased in duration due to its persistence for a longer time than the duration of the first period of impurity. He clarifies this very point with an illustration, beginning with the words "Just as," and so forth. This is the meaning: when a three-night period of impurity arising from birth or death has already commenced, if a ten-day period of impurity arising from birth or death should enter—that is, if a ten-day period of impurity, which lasts longer than the three-night period, should again arrive—then purification occurs upon the conclusion of the latter impurity. Likewise, in other cases as well, an impurity involving an increase in affliction (*aghavṛddhimad-āśauca*) that enters during the midst of a previously commenced one-night impurity is purified by its own specific duration alone. And thus it was stated by Uśanas: [61]

"If, however, during a period of short impurity (alpāśauca) a long period of impurity (dīrghāśauca) should occur, there is no purification by the former; one is purified only by its own [specific] time. But Devala has stated, by way of a particular formulation, that an increasing period of impurity—due to its persistence for a longer duration than the duration of the initial impurity—is purified by its own time. An exception to this rule has also been stated in certain cases.
"Beyond that point, impurity is prescribed for an increase in sin;
however, if [the death] occurs on the fifth day or later, it is distinguished by the preceding [period of impurity]. Thus it is said.

The meaning of the first half-verse is as follows: when there is an increase in the duration of impurity (*aśuddhi*) due to another [event]—whether that other event is of the same kind (*sajātīya*) or a different kind (*vijātīya*)—the impurity lasts until the end of the entire period of the subsequent impurity; beyond that, there is purification. This is the literal sense of the second half-verse, which serves as an exception (*apavāda*) starting from the words "If, however, from the fifth day... and so forth: if the prior impurity, even though shorter in duration than the subsequent one, should extend for several days beyond the fifth day (the fifth day inclusive), then by means of the former—the remainder of the prior period of impurity—the purification of the subsequent impurity is specifically ordained. Thus it is said: even if the subsequent impurity is of long duration, if the prior impurity should last longer than half of the duration of the subsequent impurity, then purification of the latter occurs by means of the former alone. An example of this is as follows:
If birth occurs before the ninth month, purification shall take place at that time;
whether he has died or is still living, it is accomplished by days equal in number to the months [of gestation].

By this statement, it is declared that for a birth in the seventh month, the impurity lasts seven nights; for a birth in the eighth month, eight nights. For births from the ninth month onwards, the impurity for both that birth and death is ten days; thus, by the ninth month itself, ten nights are prescribed. In that case, when a ten-night impurity occurs within the midst of a seven-night impurity, because it exceeds the former by half, the purification of the subsequent impurity occurs through the remainder of the preceding impurity. Likewise, in other cases as well, when the duration of the subsequent impurity exceeds by half the duration of the preceding impurity, it should be understood that the second impurity is purified by the remainder of the first alone. And so it was stated by Śaṅkha:
It was not equal to the second [command], just as the word of the King of Dharma.

Thus, regarding what Prajāpati stated, "Likewise, there is lightness for one who departs," and what Hārīta stated, "By the light [impurity], that [heavy one] is not [purified]," the meaning of Śaṅkha’s statement has already been demonstrated. The meaning of the statements of Prajāpati and Hārīta is this: heavy impurity, due to its long duration, is not purified by a preceding light impurity of short duration. These [rules] are to be understood as applying to cases where an impurity must be removed by another impurity whose duration exceeds half of the duration of the subsequent impurity. However, when there is a concurrence of two full-term impurities—one prior and one subsequent—on the first or the last day of the subsequent one, Śaṅkha and Likhita state a specific rule: "Now, if a death or a birth occurs during the remaining days of the [first] period, one shall be purified by those very remaining days; if at the end of the day, by two [nights]; if at dawn, by three. "End of the day" (*ahaḥśeṣa*) means the remainder of the day-and-night (*ahorātra*). This is what is meant: when a second full-term impurity occurs within the final day-and-night of a first full-term impurity, purification does not take place through the remainder of the time of the first impurity; rather, purification occurs after that remainder by two nights. But when the concurrence of another full-term impurity occurs during the eighth watch (*yāma*), then purification is by three nights starting from after that eighth watch. Śātātapa also says: [63]
"If the night remains, purification occurs after two days; if one watch of the night remains, one becomes pure after three days. Thus it is said.

The statement "on the remainder of the night, purification occurs after two days" should be understood to mean "on the remainder of the day, purification occurs after two days. This specified rule should be understood to apply to cases where the period of impurity (*āśauca*) is complete. As Bodhāyana says: "Now, if there is a coincidence of two ten-day periods of impurity, the first ten-day period of impurity lasts until the ninth day. The meaning of this has been described in the *Dharmapradīpa*; here it is also explained: the meaning is that until the completion of the ninth day, the end of the subsequent period of impurity coincides with the time of the days of the preceding existing period of impurity. Here, the mention of the "ninth day" is for the purpose of indicating the penultimate day. And thus, this is indicated even in the case of twelve-day periods and so forth, as explained by the Teacher (*Guru*) in the following passage: "And therefore, when the onset of an impurity occurs during the day on the tenth day, then too it should be understood that [purification occurs] after two days"—up to the end of that text. Regarding the phrase "when the onset of an impurity occurs during the day on the tenth day," the *Dharmadīpa* states: "The expression 'on the tenth day' is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the twelfth day and so forth; and therefore, when the commencement of a full second period of impurity occurs on the tenth day of a Brāhmaṇa’s prior impurity, on the twelfth day of a Kṣatriya’s prior impurity, on the fifteenth day of a Vaiśya’s prior impurity, or on the final day of a Śūdra’s prior impurity—then too it should be understood that this specific rule applies: 'after two days. For this very reason, Gautama says: 'If that [impurity] should occur again within [the first], one is purified by the remainder; if it occurs on the remainder of the night, after two days; if at dawn, after three days—for all four castes without distinction' (GDh 14.6–8). Having stated that 'in the event of a coincidence of impurities, they are purified by the remainder,' the fact that he said 'if on the remainder of the night, after two days; if at dawn, after three days,' should be understood to apply 'for all four castes without distinction. Thus, in the case of a coincidence of incomplete periods of impurity, on the final day of the [first] complete period of impurity, purification by the remainder of the first impurity should be understood to apply prior to midnight of that second incomplete period. However, in the case of the two impurities resulting from the death of a mother and a father, even if they coincide with each other before the final day, there is no purification by the remainder of the first impurity. As Śaṅkha says:

"If the mother dies first and the father dies while the impurity [from the mother's death] still persists, his purification shall be by the remainder of the father's period; however, he should observe a *pakṣiṇī* [period] for the mother. Thus it is said.

Although it may appear here that the purification of the subsequent impurity (*āśauca*) arising from the father’s death occurs by means of the mere remainder of the mother’s death-impurity, and the purification of the subsequent mother’s death-impurity occurs by means of the remainder of the father’s death-impurity augmented by an additional *pakṣiṇī* period, this is not the intended meaning of the statement. For it would be an improper interpretation to suggest that there is purification by the mere remainder of a prior [impurity] for one (the father’s) which is heavier due to its cause than the mother’s death, while there is purification by the remainder of the prior impurity augmented by an additional *pakṣiṇī* for the other (the mother’s), which is lighter due to its cause than the father’s death. Therefore, it must be explained otherwise. And it has been explained otherwise by the venerable Vijñāneśvara:

If the father should pass away during the period of impurity caused by the mother’s prior death, purification does not occur through the remainder of the former period; rather, purification must be performed according to the period of impurity occasioned by the father’s passing. Furthermore, even if the mother dies while one is still within the period of impurity for the father’s passing, purification does not occur merely through the remainder of the former period; instead, having completed the previous period of impurity, one must observe an additional *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night) thereafter. Thus it is said.

In the *Ādipurāṇa*, however, regarding the occurrence of a second impurity during the latter half of the first impurity, the opinion of certain authorities is presented—that purification does not occur through the remainder of the first alone, but rather by its own specific time. This is stated with the intention that all such views should be examined because they contradict the *Dharmaśāstras*:

"O Bhārgava, as long as one impurity (*sūtaka*) lasts when another impurity occurs, and when the [first] impurity has fallen away from this [second] impurity, purification is desired from that [second] impurity. [65]

"From this point forward, purification shall occur after the second period of birth-impurity (sūtaka). This same principle should be considered for both birth-impurity and death-impurity (mṛtaka). Thus it is said.

The meaning of this is as follows: for a second period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) that enters during the first half of an ongoing period of birth-impurity, purification occurs through the remainder of the ongoing impurity; however, for one that enters after the first half, purification occurs only by its own specific duration. As for the opinion held by some—that even a period of birth-impurity entering during an ongoing period of death-impurity (*śāvāśauca*) is purified in exactly the same way—that must be examined and is to be considered, because it contradicts the *Dharmaśāstra*.
Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, regarding the resolution of various concurrent impurities (*āśauca-saṃnipāta*), it has been stated that there are many kinds of impurity:
immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*), as well as one day, three days, and likewise four days.
Six, ten, and twelve days, as well as a fortnight and likewise a month.
And so forth. It has been established that this entire [rule] is an exception (*apavāda*) for those in stages of life other than the householder's. As it is said:

"For those who have reached the final goal (*naiṣṭhika*), forest-dwellers (*vanastha*), ascetics (*yati*), and celibate students (*brahmacārin*), no impurity (*aśauca*) is declared in the case of birth (*sūtaka*) or likewise in the case of death (*śāva*)."

The meaning is that the period of impurity (*āśauca*) prescribed for *sapiṇḍas* and others never applies to those in stages of life other than the householder. Although, by virtue of the general statement "there is no impurity" here, it might appear to be an exception to immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*), nevertheless, because of the contradiction with the statements to be cited later [verse 66], it should be understood as an exception to impurities other than that. Thus, it should be understood that for lifelong students (*naiṣṭhika*) and others, there is immediate purity in place of the various periods of impurity such as one day, two days, and so forth. And so says Yājñavalkya:

Likewise for officiating priests and those who have been consecrated while performing sacrificial rites, as well as for those observing the sattra vow, celibate students, donors, and knowers of Brahman.
"In the case of giving, marriage, sacrifice, battle, the ruin of a country,
and even in times of dire distress, immediate purification is ordained.
Regarding this, the meaning of the term *ṛtvij* (sacrificial priest) has been stated by Manu:

"He who performs the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), and the soma-sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma for one who has been chosen—him one calls his officiating priest (ṛtvij) in this world. Thus it is said.

"Vṛta" means consecrated by the act of selection (*varaṇa*). And since that consecration of selection persists from the commencement of the *agnyādheya* sacrifice until its completion, the connection is as follows: for the duration of that persistence, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is ordained for officiating priests even amidst long-term impurity. "Dīkṣita" refers to one possessing the consecration called *dīkṣā*. That consecration arises through the *dīkṣaṇīyā* offering and other rites, and it departs with the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛthasnāna*). Thus says the *Padmapurāṇa*: "For such a person who has received initiation in the great sacrifice of the three Vedas..."
As long as he remains engaged in the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha), he is not subject to the impurity of birth (sūtaka).

This is what is meant: the purificatory rite known as *dīkṣā*, produced by the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites, persists in both the sacrificer and his wife; as long as it continues, even during a period of long-term impurity, no such impurity exists for them, because of the injunction regarding immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). The meanings of the terms *satrin*, *vratī*, and *dātṛ* have been shown by the author of the *Saṃgraha*: "A *satrin* is one who has undertaken a vow at a sacrifice or in giving and is consecrated (*dīkṣita*);
a *vratī* is one who performs the *Cāndrāyaṇa* and other observances, as well as a religious student (*brahmacārin*)."
"One who has taken a formal resolve (saṃkalpa) regarding a śrāddha is declared to be a *vratī* (one observing a vow) and an eater;
one who always gives and does not receive is proclaimed as a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*). Thus it is said.

In the context of sacrifice (*yajña*), such as the Soma-sacrifice and the like, and in giving (*dāna*), specifically the constant giving of food, the term *satrin* refers to one who has undertaken a vow (*gṛhītaniyama*) or made a formal resolve (*kṛtasaṃkalpa*). Although one who has undertaken a vow for a sacrifice is also a consecrated person (*dīkṣita*), nevertheless, because the *dīkṣita* was already mentioned previously, the word *satrin* here—following the maxim of the "cow and the ox" (*gobalīvardanyāya*)—is intended to refer to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) in a state other than that of the consecrated. Thus it is said: "In sacrifice and giving, the *dīkṣita*. By the term *vratī*, one who performs the *Cāndrāyaṇa* and other penances, having made a resolve regarding them, is included; as is the son or relative who has made a resolve for a *Śrāddha*; and even the invited Brahmin (*vipra*) at a *Śrāddha* ceremony intended for eating is mentioned. This is because both possess the application of the term *vratī* due to their engagement in a vow (*vrata-yoga*). Although the term *vratī* applies to an initiated student (*brahmacārin*) as well—since the grounds for its application exist there too—it is stated "the *brahmacārin*" in order to show that, by the *gobalīvardanyāya*, the word *vratī* here refers to those observers of vows other than the *brahmacārin*, given the proximity of the term *brahmacārin*. By the word "giver" (*dātṛ*), forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) are designated here, according to the maxim: "Designations are made by what is not common [to others]. With this in mind, it is said: "The giver is always proclaimed to be a non-receiver (*anādātā*), namely a *vānaprastha*. Here, "non-receiver" means one who does not accept gifts. A "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*) is a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), because knowledge of Brahman generally exists in him. In this context, for these observers of vows (*vratiṣu*), immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed as an exception to the long period of impurity that would otherwise apply until the completion of the vow. It should be understood that for the *brahmacārin* and others, immediate purification is prescribed for as long as they remain in their respective stages of life (*āśrama*), setting aside the long periods of impurity that would otherwise apply. Now, an objection may be raised: since immediate purification is already established by the term *satrin* itself in the context of giving and sacrifice, the separate mention of "giving and sacrifice" in the verse "In giving, in marriage, and in sacrifice" is redundant. The answer is: regarding giving, the word "giving" is repeated to prescribe immediate purification for certain specific types of giving other than the mere gift of food. Regarding sacrifice, the word "sacrifice" is repeated to prescribe immediate purification even for sacrifices that have not been formally resolved upon. Thus, it is not redundant. As the author of the *Saṃgraha* says: [68] "Immediate purification is prescribed for giving, marriage, sacrifice, the birth of a son, and when a king arrives.
