The purity of giving to one afflicted by disease is said to be distinguished;
even regarding impermanence, he who desires to give away his possessions or perform fire-offerings and the like [is likewise pure].
When the sacrificial materials have been gathered for the sacrifice...

And so forth. For one afflicted by disease, "purity" (śuddhatā) is declared regarding a special gift—namely, the giving of a buffalo or similar animals for the sake of curing the illness—as well as regarding gifts made for the purpose of accumulating merit; the meaning is that "immediate purity" (*sadyaḥśauca*) is declared. As for the phrase "when the preparations for a sacrifice have been gathered," that will be explained in detail below. When it is asked to whom immediate purity applies in the case of a marriage, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states: "...and there shall be no [impurity] for us in the giving away of the girl, nor in the marriage of the maiden, nor in the ritual acts such as the offering of parched grain (*lājahoma*). [69]

In the giving away of a daughter during the marriage ceremony—from the initial selection of the bridegroom until the completion of the wedding—neither for the giver nor for the receiver shall there be that long-lasting impurity; the meaning is that such impurity does not exist, because immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is ordained even in the case of marriage. In battle, that is, in war: according to the rule of Āśvalāyana stating, "One should equip the king in times of distress," there is immediate purification from impurity during the rites of equipping him or the propitiatory *prāsthānika* fire-offering. When a country is afflicted by epidemics and the like, or in a rebellion due to fear of the king, there is immediate purification during the propitiatory rites performed to quell those disturbances. Likewise, even in a dire calamity, for one whose livelihood is contracted and who has a large family including parents exhausted by hunger, there is immediate purification when accepting what is necessary for their protection. This is also stated in another Smṛti:
"Immediate purification is declared for kings, for those observing a vow of sacrifice, during the calamities of marriage and the like, in times of forest distress, and in battle.
When it is asked in what action immediate purification applies to a king, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
But that by which the loss of the kingdom might occur for the king within his own domain,
when he is about to depart for battle or when the rite of departure is being performed, [should be avoided].
Or during the propitiation following a mantra, or in rites for the peace of subjects,
or at the beginning of auspicious ceremonies for cattle and the like for Vaiśyas when the time for agriculture has passed.
"Let there be no impurity in the world; it exists everywhere except [in this case]. Thus [it is said].

The meaning of this is as follows: when a king has commenced a task without which—by the non-performance of that act—the kingdom would perish through the failure to protect the subjects; or when a *prāsthānika* oblation intended for departure is being prepared for one about to go to war; or when the propitiation of malevolent planets is being undertaken with mantras and other offerings of worship; or when a communal rite of pacification (*śāntikarma*) for the subjects is being undertaken; or when a rite such as the auspicious cow-ritual (*gomangala*) established by worldly custom among Vaiśyas is being undertaken; or when a rite such as the worship of Vināyaka is being undertaken for the sake of agriculture and similar activities—in these cases, there is no impurity (*āśauca*) for kings or Vaiśyas for a long duration, because of the rule of immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). Elsewhere—that is, in cases other than those mentioned above, such as in rites like the *vaiśvadeva*—impurity does exist, because there is no provision for immediate purification in those instances. As for the statement of Aṅgiras:
Impurity does not exist at birth or death in these three cases:
during a sacrifice, at the time of a wedding, and likewise during a ritual to the gods.

Thus—*yajña* refers to Vedic rites such as the Soma sacrifice; *devayāga* refers to worldly sacrifices to deities such as the Mothers (*mātṛkā*) or to the worship of a *gaṇa*; and as for the statement of Paiṭhīnasi:

"In marriages, sacrifices, times of distress, on journeys, and in rites at sacred fords (*tīrtha*), there is no impurity (*sūtaka*) therein; likewise, one should have sacrificial and other rites performed."
Thus, as for the statement from the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"In the case of a desired installation of a deity, in rites such as the sacrifice to the Gaṇas,
in the *śrāddha* and other ancestral sacrifices, and in the giving away of a daughter, [the *parvan*] shall not apply for us."

Thus, it should be understood that these statements, which concern rites such as sacrifices already commenced, are intended to prescribe immediate purification through a particular mode of expression. For this very reason, an exception to this rule is stated in certain places in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"In some cases, even for one who has gathered extensive materials for the sake of a sacrifice, there shall be no impurity... and so forth.

And thus the meaning is this: for one who has gathered the necessary materials for a sacrifice—that is, one who has prepared all the articles required as means for the sacrifice—there is purification at the moment prior to the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding a sacrifice to be performed in that year, even if the resolve has not yet been made. This is because, after the lapse of impurity (*āśauca*), it may be impossible to find a time for the ritual within the spring season; therefore, purification occurs before the moment of the resolve concerning that sacrifice which would otherwise be missed in that year. The mention of "sacrifice" (*yajña*) is intended to include consecrations (*pratiṣṭhā*) and other such rites by way of illustration. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "There is no impurity for one who has again gathered the materials for the consecration of a deity or for a marriage. The meaning is that for the performer of the consecration of a deity or a marriage where many materials have been gathered, there is no impurity even prior to the commencement of the rite. What is being said here is this: as long as it is possible to maintain the collection of many materials, if another specific time required for an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of the consecration or similar rite cannot be obtained within that interval, it is precisely in such a case that there is an absence of impurity prior to the resolve. This is also stated in another Smṛti.

"In a sacrifice when the materials have been gathered, in a marriage, and in the rite of *śrāddha*. Here, the phrase "when the materials have been gathered" (*saṃbhṛtasaṃbhāre*) is connected to every instance. In this case as well, it should be understood that the scope of the subject matter is identical to that of the Vaiṣṇava statement. Regarding the *śrāddha*, the state of having "gathered the materials" refers to cooked substances; for if it referred to raw substances, it would result in a contradiction with the statement of another Smṛti which will be cited below. For it says: "When an obstacle to the *śrāddha* has arisen, or if death or birth-impurity occurs in the interval..."
"Or one should perform it on the new moon day; some wise men say it should be done when [the woman] is pure. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is as follows: between the preparation of raw materials and the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), if an obstacle to the *śrāddha* arises—whether due to divine or human causes, such as birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*)—one should perform the *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), or immediately after the period of impurity has passed. Between the preparation of cooked materials and the formal resolve, if birth-impurity or death-impurity should arise, it should be understood that the *śrāddha* must be performed on that very same day, by virtue of the previously mentioned rule regarding immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). If the impurity of a Brahmin guest occurs before he has been invited, another Brahmin should be invited and the *śrāddha* performed. If the impurity of a Brahmin occurs after he has been invited, his purification is shown in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
"For a Brāhmaṇa who has been invited and is devoted to his private Vedic study,
there is never any impurity (āśauca) as long as the ancestors remain within his body.
As for that which has been stated in another Smṛti:
"Objects become impure through their connection with an owner during that period of impurity;
they are purified by the purification of the owner alone, even when merely sprinkled with water.
This refers to objects not intended for sacrifice prior to the onset of that impurity.

"An item previously intended for donation does not become defiled when it is given. This is because of the traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) regarding sacrifices. The meaning is that an item intended before the onset of impurity (*āśauca*) does not become defiled when it is offered to a deity or given to Brahmins. Some statements declare that certain items do not become defiled even if they were not previously intended:
"In the case of salt, honey, meat, and flowers, roots, and fruits..."
In vegetables, wood, grass, water, curd, clarified butter, and milk;
"Regarding sesame, medicinal herbs, and skins, as well as the taking for oneself of cooked or uncooked food, and indeed all articles of trade—there is no impurity during death or birth [impurity].

"Raw grain is not censured for those engaged in the distribution of food;

however, having eaten their cooked food, one should drink milk for three nights. The phrase "of these" refers to those who are aware of the occasion for impurity, such as a death. Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:

If the impurity of a birth is recognized, one should stop eating and then perform the purification rites. This is the rule for those who have already eaten. If the impurity is recognized while one is still eating, the *Smṛtyantarasārasamuccaya* states: "If, while one is eating, the impurity of a death is recognized, one should stop eating and then perform the purification rites. If the impurity of a birth is recognized, one should stop eating and then perform the purification rites. This is the rule for those who have already eaten. If the impurity is recognized while one is still eating, the *Smṛtyantarasārasamuccaya* states: "If, while one is eating, the impurity of a death is recognized, one should stop eating and then perform the purification rites. If the impurity of a birth is recognized, one should stop eating and then perform the purification rites. This is the rule for those who have already eaten. If the impurity is recognized while one is still eating, the *Smṛtyantarasārasamuccaya* states: "If, while one is eating, the impurity of a death is recognized, one should stop eating and then perform the purification rites. If the impurity of a birth is recognized, one should stop eating and then perform the purification rites. This is the rule for those who have already eaten. If the impurity is recognized while one is still eating, the *Sm
"And while the Brahmins are eating, if a death or birth occurs in the interim, they are all considered pure once they have rinsed their mouths with water from another house. Thus it is said.
Thus concludes the section on exceptions to impurity (*āśaucāpavāda*) in the *Smṛticandrikā* [74].
Now follow the rules regarding impurity (*āśaucaniyamāḥ*).
Regarding this, Jābāli says:

"The twilight prayers, the five great sacrifices, the daily rites, and the duties prescribed by the Smṛtis—one should certainly omit these during that interval; at the end of ten days, the performance is renewed."

Because of its association with the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), the term *naityaka* here refers to the obligatory daily *śrāddha*. "Ritual acts prescribed by the Smṛtis" refers to rites such as the worship of deities mentioned in the Smṛtis. "In the midst of that" means during the period of impurity. "One should omit" means one should abandon them. Regarding those [rites] dependent on the *saṃdhyā*, there is a "re-performance" (*punaḥkriyā*)—that is, a renewed performance—at the end of the ten days, when the impurity has ceased. The statement "one should abandon the *saṃdhyā*" is said with reference to the *saṃdhyā* consisting of the recitation of mantras, and not with reference to the *saṃdhyā* in its entirety. As Pulastya says: "One should perform the *saṃdhyā*, the *iṣṭi*, the *caru*, and the *homa* for as long as one lives."
A twice-born man should not abandon [his duties] even during a period of impurity; by abandoning them, he would go to a lower state.
"During both birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka), a twice-born man should perform the twilight rites;
he should recite the mantras mentally, with the exception of breath control (prāṇāyāma). Thus [it is said].

This is its meaning: one should mentally recite the mantras other than those for *prāṇāyāma*. However, one should not even mentally recite the mantras for *prāṇāyāma*; the point is that one should perform *prāṇāyāma* entirely without mantras. The instruction to "recite mentally" applies to matters other than the throwing of the joined palms (*añjali*). For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi says: "During birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), having thrown the joined palms with the Sāvitrī mantra and having circumambulated, one should bow to the Sun. The repetition of the Sāvitrī mantra mentioned in the ritual for the *saṃdhyā* is for the purpose of precluding mental recitation; therefore, the recitation of the Sāvitrī mantra must be performed vocally. Viṣṇu also states the actions to be avoided: "During impurity, the fire-oblation (*homa*), giving, receiving, and Vedic study cease; during impurity, one should not eat the food of anyone. Here, the *homa* intended is the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
"A Brahmin shall remain for ten days excluded from the Vaiśvadeva rite," because Saṃvarta has thus specified this particular rule; and Śaṅkha also, with reference to the Vaiśvadeva, states:
"Giving, receiving, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and rites for the ancestors [are suspended]."
Except for the offering of funeral cakes to the departed, one should suspend [all other rites] during the period of impurity.

"Pitṛ-karma" refers to rites for the ancestors, such as the *śrāddha* on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) and so forth. One should not suspect that by the force of this general statement, "and no fire-oblation," even the *agnihotra*, *aupāsana*, and other such rites must be discontinued; for Yājñavalkya says:
"The *vaitāna* (sacrificial) and *aupāsana* (domestic) rites, as well as those actions enjoined by the *Śruti*, must be performed."

The *vaitāna* rites are those accomplished by means of many fires, such as the *gārhapatya* and others, as enjoined by Vedic injunctions such as, "One should perform the *agnihotra* for as long as one lives," and "One should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* for as long as one lives. Likewise, the *aupāsana* rites are those accomplished by means of the single domestic fire; the meaning is that the *aupāsana-homa*, the *pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka*, and so forth, must be performed. And there is another *smṛti*: "Having bathed and performed the ritual sipping of water (*upasparśana*), one should personally perform the *vaitānika* rites."

The meaning is that immediately after the onset of impurity (*āśauca*), one should bathe, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and personally carry out the *vaitānika* rites, such as the *agnihotra*, at their proper time. It should not be argued that an injunction regarding *vaitānika* rites is untenable while impurity—characterized by unfitness for religious duties (*dharma*)—persists; for it is precisely through the force of the injunction itself that fitness for religious duty is understood. And so it has been stated by Gobhila: "In the case of the *agnihotra*, however, purification for the purpose of the oblation is considered to be momentary (*tātkālikī*). But he who is impure shall not perform the five great sacrifices (*pañcayajña*); he remains [impure] until [the rite is completed]."

In rites such as the *agnihotra*, where a rule exists for performance during a period of impurity (*āśauca*), there is purification for that specific occasion. From the moment prior to the initial resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for the rite until the completion of the Vedic ritual (*vaitānika-anuṣṭhāna*), one should understand that there is a purification characterized by fitness for dharma. In this regard, however, there is no rule stating that the five great sacrifices (*pañca-mahāyajña*) must be performed during that impurity; since there is no rule indicating purification in that case, the meaning is that there is simply unfitness for the rite. Thus, even when fitness for the rite has been indicated by the rule, if a man does not offer the oblation, he must perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). For this very reason, Manu says:
"One who, out of delusion, abandons the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices as well as any Vaitānika rite even during the period of impurity (sūtaka), must indeed perform an expiation.
The mention of "Vaitānika" is intended to include Smārta rites prescribed for the period of impurity as well. For this very reason, Jātūkarṇya states:
When impurity (sūtaka) has arisen, how should the Smārta rite be performed?
One should have the Piṇḍayajña, the Caru, and the Homa performed by one who does not belong to the same Gotra.

The *piṇḍayajña* is the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. The *caru* is the *pārvaṇasthālīpāka*. The *homa* is the daily *aupāsanahoma*. By the force of the injunction "one should cause it to be performed," it is understood that regarding Smārta rites—specifically those rites consisting of renunciation (*tyāga*)—impurity characterized by unfitness for religious duty (*dharmāyogyatva*) applies only there and not elsewhere. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:

"In the case of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), when one is unable to eat at a *śrāddha*, or due to causes such as being away on a journey, one should have the oblation offered (*hāvayet*), but one must not let it lapse (*na tu hāpayet*)."
"One should not let it lapse" means one should not abandon it. And so Jābāli says:
"In the case of a Vitāna sacrifice, there is no abandonment of ritual acts even upon birth or death;
the oblation must indeed be performed in the domestic fire by those born of other lineages."

The *homa* performed in the domestic fire (*śālāgni*) is called *aupāsana*; because of the rule that this must be performed by those belonging to other lineages (*gotra*), whereas there is no such restrictive rule for the *homa* related to lineage and other matters performed in the sacrificial fires (*vaitānika-agni*), it is understood that one may perform it oneself.
"One should avoid performing obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and other rites during a period of impurity (*sūtaka*).
For one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), purification is ordained to occur immediately at that time. Thus [it is said].

In this regard, it should be understood that the first half [of the verse] concerns obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites and so forth during a period of impurity (*āśauca*), while the second half concerns those who maintain the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). In the same way, the scope of Paiṭhīnasi’s statement—"Obligatory rites should be suspended, with the exception of those pertaining to the sacrificial fires (*vaitāna*)"—must also be understood; for there is no counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the rule that Vedic (*śrauta*) and Smārta rites are to be abandoned. Even for Vedic rites such as the *agnihotra*, abandonment occurs at the time of their initial commencement during impurity, because the counter-exception rules apply to the *agnihotra* and other rites to be performed after the initial commencement. Pulastya states [the following] regarding optional (*kāmya*) rites, while the terms "obligatory" and "occasional" continue to apply: [78]
Having touched the waters at Saṃnihatyā when the sun is seized by Rāhu,
for one who has entered into the duty of a sacrificial session and desires the fruits of the act of giving.

The meaning is this: even for one who desires the fruit of the act of giving, having touched the *saṃnihati* and bathed in a specific sacred ford (*tīrtha*), there is immediate purity (*sadyaḥśauca*) when proceeding with the gift; likewise, for one engaged in the duty of a food-distribution (*annasatra*), there is immediate purity even if he seeks the fruit of that giving. Regarding occasional rites (*naimittika*) as well, Vṛddha-Bṛhaspati states for the purpose of providing an exception (*pratiprasava*): "In the marriage of a daughter and during a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), there is never any birth-impurity (*sūtaka*). For the purpose of providing exceptions even for obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites, Jāmadagnya says:
"Whether during birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka), one who has immersed oneself in the waters of the Jāhnavī,
standing in water reaching to the navel, may perform acts such as giving gifts and recitation;
this applies especially to the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites."
As for the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, which states: "One should never neglect the performance of obligatory duty;
by its non-performance, however, there is bondage and nothing but rebirth after death."

Thus, that [statement] refers to the suspension of rites such as the *agnihotra* which are specifically enjoined; it does not apply to daily obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) such as the *tarpaṇa*, which lack such specific injunctions, for that would result in a contradiction with the previously cited texts. Furthermore, he himself has stated:
"A Brāhmaṇa should remain for ten days, avoiding gifts, *homa*-offerings, and the like;
a Kṣatriya for twelve days, and a Vaiśya for half a month."

And "A Śūdra shall remain for a month deprived of his obligatory duties" (79)—this is intended as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) even of the full periods of impurity prescribed according to one's age and stage of life. As for that which was stated by Hārīta:
"Then, on the eleventh day, sacrifice and Vedic study may indeed take place."
And indeed, ritual actions proceed [from this]; thus Manu has declared.

Thus, the phrase "then on the eleventh day" is intended to indicate the day immediately following the final day of the period of impurity (*āśauca*). Regarding the religious student (*brahmacārin*), Kātyāyana says:
"One should not abandon ritual action during *sūtaka*; nor should one who observes a vow ever abandon it.
For him, there is no *sūtaka* as there is for a householder; rather, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is mandatory.
Thus concludes the section on the rules for impurity in the Smṛticandrikā; now follow the duties of one who is about to die, according to Vyāsa:
Having seen a man dying, the performer [of the rite] should act upon the ground in a pure place,
in a temple, on a riverbank, in the waters of the Gaṅgā, or at the foot of a great tree.
One should offer a cow, with its face upward and its neck toward the south, dedicated to that [deceased];
and one should cause gold, a gift of land, and sesame seeds to be given according to one's capacity.
That gift which is given with affection to one who is a householder, poor, learned in the Vedas, and ascetic— that gift is the means for attaining heaven.
Whether it be the afflicted person or their son,
close relatives should whisper into the ear the words of the Lord as proclaimed in the scriptures and other authoritative sources.
And Śātātapa says:
For the sick, a physician is a friend; for one who is dying, charity is a friend—namely, food, drink, horses, cattle, clothing, land, beds, and seats.
[80] “In the world of the *pretas*, eight types of gifts are especially praised;
therefore, one should by all means perform acts of giving at the time of death.
Thus ends the section on what must be done by one about to die in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination regarding the fire.
Yājñavalkya states the rule for the offering of fire and water upon death after the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*):
"If he has been initiated, he should be cremated according to the procedure for one who maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), provided there are the necessary materials."

If one who has been initiated dies, he should be cremated according to the procedure for the consecration of one who maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), so that it is purposeful—that is, effective—according to the manner prescribed for such a person. This is the intended meaning: those purificatory rites prescribed for one who maintains the sacred fires, such as the clearing of the ground, the spreading of *darbha* grass, and the sprinkling with water, must be performed insofar as they serve a functional purpose as the means (*dvāra*) to the ritual action. However, those rites whose purposes have ceased, such as the joining of the sacrificial vessels (*pātra-saṃyojana*), need not be performed. This is just as, in the case of *kṛṣṇala* beans where the rules are extended (*atideśa*), threshing, sprinkling, and other such acts are not performed because their functional means are absent, whereas sprinkling and similar acts are indeed performed. And the same applies to the fire used for a funeral (*sāntatika*), because of the injunction regarding the fire of Mitra and Varuṇa. Regarding the "funeral fire" (*sāntātika*): all rites for the youth are performed in that very fire which has been maintained since his birth-ceremony (*jātakarma*) until his marriage, starting from the tonsure (*caula*). For students (*brahmacārin*), the uninitiated, and maidens, cremation is performed using either a common fire or a fire from a skull-bowl (*kāpāla*). Its production is like the production from the two kindling woods (*araṇī*). The mention of a "common fire" is because of the absence of the fire produced from the kindling woods; however, if those are present, the fire should be taken by churning them. [81]
And likewise, Yajñapārśva says:
"The cremation of the child should be performed with fire from a human skull;
others say it should be with ordinary fire, while still others say it should be with fire produced from a fire-drill."
Kātyāyana also says:

"The cremation of celibate students who have died without having maintained the sacred fire, of widowers, of ascetics, of those who have fallen from their status, and of women [who have likewise died without maintaining the fire]..."
The cremation with the fire of the skull (kapālavahni) is performed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch;
likewise, one should cremate the householder with the fire produced at the time of marriage.
"It is the consensus of those learned in sacrifice that [the fire] for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) is by means of the three sacrificial fires (*tretāgni*).

Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "The *kapālāgni* is the fire produced when a potsherd heated to the color of fire is placed inside a heap of dried cow-dung (*karīṣa*) and so forth. [This is stated in] the *Gṛhyakārikā*.
For one who has died without a wife, the fire shall be either the *uttāpana* or the common worldly (*laukika*) fire.

"And likewise for a woman who has no husband, before her marriage, during her menstrual period, or while she is impure. Thus says Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya: "One who has maintained the sacred fires should be cremated according to rule with the three fires."
One who has not maintained the sacred fires [is purified] by one worldly [fire], and other people by another.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha also says:
"One may burn a maiden with a fire of chaff, or with rice, or with barley;
or else with a fire of heated iron, or with a fire of potsherds."
One should burn an ascetic who observes the celibate life with the fire of a skull-bearer;
or, according to others who know, with the parching chaff of grain.
Having established the fire upon *darbha* grass, he remains again upon *darbha* grass; the fire is traditionally known as *uttāpana* when it is again upon a third layer of *darbha* grass.
Having cast the skull into the fire, one should throw parched grain husks (tuṣa) into it;
or, having thrown dried cow dung (karīṣa), once it has ignited, there arises the "husk-fire" (tuṣapāvaka).
As long as fire arises solely from a heated skull,
so long is that fire proclaimed to be produced from a bundle of grass.
If one dies in a place other than where the sacred fire was maintained,
a *pāthikṛt* oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) must be performed, or else a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Having led [the body] to a place near the *aupāsana* fire, one should perform the funeral rites for the deceased after offering either the *pāthikṛt* sacrifice or the *pūrṇāhuti* into that fire; otherwise, one should cremate it according to the rules in another location. In that case, the *pretādhāna* (establishment of fire for the deceased) must be performed. As for the fate of the fire during that interval, it is said: "The milk-offering for a cow whose udders have flowed is prescribed to be made with her milk until the cremation of the body, using the calf of another."

"Even for another [deceased person], one should offer oblations with milk in the absence of that [milk]; however, one should cremate him who has been burnt by a fire other than the *aupāsana* with the fire prescribed by the injunctions. Thus, even if he has been cremated according to a rite other than one's own *śākhā*, one should cremate him again according to the rite prescribed in one's own *śākhā*. Likewise, [83]
"But one should purify again what has been burnt by a fire that is not fit for worship;
and one who has been burnt by a non-scriptural [teaching] should be purified according to the scripture.
As for the statement:
If the fire is located in another country and the deceased has died in a distant land,
the funeral rites for the departed must be performed by the best of the twice-born after they have produced a fire.

Thus it has been said, and this is respected by the learned. If one who has died is found to have had his *āhavanīya* fire-lineage interrupted, he should perform the reconnection according to the rule and offer twelve portions (*dvādaśagṛhīta*). This has been stated by Āpastamba:

If one who has established the sacred fires dies—whether his fires have been extinguished, his fires have become disordered, or he has abandoned his fires—they do not cremate him with other than the three *tretā* fires. Therefore, wearing the sacrificial cord over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), having dug up the fire-places and sprinkled them with water, he places the deceased in the sacrificer’s place. Having placed the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) behind the *gārhapatya* fire, he churns [the fire] with the mantra: "Those fires of his who, desiring flesh, long for the sacrificer's flesh when he offers oblations—let them know this; let them lead this deceased man to the heavenly world for this offered oblation. Having silently spread out the fires, he fills the *sruva* ladle with twelve portions of clarified butter and offers it silently. Then the funeral rites beginning with "The attendants [should follow] the deceased" are undertaken. Thus it is said.
Regarding the fires mounted upon the self and so forth, it has been stated by him [the author] himself in the event of the sacrificer's death:

If the sacrificer should die while the fires have been consigned to the two kindling woods (*araṇī*) or within himself, one should proceed as before: having dug up the fire-places and sprinkled them with water, one places the deceased on the sacrificer’s place; then, having established a fire in the *gārhapatya* hearth, one takes hold of the right hand of the deceased. His son, brother, or another close relative mutters the formula, "Bring it down" (*upāvaha*), or, if the fire had been consigned to the two kindling woods, he brings it down into them and churns [the fire]. While the fire is being produced, he should cause the deceased to touch it and mutter this mantra. Thus it is said.
And likewise, another Smṛti states: [84] "If this person has died while his consciousness was fixed upon the Self, then the Śruti says:
having taken hold of the right hand of the deceased, one should recite this."
"Descend, O Jātavedas; if [the fire is] in the two kindling woods, one should mutter thus.
Having churned the fire and established it, [one should place it] to the south of the other fire. Thus [it is said].

When husband and wife die simultaneously, the *pitṛmedha* (funeral rite for the ancestors) is performed together. Regarding this, Āpastamba has stated: "If they have died together, the *pitṛmedha* is performed together. On this point, some desire that the offering of the fire be divided; however, the Commentator has declared that this is incorrect. In the case of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*sarvādhāna*) and has many wives, if the eldest wife dies first, he should relinquish the fires there and perform the *ādhāna* (establishment of the fires) and subsequent rites with the second wife. If she too later dies, he should relinquish the fires there and perform the *ādhāna* with another wife. In the absence of another wife, he should marry again and perform the *ādhāna* and subsequent rites with her. If he is incapable of marrying again, he should perform the *ādhāna* for his own sake alone. Thus says Śaunaka.

"If one wife of a husband has died, the householder, having cremated her with that very same fire, may again establish the sacred fires together with another woman according to the ritual procedure for the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*). Thus [says the text].
The author of the commentary on the *Āpastamba-kalpa* also [states]:

"Even though there are two wives, when one wife has died, they should cremate the deceased together with the very same fire. After this, the reuniting of these two with the fire and their wealth shall take place again according to the prescribed rule. Thus it is stated; and also in another Smṛti:

But in the case of having many wives, if the eldest dies first, one should cremate her with the *agnihotra* fire; the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādheya*) must then be performed with another wife.
They should fetch all [the fires] from the churning fire alone, and not from the ordinary fire.

In that same case, if the sacrificer dies first, the *pitṛmedha* (funeral rite) is performed with his three sacred fires (*agnitretā*) of the *agnihotra*. For the wives, however, there is only the *pretādhāna* (the kindling for the deceased) as previously described. But in the case of the *ardhādhāna* (half-kindling), if the sacrificer who has only one wife dies first, the *pitṛmedha* is performed with his three sacred fires; the wife’s rites are performed with the *aupāsana* fire. This is because of the traditional teaching of Āpastamba: "Of those two, whichever dies first, the *pitṛmedha* is accomplished with his three sacred fires; whichever dies later, [it is accomplished] with the *aupāsana*. If the wife dies first in this very situation, one should either abandon the *agnihotra* or the *aupāsana* fire there, perform the *punarādhāna* (re-consecration), and then perform the *ādhāna* together with her. This is because, starting from the passage "Then he fasts," up to "Before the *sabhyāvasathya* and the *aupāsana*," there is a rule for the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the *aupāsana* fire as well. If she dies again, this same principle applies there too. If there is an inability to perform the re-consecration, then the *ādhāna* and other rites are for oneself alone. However, in the case of the *ardhādhāna* for one who has multiple wives, if the sacrificer dies first, the *pitṛmedha* is performed with his three sacred fires. But for the wives, it is performed with their respective portions of the *aupāsana* fires. And so says the *Trikāṇḍi*:
One who has maintained the sacred fires should be cremated according to the rule with three fires;
one who has not maintained them with one fire, as was previously the case for husband and wife.
If one of the two wives should die, having cremated her with the very fire used for domestic worship (*aupāsana*),
he should perform the formal offering of the fire according to rule and then take up another domestic fire.

[86] "Or, if there is a worldly fire, one should divide the fire that has been maintained by two wives and give [the portions]; then one may take another portion of the fire. But if the former fire is lost, one should subsequently obtain it again.
Thus ends the determination of the fires in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination of the performer of the consecration (*saṃskartṛ*).
In that regard, when there are many sons, the offering of the fire (*agnipradāna*) must not be performed by all; rather, it must be performed by the eldest alone. And so says Marīci:
"Whatever has been performed by the eldest alone, after having obtained the consent of all..."
"And by means of the undivided property, it shall be as if performed by all.
Thus [it is stated]. Also in the *Matsya Purāṇa*: "The son of the deceased should perform the cremation and other rites; even a son born of a concubine (aiṣa) may do so."
"But when there are many [sons], the one possessing special qualities (guṇin) should give; when they are equal, however, the eldest alone [should give]. Thus says Ṛṣyaśṛṅga:
"Whether it be the middle son, the youngest, or even the eldest among the sons..."
And whatever is most dear to his father, he should have all of that performed by him alone.

"All sons, even if they hate their father, as well as the wife, brother, or friend, shall perform the rites such as the cremation fire for the father; so too shall daughters and others. [87] Thus it is said.
Regarding the eligibility for the offering of the cremation fire, Jamadagni states that if one is incapacitated by illness or other causes:
The eldest son must perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and the water rites;
even if he is incapable, the son who provides the fire should have the remainder performed by another.
Vasiṣṭha also says: "When the eldest son is present and capable, or when another ritual act is being performed,
the funeral rites for the parents must be performed by the second son or the younger brother."
If the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the parents has not been performed by the eldest son,
it must be performed again by that eldest son once the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) has been completed.
If the death of both husband and wife occurs within ten days of each other,
the funeral rites for the parents must be performed by the elder brother alone.
Likewise, in the absence of a son, the rite should be performed by a sapinda or others. Thus says Paraskara:
"Whether it be a son, a brother, a daughter's son, a cognate, or even a son-in-law—whoever offers [the water] on the first day, he shall complete the ten-day period."

In the absence of a son, the paternal *sapiṇḍas* and disciples [should perform the rites]; in their absence, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the teacher (*ācārya*), and so forth. Bhṛgu also says: "Whether of a different lineage or the same lineage, whether a woman or a man, whoever offers [the first water] on the first day shall complete it for ten days."
If the son arrives before the collection of the bones,
then from that time forward he should perform the rites, and the cremator should release the remains.
"If a son arrives after the collection of the bones, he who offers [the first rice ball] on the first day shall complete the ten-day period.
Likewise, whatever substance is intended for the rice ball on the first day remains that same substance until the end of the ten days. This was stated by Śunaḥpuccha:
One should offer the oblation with rice, or with barley meal, or even with vegetables;
whatever substance is used on the first day shall be used until the end of the ten days.
Yajñapārśva says:
One who is close to a man without a son should offer the funeral cakes, water, and other rites until the completion [of the period];
otherwise, he becomes a sinner.

In the consecration (saṃskāra) of the parents, the eldest son alone is the performer; in his absence or when he is not present, the younger son; and in the absence of sons, a near *sapiṇḍa* or other relative. In the absence of such, the next closest person performs the rite accordingly, so that even if another close relative is present within the ten-day period (*daśāha*), the former shall complete the ten days, and not beyond them. If a son or other relative becomes incapable due to illness or similar reasons, then another should have the rites performed until the end of the ten days, because a substitute is seen to be permissible in cases of distress (*ārta*), whereas no such substitute is seen for expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*). However, when the performer belongs to a different Vedic school (*śākhā*)—as indicated by the rule "one who is not of the same *gotra*, one who is of the same *gotra*"—then the *Pitṛmedha* must be performed according to one's own school. Otherwise, the consecration must be performed again. Thus says Kātyāyana.
The learned who accomplish their tasks have declared that ritual procedure is threefold:
non-performance, performance by another, and thirdly, improper performance.
The dull-witted person who abandons the injunctions of his own Vedic branch and instead relies on those of another branch acts in vain; for him, that action and its fruit are both lost.
That which is not prescribed in one's own Vedic branch, provided it is not contradictory,
should be performed by the learned, just like the Agnihotra and other such rites.

If the material for a rite has been prescribed as stated, and the performer should act otherwise, he should perform that rite again as prescribed; however, if there is a lapse in the ritual manual (*tantra*), there shall be no further performance.
"But when the primary act has not been performed, it should be performed again along with its subsidiaries;
however, if a subsidiary has not been performed, one should perform the expiation, and not that [primary] act.

Here, in the case of the non-performance of the primary act, that very act must be performed again together with its subsidiaries. In the case of the non-performance of a subsidiary, there is no repetition of that primary act, nor is there the performance of only that specific subsidiary; rather, only the expiation (prāyaścitta) is to be performed.
Now the rite of entering the fire by women is described:
entering and following [the husband] in death is ordained for women alone;
however, the procedure for entry for Śūdra women is said to be without mantras.

When the time of death has arrived for any Brahmin whatsoever, his wife—having performed an auspicious bath, put on clean garments, sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), and taken hold of perfumes, flowers, and other offerings—approaches her husband and summons Brahmins. Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "On this meritorious lunar day, characterized by the aforementioned specific qualities, I shall follow my husband in death for the sake of attaining residence in the world of Brahmā together with my husband, who is the very form of Viṣṇu," the devoted wife sits down facing the east, holding water along with *darbha* grass and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
To this Viṣṇu, the bestower of all desires and my worthy husband,
I shall offer my body so that I may indeed dwell in the celestial abode.
The earth, the sky, water, fire, and wind are the lords of the world;
the seven seers, time, and all the gods are the witnesses.
Whatever sin has been committed by me, arising from mind, speech, and body— may all that go to destruction as I cast off my body into the fire.

The giver of life should perform the rite, saying: "I give this to you, [Name], of such-and-such lineage, who desires the attainment of residence in my world of Brahmā for your husband, who is the very form of Śrī Mahāviṣṇu; it is not mine. The performer, having spread Darbha grass with its tips pointing south upon a seat and placed the corpse there, and having placed the wife of the deceased on the left side of the corpse, binds the wife of the deceased with a cord of Darbha grass while reciting "Saṃgacchadhvam. Following the deceased as he is carried away by the bearers, he establishes the fire on the southern side of the funeral pyre. At the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he places the corpse on the pyre with its head to the south, and places the wife on its left side. Having placed the fire between their two arms while reciting "Mainam agne," the performer then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnavītī*), holding Darbha grass in his hand, and joining his palms in reverence, consecrates the act with "Sūryaṃ te cakṣuḥ śarīrair agne... He takes clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle and offers it into the fire with "Ya etayoḥ patho goptāraḥ svāhā," and then he should cremate the body.
Thus concludes the procedure for following [the deceased];
now the method for entering the fire is described.

When the husband has died and the wife, being unable to follow him in death, desires to abandon her body by entering the fire, then the performer—such as a son—should cause that devoted wife (*pativratā*) to enter the fire. When the husband has died, the devoted wife should first bathe and sip water (*ācamana*), perform the rite of restoring life to the husband (*prāṇadāna*), and, after consecrating the deceased being carried by the bearers, go to the cremation ground. At the conclusion of the husband’s funeral rites, she should bathe in a pond, a river, or the like, apply turmeric ointment, wear fragrant flowers and ornaments, and don yellow garments. Having sipped water, she should approach the husband. Then the performer—such as a son—having spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south on the northern side of the funeral pyre (*citī*), should seat her there, facing south. He should purify her with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) while reciting "Āpyāyasva," and purify her again with "Āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ" and "Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ. Then, having placed the wife of the deceased near the deceased, he should offer oblations of clarified butter (*ājyāhuti*) and the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the portion of the deceased's hand while reciting "Ya etasya," and so forth. He should then place the vessel of clarified butter, the *sruva* ladle, and the fire behind the pyre, and seat the wife of the deceased facing east. Bringing more clarified butter, he should perform an *ājyahoma* over her head with the tip of a *darbha* blade in a continuous stream, reciting: "Bhūḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Bhuvaḥ svāhā! Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā! Thereafter, the wife of the deceased, standing on the northern side of the pyre facing south, should take a handful of water along with rice grains in her joined palms (*añjali*).

O you who consist of the three Vedas, whose nature is the triple form, the sole lamp of the three worlds, leader of the planets, and possessor of seven horses—accept this arghya; salutations be unto you!
Having thus offered the *arghya* to the Sun:
"O Seven-Tongued One, may you quickly destroy whatever sin has arisen from my mind, speech, and body, as well as that born of transgressing the words of my husband; salutations be unto you!"

Having thus offered one fruit into the fire, preceded by the gift of the right foot, he should enter the fire. Having cremated the deceased in this manner, immediately thereafter, all the relatives should have their hair shaved. Regarding the case of another performer, the specific injunctions concerning the performer as already established are found in the section on *śrāddha*.
Thus ends the determination of the performer of the sacraments in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follow the matters concerning the cremation of the deceased and related rites.
In that regard, the ornament of the three sections [states]:
"When [the food] is directly perceived and the purification by refinement is unimpeded,
one should perform three *prājāpatya* penances for consuming the leavings of a lower [caste]."
Likewise, if one eats while leaving food on the upper part of the body, one should perform six Prājāpatya penances;
however, Parāśara says three, Bhṛgu says five, and Aṅgiras says six.
Gautama has declared that for dying after touching one who is untouchable, six *kṛcchra* penances are required;
however, for everyone else, one who is capable [of performing the full penance] must undergo a twelve-year penance.
According to the words of the Brahmins, the procedure for the counter-teacher is as follows:
having performed the cremation, he should carry out the rite; otherwise, he would become a sinner.
"For the sake of accomplishing his qualification as the performer [of the rite], he should perform three, five, or seven *kṛcchra* penances;
or else, he should perform the *paitṛmedhika* rites through gifts and other means. Thus it is said.
The cremation and subsequent rites must be performed immediately after the ritual bathing. Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
Having bathed the weak person and clothed him in clean garments,
one should place him on the ground strewn with *barhis* grass, with his head toward the south.
Having anointed him with ghee and bathed him, [he should place him] wearing a garment and the sacred thread,
his entire body sprinkled with sandalwood paste and adorned with flowers.
Likewise, having bound a garland made of reeds and adorned him,
they threw pieces of gold into his seven openings.
[93] "Having covered his face with a cloth, the sons and others should carry him out; wearing the *prācīnāvīta* [sacred thread] over the right shoulder, they should proceed while observing silence.
Regarding this, the restriction of direction for the carrying out of the corpses of Brāhmaṇas and others has been shown by Manu:
"One should carry out a deceased Śūdra by the southern gate;
for the twice-born, one should do so by the western, northern, or eastern gates as appropriate," thus says Vasiṣṭha.
Then they should carry the corpse, face upward, upon an Audumbara post or a throne;
they should not lead it facing toward the village, nor downward, but with its head directed toward the south.
The elderly women and children of the deceased should stand in front, while the others behind;
they should have their upper garments cast down and their hair loosened.
"The kinsmen should follow behind; there should be no interval between the fire and the deceased," so says Kātyāyana.
Taking food in an unbaked earthen vessel, [they lead] the deceased preceded by the fire.
"One person should follow after [the body] for its sake; he should leave half of it on the path on the ground.
Having reached the cremation ground, sitting facing south and bending his left knee, he should slowly perform the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) with sesame seeds. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is that, according to the procedure for offering the funeral ball (*piṇḍa*), one should sit on the ground from the time of cremation until the end at the cemetery and cast [the offerings] down. Gautama says: "One should prepare the place of cremation either in the south-east or the south-west, having cleared away thorns, trees, and even the forest plants and medicinal herbs."
[94] They should construct a pit measuring five *aratnis* in length, extending from east to south, with its opening facing upward toward the south and reaching twelve finger-breadths in depth.
"Having spread out *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing south, and having scattered sesame seeds and then barley grains,
one should cremate [the body] with wood, face upwards, but not naked, just as an oblation [is not offered naked].
Thus says Vyāghra.
They should not cremate [the body] face-down, nor naked, nor defiled by impurities;
nor with fuel-sticks unfit for sacrifice, nor with those brought from outcasts (caṇḍāla) or the fallen (patita).
One should not burn cloth that is infested with worms, insects, and the like, nor that which is very old;
one should discard half of it and wear the other half.
And Pracetas says:
The sons and other relatives should perform the bathing of the deceased, followed by worship;
one should not burn the body naked, but rather some cloth should be offered and discarded [with it].
The meaning is that half [of the merit] is to be given to the one who dwells in the cremation ground. Vṛddhaparāśara states:
"In the rite of purification following contact with a corpse, a Brāhmaṇa is not at all defiled;
both the carrier and the fire-kindler become pure immediately after bathing."
This refers to the case of a destitute Brāhmaṇa:
"Those twice-born who carry a deceased Brāhmaṇa who is destitute obtain,
step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in due order."
For those of virtuous deeds, there is no impurity whatsoever, nor any evil;
for them, purification is ordained immediately, like one who has emerged from the water after bathing.

Because it has been stated thus. As for that which was said by Devala: "If one should perform the cremation during the day, after the setting of the sun, the Brahmin, having bathed, may enter his home; if [the cremation occurs] at night, [he may enter] after the rising of the sun."

Thus, as for what was stated by Hārīta: "Upon touching a corpse, they should not enter a village until the appearance of the stars at night, or until the sun [rises] during the day," that should be understood as applying to cases where the act is performed out of delusion or similar causes. However, as for what was stated by Aṅgiras: "Whoever, even if not a sapinda relative, should somehow carry out a corpse, he becomes pure on that very day after bathing with his clothes on and touching fire."

Thus, this [text] intends to show that there is impurity (*āśauca*) even for one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* when he performs the removal of a learned (*śrotriya*) Brāhmaṇa out of greed for wealth and the like. And so says Manu: "A Brāhmaṇa, having carried out a deceased twice-born person who is not a *sapiṇḍa* like a kinsman, becomes pure after three nights; likewise for the mother's close relatives."
"If he eats their food, he becomes pure after ten days;
but if he does not eat their food, he is purified in a single day, provided he does not dwell in that house."

But he who, having performed the removal of a corpse, dwells in that very house and does not eat food there, must observe impurity for three nights. Gautama states: "If a lower caste person touches a higher caste person, or a higher caste person touches a lower one, the impurity in that case is as prescribed for a corpse. "Touching" here means "removal. The meaning is that if a Brāhmaṇa performs the removal of a Śūdra's corpse, his impurity lasts for ten nights. Vyāghra, however, says that for one who performs the removal of a corpse of a different caste out of greed for wealth, the impurity is double. [96]

"If an inferior person carries out the funeral rites for a superior, or a superior for an inferior, he shall observe impurity like a corpse-bearer; if it is for a visible purpose, the impurity shall be double.

The meaning is that regarding the carrying out of a funeral for one of a different caste (*asavarṇa*), the impurity that has been prescribed becomes double the impurity when it is for a visible purpose. As for the *Ādipurāṇa*:
But having taken a person of a different caste by paying their value, a man should cremate them;
his period of impurity shall always be equal to that of the deceased's own class.

Thus, that [rule] refers to a case where the deceased is not a *sapiṇḍa*. However, for one who carries out the funeral procession (*nirharaṇa*) of a *sapiṇḍa* relative, there is no increase in the period of impurity (*āśauca*), because carrying out the deceased is prescribed as a duty. As Devala says:
"The carrying out of the deceased and so forth is indeed prescribed for *sapiṇḍas*;
whoever among them performs it for them, for him no increase [in impurity] exists."
"Excess" means an excess of impurity (*āśauca*). In the case of carrying out the corpse of a *samānodaka* relative, the impurity lasts for ten days. To this effect, that same author says:
"He who carries or burns the corpse of a *samānodaka* relative shall have impurity for ten days; for others, however, they know it to be three days."

For a religious student (*brahmacārin*), there is indeed a violation of his vow (*vratalopa*) when carrying out the removal of a corpse. Thus says Devala: "A religious student shall not perform rites such as the cremation of a corpse;
if he should perform them, he must undergo the *kṛcchra* penance and the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) again."
However, there is no fault in cremating the corpse of one's father or others. Regarding this, Manu and Devala both state:
"Having carried out the body of his teacher, his sub-teacher, his father, his mother, or his guru, a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) is not deprived of his vow. [97]
One should not employ a Śūdra for tasks such as carrying the corpse of a Brāhmaṇa. Regarding this, Manu says:
"While his own kinsmen are present, one should not have a dead Brāhmaṇa carried by a Śūdra;
for that offering, defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven."

In this context, the statement "while his own [kinsmen] are present" is not intended to be emphasized, because of the scriptural hearing of the fault that it leads away from heaven: "A Śūdra shall not carry out a deceased twice-born man, nor shall a twice-born man carry out a Śūdra."
Thus ends the section concerning the cremation of the deceased and related matters in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination of what is to be done after cremation.
Regarding what is to be done after cremation, Yājñavalkya says:
"From the seventh or even the tenth day, the kinsmen approach the waters, saying:
'May this [water] cleanse away our sin; through this, may the ancestors turn their faces away from us.'"

The meaning is that from the seventh day until before the tenth day, the kinsmen—those of the same lineage (*samānagotra*), those within the sapinda relationship, and those entitled to the water offering (*samānodaka*)—should approach the waters facing south while reciting the mantra, "May sin burn away from us. This rite should be performed on odd-numbered lunar days (*tithi*), because of the traditional teaching of Gautama: "The water-rite is performed on the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth [days]. However, Pracetas states that it should be done for as long as the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts:
"Day by day, they should offer full jars of collyrium for the sake of the deceased."
The increase should be carried out until the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) is completed;

the meaning is that the increase of the *añjali* (handfuls of water) should be performed accordingly. In this matter, with regard to the specific benefit for the deceased spirit (*preta*), the offering of water should be repeated for as many days as the period of impurity (*āśauca*) lasts. Yājñavalkya states that the offering of water must be performed even for those other than one's own kin: "In this manner, the water-rite is performed for the mother, the father, and the deceased teacher."

"One may offer water out of desire for one's friends, for married daughters, for sisters, and for the sister's son, the father-in-law, and the officiating priest. Here, "married" (*prattā*) refers to a daughter or a sister who has been wedded; "sister's son" (*svasrīya*) refers to a nephew. In this case, the offering of water for deceased maternal grandfathers and others who are not *sapinda* relatives must be performed as an obligatory duty (*nitya*), because it is heard in scripture that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) if it is not performed. However, for friends and the others mentioned, it is done out of desire (*kāma*); if performed, there is spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*), but if not performed, there is no transgression.

Herein is the procedure for the water libation (*udakadānavidhi*). Restraining their speech, the *sapiṇḍas*, the *samānodakas*, and other kinsmen, beginning with the elders, should pour water once each day, saying: "May the deceased, named so-and-so and belonging to such-and-such a *gotra*, be satisfied. Thus they should pour water only once daily. This is also stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
Having cremated the corpse according to the rule and beheld the celestial lights, the kinsmen,
accompanied by their sons, should proceed while carrying sesame seeds and embers before them.
Then, having taken a stone that is pure, uncracked, smooth, and either dark or red, one should go there to a great body of water.
Having bathed with his clothes on like a staff, having washed away the impurity born of the body,
and having entered deep water, he should cleanse his garment with water.
[99] Having bathed again with their clothes on, restrained in speech and well-composed,
the elders, those of the same lineage, kinsmen, and those related by water-offerings [should assemble].
The sapindas and the sons, in their respective order, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin),
all facing south, [should sit] upon kuśa grass with its tips pointing toward the south.
Having cast a stone there and made a pit in front of it,
he should pronounce the name and lineage [of the deceased], saying, "May the departed spirits be satisfied."
They should pour a single handful of water filled with sesame seeds into the pit;
however, for the parents, they should offer handfuls of water for as long as the period of impurity lasts.
Or else, one may offer a hundred handfuls; on the first day, one handful;
on the second, three handfuls; and on the third, five and seven.
On the fourth and fifth days, one should offer nine handfuls of water;
on the sixth day, eleven handfuls; and on the seventh, thirteen.
On the eighth day they should offer fifteen añjalis; then on the ninth, seventeen;
and on the tenth, they should give one hundred añjalis.
Some [offer] seventy *añjali*s; others three, seven, or five;
they may be numbered as seven, eight, or nine; but on the second day, there are exactly ten.
Those who are subject to a three-night period of impurity should offer thirty handfuls of water on the first day, forty on the second day, and thirty thereafter; thus they become pure.
"But in the case of seventy *añjali*s, one who is pure should give twenty-one on the first day, twenty-one on the second, and on the third, the remainder. Thus says Prajāpati.
Also, Prajāpati:
Day by day, one should offer full handfuls of water for the sake of the deceased;
the increase [of the offerings] should be continued until the final rice-ball (piṇḍa) is completed.

The meaning is that the number of *añjali*s (handfuls of water) should be increased accordingly. Paiṭhīnasi says: "Having bathed and become pure, meditating on the deceased in his mind, facing south, he should pour out three *añjali*s of water; he should cease [this practice] on the eleventh day from the cremation of the body. Vasiṣṭha says: "Having consecrated the body with fire, they enter the water without looking back; they should perform the water-rite with their left and right hands respectively, facing south on odd-numbered days. Hārīta says: "Having carried out [the body] and performed the consecration, the performer goes to the water, bathes, and pours out an *añjali* of water, saying, 'May so-and-so be satisfied. Śaṅkha and Likhita say: "Now, regarding the water-rite for the deceased: the kinsmen, having entered the water according to their seniority, should not step out; they should sprinkle water once while facing south—facing north for a Brāhmaṇa, and facing east for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya—wearing their garments and sacred threads over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), saying, 'This for you, O Father' (?). Kātyāyana [says]: [End of excerpt]
Likewise, all those who have touched the corpse shall go to the water without looking back;
having bathed with their clothes on and sipped water, they should offer water for him on dry ground.
Immediately after reciting the name of the lineage followed by the words "I satiate," one should place *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing south and offer sesame seeds separately for each.
"Day by day, one should offer a full añjali for the sake of the deceased;
the increase [of the offering] should be continued until the piṇḍa is completed. Thus says Pracetas.
Having likewise gone to the riverbank and performed purification according to the rules,
one should first thoroughly cleanse one's garment and then perform the bath.
But one who is clothed, having bathed again, being pure and with a restrained mind,
should take up a stone and offer ten handfuls of water, O Brahmin.
A Kṣatriya should give twelve; for a Vaiśya, fifteen are prescribed;
thirty should be given by a Śūdra; thereafter, he may enter his own home.
"Then a bath must be performed again, and one should cause the purification of the house to be done.
Regarding children for whom the naming ceremony has not yet been performed, Manu says that nothing at all need be done:
"Those children who have not yet grown teeth, and those who have just emerged from the womb..."
"For them there is no cremation with fire, no ritual, and no water-offering.
Thus says Āpastamba.

For those related to the mother by blood and for those related to the father up to the seventh generation—provided their connection is known—if they have died, there shall be the touching of water (libation), excepting the case of a fetus that has not yet reached one year; the parents alone [perform this] if the death occurs within a year. Furthermore, upon the death of a wife or a supreme guru, they shall remain without food until the time of the next dawn and wear the dress of the sick. Having disheveled their hair and scattered dust, wearing a single garment, facing south, they shall touch water once, emerge, wring out their clothes, and sit down. In this manner three times; then, having pronounced the name together with the *gotra*, they shall pour out water mixed with sesame. Without looking back, they shall enter the village silently. Whatever women say, that they shall do; and some maintain that this same rule applies to others as well.

The ritual formula is: "I give this water with sesame seeds (tilodaka) to [Name], of [Gotra] lineage. Having thus given the water, they should return to the village without looking back, enter their home, and do whatever women say. Regarding others who have died—those other than wives and so forth—some teachers extend the rule that one must abstain from food until the end of the day; however, his own view is that this applies only to mothers, fathers, and gurus. Following the aforementioned procedure, after the offering of water, the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) must be performed. This has been stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
Outside the village, in a clean place smeared with cow dung,
having established the common fire (laukikāgni) and bathed, [he should offer] with a vessel made of metal.
The cooking may even be performed with an earthenware vessel, as in the Pitṛyajña;
having poured clarified butter over it, removed it from the fire, and then poured clarified butter over it once more.
Having placed a stone in front and remaining silent while facing south,
one should spread *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing south and pour water upon them once.
Having pronounced the name and lineage, one should offer the funeral ball (piṇḍa) accompanied by mantras;
furthermore, one should offer water with sesame seeds in this manner for ten days.
If one is unable [to perform the rites], it may be done on the first day, or on the fifth, or even on the tenth;
when the three-day impurity has arisen, there should be three funeral cakes (piṇḍas) or ten.
Having offered water and the funeral ball, one should again pour out water;
remembering the boon granted by Vaivasvata, one should give an offering to the crows.
Having cast [the remains] into fire or water and bathed, one should always return home;
ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas) are prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa, and twelve for a Kṣatriya.
"Fifteen [days] are prescribed for a Vaiśya, and thirty are proclaimed for a Śūdra. Thus [says the text]. Śātātapa also says:
"But when there is a reduction in the period of impurity, one should offer exactly ten funeral cakes (piṇḍas)."

The regulation of ten funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) pertains to the Brāhmaṇa. In this regard, a specific rule concerning the number of funeral cakes has been shown by Yama: "Ten funeral cakes for a Brāhmaṇa, twelve for a Kṣatriya, fifteen for a Vaiśya, and thirty indeed for a Śūdra."
Also in another Smṛti:
"With a concentrated mind, one should offer nine funeral cakes (piṇḍa) over nine days;
having offered the tenth cake, one becomes pure at the end of the night."
As for another Smṛti text:
"In the evening and in the morning, for the foremost of the twice-born, there is then the rice-ball and water;
by discarding twenty rice-balls, a Brāhmaṇa attains purity."

Thus, this [rule] applies only to those followers of the Vedic branches for whom it is stated in their *Gṛhya-sūtra* that [the rites] are performed "in the evening and in the morning," and not for others. Regarding the alternative of shortening the period of impurity (*āśauca*), Pāraskara says:
"On the first day, one who is well-composed should offer three funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*);
on the second day, he should offer four, and thereafter follows the collection of the bones."

"But on the third day, one should give three [offerings]; thereafter, one should wash the anus and other parts. Thus says Viṣṇu: "Having performed the pouring of water for the deceased, they should offer a single *piṇḍa* upon *kuśa* grass. The word "each" (*pratyekam*) is to be supplied as the remainder. The phrase "they should offer" (*dadyuḥ*) is an elliptical expression indicating both the offering of water and the offering of the *piṇḍa*. Regarding the specific details for the offering of sesame-water and the *piṇḍa*, Viṣṇu states:
"Likewise, the sesame-water, the *piṇḍa*, and similarly the *navaśrāddha*..."
"One should not perform [the rite] at night, nor during the twilight; if one were to do so, it would be fruitless.
Regarding this, Pāraskara states that there is an exception:
"Having taken the *pretapāṣāṇa* (the stone for the deceased), one may go [to the river] even when the region is unfavorable."
One should perform [the rite] even by drawing back [the breath], but one must not leave this remainder.

"Whatever [rites], such as the offering of water and the giving of funeral balls (*piṇḍa*), are to be performed within the ten-day period—during that ten-day period, one should perform all of them as previously prescribed. Thus [it is said]. Regarding the reversal of the [proper] stones and so forth, there is another Smṛti text:
If the stone should be lost during the period of impurity,
one should offer water-libations with another stone and complete the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
On the first day, whether it be a woman or a man who is the performer of the rite,
one should perform the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) and the water-libation rites for ten days.
"If the performer has fallen away from his duties or has died, another person may complete [the rite];

he alone shall cause the *piṇḍas* to be offered, but the water-libation (*udaka*) must be performed by the *sapiṇḍas*. Thus says Ṛśyaśṛṅga regarding the occurrence of the tenth day or other such occasions within the ten-day period (*antardaśāha*).

"Gautama says: 'If a new-moon day (darśa) should occur during a period of impurity (āśauca), those of all castes should complete the rites for the deceased. Thus [it is stated] in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa.
"But for one who has entered into the ritual procedures for impurity, whatever *darśa* offering is to be given,
having completed the water-libations and the *piṇḍas*, he should perform only the ritual bath. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi.
The offering of funeral cakes and the water-rites should be performed during the first lunar day of the moon;
however, one who performs them during the second lunar day incurs the impurity of death once again.
If one's death occurs on the thirteenth lunar day when it consists of only a single digit (kalā),
one should perform the water-libation rites for that person without waiting for the passing of the Sinīvālī phase.
Aṅgiras states: "One who dies on the fourteenth day attains the status of an *atithi* (guest) thereafter;
one should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) and water until the end of the ten days on that very same day."
"Aṅgiras has declared that one should perform the *śrāddha* on the eleventh day.
All of this refers to cases other than those involving one's mother or father. Regarding the distinction between two lunar days (*tithi*), Gālava says:
"If the new moon (*darśa*) should coincide during the period of impurity (*āśauca*) for one's parents, [it should be completed]."
"The subsequent ritual procedure shall conclude within three days at the very most. Thus it is stated; and in another Smṛti as well:
"If the new moon (darśa) occurs during the period of impurity for the parents, [the rite] shall take place after three days."
It is certain that the Uttara-tantra is concluded at that very point.

"Vasiṣṭha says: 'If the new moon (darśa) occurs within the ten-day period, one should conclude the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa-dāna) and the water with sesame seeds (tilodaka) for others— excluding the two parents— by means of the new moon [offering] alone.'"
If the new moon occurs within ten days [of death], one should complete the entire ritual procedure;
however, regarding the parents, one should perform it without weariness for as long as the period of impurity lasts.

[106] "If a new-moon day (darśa) or a transit (saṃkramaṇa) should occur within ten days, others hold that the remaining funeral rites for the deceased must be completed; provided that the specific lunar day has not been passed, as it does not release one from the state of being a preta. Thus it is said.
Gālava says:
If a new-moon day (darśa) should occur during a period of impurity for anyone of all castes,
one should postpone all offerings of rice-balls (piṇḍas) and water, and complete them [at the proper time].
"One should offer water to the sapinda relatives as well as to the samānodaka relatives;
by the sight of a second moon, all ritual action perishes immediately. Thus ends the section on the determination of duties following cremation in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now follows the determination of the consolation of the afflicted and so forth.
Yājñavalkya states that after the offering of water, the relatives must perform the consolation:
"When they have offered the water, emerged [from the river], and are seated upon soft, grassy ground..."
"They should address those who have bathed with ancient historical narratives. Thus [says] Kātyāyana as well:
"When they have thus properly offered water and are all seated upon a grassy spot..."
Having bathed and sipped water again, those followers were made to know [the rites].
Do not grieve over that which is impermanent and subject to the nature of all living beings;
practice the Dharma with diligence, for it is that which will accompany you.
He who seeks a core in human existence— which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree and resembles a bubble on the water— is utterly deluded.

If the body, which was composed of five elements, has returned to the state of the five, what cause for lamentation is there regarding that, since it arose through actions produced from one’s own body? [107] The meaning is this: if the body—which was accumulated and constructed in five ways as the nature of the five great elements, such as earth and so forth, by means of one's own actions performed in previous lives for the sake of experiencing their respective fruits—has, upon the cessation of the experience of those fruits, returned to the state of the five and attained the form of earth and the other elements, why do you lament over that? Since it serves no purpose, you should not do so. Furthermore:
The earth, which supports all beings, goes to destruction, as do the oceans and the gods;
how then will the world of mortals, which resembles mere foam, not go to destruction?
The meaning is that death is simply appropriate for bodies; therefore, grief is useless. He states the fault in weeping as follows:
"Since the deceased, being powerless, must consume the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should certainly not weep; rather, the funeral rites should be performed with diligence. Thus he says.
Pāraskara states the fault in weeping for others, such as kinsmen and so forth:
"Before the collection of the bones, one should perform a bath after weeping;
for a Brahmin, within ten days [of death], rinsing the mouth is prescribed."
Within ten days of the death of a Brāhmaṇa, before the collection of the bones, a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or others, having wept, should perform a ritual bath.
As long as the bones of the deceased Brāhma�anya have not been removed,
any relative who weeps there along with the other relatives [must likewise bathe].
From bathing, his purification shall come; thereafter, sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed.
For others, however, bathing with one's clothes on is required once the collection of bones has been performed;
but for those born as Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, bathing alone is required after that.

[108] In the case of the death of a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra, for a Brāhmaṇa, the period of impurity (*āśauca*) due to weeping lasts for one day until the collection of the bones (*asthisaṃcayana*), after which there is merely bathing. Regarding this, Pāraskara says: "If a Brāhmaṇa weeps at the collection of the bones of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, he becomes pure by bathing with his clothes on on the second day."
But when an accumulation has occurred, O Brahmin, the twice-born becomes pure by means of bathing alone.
Also in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"If a Brahmin should shed tears before the collection of the bones,
he shall become impure for three nights after going to the house of a deceased Śūdra."
After the collection of the bones, for as long as one month,
the twice-born are purified by a single day and night, along with the washing of their clothes.

If the death is unknown, a Śūdra becomes pure by fasting for two days in the case of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya; otherwise, if he has touched them without following the corpse, he is purified by eating only at night.
All this has been prescribed according to rule for the sapindas;
indeed, the removal of the corpse and other such rites are ordained for the sapinda.
There would be fault for one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* if they fail to perform the funeral rites for such a person;
