however, there is no fault for *sapiṇḍas* in weeping [for the deceased] until the cremation ground.
"After the death [of a relative], there is no fault [in following the corpse] for the kinsmen; [it is purified] by three nights alone.
Thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya speaks of the fault in following a corpse:
"A Śūdra must not be followed by a Brāhmaṇa, nor should a twice-born man ever [follow one]."

"Having followed [the corpse], bathed in water, touched fire, and consumed ghee, one becomes pure. (109) Thus, since there is no authoritative basis for prescribing the consumption of ghee as a substitute for the act of eating, there is no prohibition against eating. It is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"If [one consumes] gold of the same color or even superior [gold] due to affection for the deceased..."
Having followed [the corpse] and bathed, one becomes pure by touching fire and consuming clarified butter.
But a Brahmin, having followed a deceased Kṣatriya like a kinsman,
shall then bathe, touch fire, consume clarified butter, and pass the day in fasting.
"Having followed a Vaiśya woman, one should observe the impurity for a *pakṣiṇī* period;

having followed a Śūdra woman, one becomes pure after three nights. Thus it is said. A Brāhmaṇa, having observed three nights of impurity upon following a Śūdra woman, shall become pure by bathing in a river that flows into the ocean, performing one hundred *prāṇāyāmas*, and consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*). However, in the case of following a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya woman, the impurity lasts for one day. For a Kṣatriya following a Śūdra woman, the impurity lasts for a *pakṣiṇī*; for a Vaiśya following a Śūdra woman, it lasts for one day; and the same applies to weeping [for them].
Thus concludes the determination of the consolation of the dying and related matters in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the collection of the bones; regarding this, Saṃvarta says:
"On the first day, or the third, or the seventh, or even the ninth,
the collection of bones should be performed during the daytime by those belonging to the same lineage. Thus says Pāraskara as well.

"On the first day, or the third, or likewise the fifth or the seventh, the collection of the bones should be performed by the kinsmen together with the relatives. Thus says Viṣṇu: "On the fourth day, one should perform the collection of the bones; their casting into the waters of the Gaṅgā [should follow]. Kātyāyana says:
On the second day, or the third, the fifth, or even the seventh;
or indeed on the ninth or the tenth, the collection of the bones shall take place.
The procedure prescribed therein by the sages is now being stated:

having performed everything up to the ritual bath as before, one should then sprinkle all the bones with cow’s milk while wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and reciting the [appropriate] mantras.
Having extracted the bones from the ashes with branches of the *śamī* and *palāśa* trees,
and having anointed them with clarified butter, one should sprinkle them with fragrant water containing cow's products.
Having placed it in a pair of earthen vessels and wrapped them with thread,
one should dig a pit in clean ground and bury them while facing south.
Having filled the pit with lumps of clay and moss,
and having leveled the surface above, one should perform the remaining rites according to the procedure for the forenoon.
This very same rule is declared for one who has maintained the sacred fires and has passed away;
the collection of the bones and the sacrifice to the deities have been proclaimed.
If one who is pure does not perform the sacrifice to the deities intended for that which has become a *preta*,
then the deities will curse him.
"The deities previously mentioned as being burned in the cremation grounds [should be offered] silently: a libation, flowers, incense, and likewise a lamp;
as well as eye-salve, ointment, water, and unguent. Thus it is said.
Regarding the specific days, lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), and lunar dates (*tithi*) for the collection of bones, it has been stated by Yama:

"One should avoid the collection of bones on Tuesdays, Sundays, and Saturdays, as well as on even lunar dates; likewise, one should avoid it when the lunar mansion has only one quarter remaining or three quarters remaining."
"Especially on the birth-star of the donor, or on a three-quarter star.

Thus [it is said] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "In the case of one who has not maintained the sacred fires, [the rite is performed] after death; but for one who has maintained the sacred fires, it is from the cremation."
The collection of the bones should be performed according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch.
Having divided the period of impurity into three parts, one should perform [the rites] during the first portion;
the middle portion would be the middle part, while the third is recorded as the lowest.
A twice-born man should avoid the afternoon and the night in every respect.
The days of the Moon and Mercury are auspicious; those of Venus and the Sun are middling;
the remaining days are inauspicious, while the two-footed signs are middling.
One should avoid the three asterisms beginning with Arka (the Sun), as well as the Bhadra-yoga and that lunar day;
having placed an elder at the front, one should go toward the cemetery facing south.
Having sprinkled [the tree] with water mixed with milk using a branch of the *śamī* tree,
[he should touch it] from the feet up to the top with his thumb and ring finger.
Having taken the bones, one should place them in a jar or cast them into a pit;
having performed the purification of the bones with the names beginning with Keśava.
Having washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should worship it thoroughly with flowers and other offerings.
[112] Having obtained the permission of the twice-born, one who is well-composed should utter the names of the lineage and the formal declaration (saṃkalpa) according to the rule, in the Gaṅgā.
With the *adhamarṣaṇa* hymn, one should dismiss the bones into the water with the words, "May there be safety for Dharma," and one should continue muttering that [hymn] as long as the bones remain.
As long as the bones of humans remain in the waters of the Gaṅgā,
for that many thousands of years they are honored in the heavenly world.

"Having bound it firmly with straps of antelope skin, wool, or thread, or with linen, silk, or cloth bands, or with a rope of *kuśa* grass, one should cast it [into the water] according to the previously mentioned procedure. Thus, in the *Matsya Purāṇa*.
Beginning with the ritual purifications along with their ancillaries, and extending from the cremation until the conclusion of the domestic rites,
[the observances] take place on the first day, the second, the third, or the fourth.
On the fifth, seventh, or ninth auspicious day,
at the time prescribed by the astrologers, according to the ritual injunctions stated in one's own Vedic school (śākhā).
Having performed the collection of the bones, one should likewise construct an altar of their ashes using either flour of barley and wheat,
flour of śāli rice, or even clay.
One should fashion the three stones with various colors and worship them;
furthermore, one should offer handfuls of water to their companions in successive order.
"Having given the bones, one should cast them into the Gaṅgā, or cast them upon the ground;
or one should dispose of them at another sacred ford (tīrtha), in a pure place, or at Kurukṣetra.
Thus ends the section on the collection of bones in the Smṛticandrikā.
as for the shaving of the head,
that should be performed on the tenth day. Regarding this, Devala says:
"When the tenth day has arrived, the bath shall take place outside the village;
there, the clothes, hair, beard, and nails are to be discarded.
Thus says Pāraskara as well.
"On the second day, the rite of shaving (kṣaurakarma) should be performed with diligence;

or on the third, the fifth, or the seventh, until the offering (pradāna). By the mention of "offering," the lack of restriction regarding the *ekādaśāha* śrāddha and others is understood. Thus says Baudhāyana.

"One who previously had unshorn hair, having heard [the injunction], should have his hair shaved on the first day, or the third, or the fifth, or even the seventh; or rather, according to another opinion, as long as the *śrāddha* is being offered. Thus it is said.
In this regard, shaving is mandatory for sons at the following seven occasions:

at the Ganges, at Māskara-kṣetra, upon the death of one's mother, father, or guru, at the time of establishing the sacred fires (ādhāna), and during the Soma sacrifice. Thus is the shaving prescribed in the Smṛtis.
Because of this statement:
"And in that case, in the absence of a son, the grandson, or his son, or the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā),
having performed the shaving of the hair, should perform the funeral rites for the father."

In this context, shaving for the *sapiṇḍas* is optional. Āpastamba states: "And there is shaving for those who follow. Those who come after (*anu*)—that is, are born later—are the younger brothers; for them, shaving must be performed before the day of the *śrāddha*. This has been stated by the author of the *Gṛhyasūtra*: "Or, having scattered their hair, the blood relatives may throw dust [on their heads]. Shaving of the head is for the performer [of the rite]; thereafter, it is for them according to their own wish."
Regarding those sapindas, the Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa states:
"The teachers of the Taittirīya school say that one should scatter the hair;
that ritual act is not mentioned by the Sāman-chanters, but according to the Śruti for the Bahvṛcas."
"According to the wish of the *sapiṇḍas* who are followers of the *Bahvṛca*, the shaving of the hair (*keśavāpana*) is permitted;
on the tenth day, the rite of shaving (*kṣurakarma*) is recommended for all. Thus it is stated. Furthermore, the shaving and bathing are mentioned in another *smṛti*:
"On a riverbank, at a crossroads, or in the vicinity of a large tree,
those who have experienced [the calamity] should perform the shaving of hair, beard, and so forth.
Thus a specific rule is stated in another Smṛti.
Upon the death of maternal grandfathers, paternal uncles, maternal uncles,
elder brothers, fathers-in-law, and preceptors— and upon the death of their wives— the impurity lasts for ten days.
"One should have the hair shaved even for the sake of a maternal aunt or a sister, or when carrying a fetus;
likewise, having heard of the death of one's parents or the death of a guru while abroad,
one should immediately perform a shaving and carry out a bath with one's clothes on."
As for the statement:
"One who bathes in the waters of the ocean, or shaves his beard,
or a husband who performs these acts while his wife is pregnant, shall certainly go to hell."
One should perform the shaving ceremony when the fetus has become manifest, at the *sīmantonnayana* rite, and at marriage;
until delivery, shaving is not prescribed except by a specific scriptural injunction.
Hair-cutting on the day of marriage is not recommended, nor at night for one's own desire;
it should be performed by the groom either before or on the fifth day after the wedding.
Thus, that [rule] refers to occasions other than the death of a father or similar relatives.
"Whatever sin whatsoever has been committed by men resides in their hair;
therefore, shaving should be performed, and thereafter the *śrāddha* is mandatory."
Thus ends the procedure for shaving in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Regarding the rites on the tenth day, the specific rituals to be performed on that tenth day have been shown by Pāraskara.
On the tenth day, in the forenoon, the shaving ceremony is performed according to the sacred tradition;
having bathed with one's clothes on and sipped water, the household impurity is removed as previously prescribed.
Having gone there with his kinsmen and relatives to that great body of water,
he silently bathed and performed the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) according to the prescribed rites.
One should offer three pindas below; the southern one is dedicated to Yama as its deity.
Having offered one in the middle for the preta, one should cast the raudra pinda upon the northern sacrificial grass.
Having offered collyrium and ointment, as well as an umbrella, sandals, garlands,
and so forth, to the deities, [he should offer] a new jar filled with water.
Then one should request the kinsmen, and those who have been requested should offer handfuls of water,
pronouncing the names and lineages, three times or even ten times.
Having placed a stone in front, or else upon the ground strewn with darbha grass,
one who wears the sacred thread should rise and cast down that stone.
In the midst of water, at the root of a great tree, or at a crossroads,
they should all perform anointing with ointments, garments, and flowers.
Having placed perfumes, other auspicious items, and vessels filled with water for elderly women at the forefront, they should go home and eat barley-rice porridge.
If the stone is lost or even stolen through negligence,
one should take another stone and pour the water previously offered upon it.
When nine days of the impurity period have elapsed and the bones have been consecrated,
one should perform cremation again, having moved the rite forward from the previous ten-day period.
Starting from the eleventh day until the twelfth month, one should perform the sixteen śrāddhas; after that, for the mother, there is the subsequent rite.

"On the eleventh day, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha; if he does not perform it, he must undergo the rite of re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). Thus ends the determination of the duties for the tenth day in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination of the excellence of the rules for dying.
The excellence of the rules for dying is stated in the Mahābhārata:
"For one whose death occurs during the northern course of the sun (uttarāyaṇa), there shall be the highest destination."
"And at midday during the bright fortnight, or on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight as well. Mārkaṇḍeya also says:
"When the sun is in its northern course, it is said to be the most excellent time."
Death occurring there during the bright fortnight is excellent, and death during the day is auspicious.
[117] Even there, at midday, death during both fortnights is excellent;
on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī), death is most excellent, bestowing liberation and granting all desires.
If it is endowed with auspicious planets, yet joined by the Sun, Mars, and Saturn, and occurs in conjunction with three lunar mansions, that is a *triyoga* and a *tripuṣkara*.
"In that *tripuṣkara* yoga, death brings about another death. Thus says Garga:
"When [the Moon] is joined with Mars, the Sun, or Saturn, and is situated in a sign containing two, three, or four *pādas*..."
For those [deeds] performed with two [factors], it would be "two-puṣkara"; that which is performed with three [factors] is "three-puṣkara."
The twelfth lunar day conjoined with the Sun, the eleventh with Viśākhā and the Moon,
the twelfth with Mars, and the second with Śukra and Rohiṇī.
The third lunar day with Mercury and Mūla, the sixth with Jupiter and Śatabhiṣaj, and the seventh of Āṣāḍha with Saturn— these seven yogas are *tripuṣkara*.
In the Puṣkara yoga, when the five asterisms beginning with Dhaniṣṭhā are involved,
one who dies in Jyeṣṭhā during the Tripuṣkara yoga incurs the fault of being burned.
To avoid that fault, one should perform the gift of gold;
having touched the heart of the corpse, one should then do so by the side of the cremation fire.
"Having offered clarified butter into those sacrificial ladles, one should cast a piece of gold [into them].
If this propitiatory rite (śānti) is not performed, one quickly perishes as a result of that [omission]. Thus says Jyotiḥparāśara.
O auspicious lady, when the asterism is Tripāda and Venus, Mars, and Jupiter are present,
that ritual performed during the *maraṇa* and *dahana* [nakṣatras] shall become threefold in efficacy.
[118] “O auspicious lady, on a lunar mansion consisting of three stars (tripadakṣa), a gift of land should be made; on a weekday, a gift of gold;
and on a day presided over by a planetary deity, the gift of clothing is praised.
Thus ends the determination of the specific characteristics of the procedure for death in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, regarding impurity (*āśauca*),
here follows the determination of the time concerning impurity starting from the day of birth or death, as stated by Pāraskara:
"Whether it be by day or by night, so too for a birth or a death..."
The period of impurity beginning from that day is traditionally recorded as one night and three days.
Upon birth as well as upon death, purification lasts ten nights;
for a *bhū* it is twelve days, and for a *vaiśya* fifteen are prescribed.
For a Śūdra, the period is thirty days; for one who conducts himself righteously, it is half of that.

One should divide the night into three parts: two parts belong to the preceding day, and the remainder is to be taken as part of the following day. This same rule applies equally when a birth occurs or when a death takes place.
Regarding the cooking of a *sthālīpāka*:
"In the case of a miscarriage after midnight, or at birth, or even at death, one should take the preceding day as the time [for the rite]; so says the venerable Yama."
From sunrise until the next sunrise is designated as a "day";
those who know the Vedas understand that the period of impurity begins with that day.
If the dust is seen at night, one should divide the night into three parts;
if it occurs during the first two parts, [the purification is] as before, but if it occurs in the latter part, it is on the following day.
In the case of birth, death, and likewise in the event of a miscarriage,
if these occur before midnight, the same rules apply regarding impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka).

[119] The day itself must be taken as the time of occurrence; if it occurs after midday, it belongs to the following day. When birth, death, the appearance of menstrual blood, or ritual impurity (sūtaka) occurs during the night, the day itself must be taken until the sun has risen.
"One should divide the night into three parts: two parts belong to the preceding day,
and the final portion belongs to the following day, both for births and for deaths," so says Kāśyapa.
"If death or birth occurs before midnight, the previous day alone is to be taken; if it occurs after, it belongs to the following day. Thus says Vasiṣṭha.

"But when the menses appear for women after the sun has risen, that day on which birth or death occurs, its night [is also counted]. Thus, if menstruation, birth, or death occurs at night, one view is that the night should be divided into three parts; if it happens during the first two parts, it belongs to the preceding day itself. Another view is that if it occurs before midnight, it belongs to the preceding day. Yet another view is that if it occurs before sunrise, it belongs to the preceding day. Since the Smṛti texts are of equal authority, the determination in this matter depends on local custom.
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā, regarding the determination of time for impurity (āśauca),
[the author] now states those who are unworthy of the offering of water (udakadāna).

"Heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*), those who have not entered an order (*anāśrita*), thieves, those who kill their husbands, unchaste women, those who drink liquor, and those who commit suicide—these do not receive the period of impurity nor the water-offering.

[120] A heretic is one unworthy due to the insignia of a religion outside the Veda. One who has "not entered an order" (*anāśrita*) is one who, despite possessing the qualification for it, has not undertaken a specific stage of life (*āśrama*); that is to say, one who is without an order (*anāśramin*). A thief is a stealer of gold and so forth. One who kills her husband (*bhartṛghnī*) is a wife-killer. An unchaste woman (*kāmukā*) is an adulteress. One who drinks liquor (*surāpī*) is one addicted to drinking intoxicants. One who commits suicide (*ātmatyāginī*) is one who, out of desire, gives up her life by means of poison, hanging, and the like. (Manu).
The water libation shall be withheld from those born of illicit unions, from those who remain in the ascetic orders,
and from those who commit suicide.
"And for women who have resorted to heretical sects, those who act according to their lust, those who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor. Thus [it is said].

Regarding the wives of others, those born of unrighteousness are those born in vain from mixed unions (*saṃkara*). Renunciation (*pravrajyā*) is a way of life pursued by one's own will through exclusion from one's father and other kin. Likewise, Yama says:
For those born of void intermixture, for those who dwell within the boundaries of a hermitage,
and for those given in marriage to a maiden, the water-libation rite shall be discontinued.
Death from a Caṇḍāla, water, a serpent, a Brāhmaṇa, lightning,
as well as from fanged beasts and wild animals, awaits those of evil deeds.
Whatever water and offerings of rice balls are given to the departed spirits, none of it remains; it perishes in mid-air.
For those slain by the rod of Brahman, there shall be no impurity, no water libations, no cremation or other funeral rites,
and one should not carry their bier.
The "brahmadaṇḍa" is the curse of a Brahmin or a malevolent incantation (*abhicāra*). By the word *kaṭa*, items such as a litter used for carrying a corpse are designated. Āpastamba states:
"He who would kill himself by means of fire, water, or other such methods—for him no impurity (*āśauca*) is prescribed, nor is the water-libation rite (*udakakriyā*) to be performed."

Viṣṇu states: "Those who commit suicide do not undergo impurity nor are they entitled to the water libations. Gautama says: "For those killed by cattle or Brahmins, or by the king's wrath, or in battle, or by means of fasting, weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling [from a precipice], [impurity lasts] as long as the sight [of the body remains]. *Prāya* refers to the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*). *Anāśaka* refers to fasting. In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"He who dies while playing with horned animals, fanged beasts, clawed predators, serpents, poison, fire, or great waters—[which should be avoided from afar]..."
Those who acted unfavorably toward the Nāgas were burned by lightning,
as were those who were ever apprehended by the king on account of the crime of theft.
And those who, out of anger, abducted the wives of others were slain by their husbands;
as well as those who engaged in conflict with those of unequal status, with those of mixed caste, and with Caṇḍālas and the like.
Having done so, they were killed by them; likewise, out of anger, they resorted to outcasts and [met their end] through poison, fire, weapons, hanging, or water.
Those lowest of men who throw themselves from mountains, trees, or precipices;
those struck by the staff of a Brahmin's curse; and those who have been killed by Brahmins.
"Those who commit great sins (mahāpātakin) and those who have fallen from their caste (patita) are thus proclaimed.
For the fallen, there shall be no cremation, no period of impurity (āśauca), and no funeral rites (antyakarma).
Nor should there be the shedding of tears, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), or the performance of śrāddha and other such ceremonies. Thus it is said.

This prohibition of cremation by fire for those killed by *caṇḍālas* and others refers to the case of one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). Regarding the case of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), there would otherwise follow the lapse of the prescribed disposal (*pratipatti*) of the fires and sacrificial vessels, as it is ordained: "They cremate the *āhitāgni* with his fires and his sacrificial vessels" [122]. Furthermore, another *smṛti* text prescribes that for the fires and sacrificial vessels belonging to an *āhitāgni* killed by *caṇḍālas* and others, the ritual disposal must be performed until its completion: "One should cast the *vaitāna* (sacrificial) fires into water and the *āvasathya* fire at a crossroads; however, if the sacrificer is killed in vain, one should burn the vessels in fire."

"There is no ritual for those who have abandoned their own lives, nor for those who have fallen [from caste]. Nevertheless, it is held that even for them, [the rite] is accomplished by placing them in the waters of the Gaṅgā. Thus it is said in the Vahnipurāṇa.
And for those who have become heretics or outcasts, for one killed by Caṇḍālas and the like,
and for those who die intentionally [at the hands] of horned animals, fanged beasts, fire, serpents, and so forth;
One should not perform the cremation or the impurity rites; if they have already been performed, one should not attend to them.
Their bodies should be cast into the Ganges, the great river.
Having cast the fires of the deceased into water and the domestic fire at a crossroads,
one should burn the sacrificial vessels when there is contact with the dead.
Purification from bathing, ornaments, clothing, wealth, cutting a rope, or shedding tears is achieved through the Mahāsāntapana penance; knowledge is the purifier of what has been heated.
"But for intentionally eating [forbidden food], there is a Cāndrāyaṇa, a Parāka, or a Pādakṛcchra;
when each of these is performed, the Pādakṛcchra is the purification.
If it is done through ignorance, there should be a fast as well as a bath with one's clothes on. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, for all those who have committed suicide and the like, there is a prohibition against cremation, the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), and the *śrāddha* rites without distinction for up to one year. Once the year is complete, the son or other relatives should perform the *śrāddha* and other rites for the deceased. Thus it has been said: "Even for those who have abandoned their own lives by means of poison, hanging, weapons, and the like, or even through fasting, drowning, or falling into fire, [the rites are performed] without [waiting for] the prescribed time."
"One should perform the entire post-mortem rite (*aurdhvadaihika*) after one year.
Even after a year has passed, one should perform the *nārāyaṇabali* and then carry out [the rites]. And so Vyāsa says:
"For those who have died by an evil path, after a year has elapsed..."

"Having performed the Nārāyaṇabali, the twice-born man should perform the subsequent rites. Thus ends the determination of those ineligible for the offering of water in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the determination of the time for re-consecration (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*).
Whether it be a child or an elderly person, or when Venus has set,
one should avoid a pilgrimage to a new deity and the performance of funeral rites for the deceased.

Whether [the moon] be in its childhood or its old age, or when Venus has set, the rites for the deceased should not be performed; nor [should they be performed] when Jupiter and Venus are both eclipsed.
If the funeral rite has been performed at an improper time, it may be repeated;
provided that the cremation ceremony for the deceased is performed again within three fortnights.

No restriction regarding time should be observed, nor should there be concern for the "infancy" (mauḍhya) of Jupiter or Venus; one may perform the funeral rites (aurdhvadaihika) even at the time of the sapindikarana ceremony, for no defect such as the infancy of Jupiter or Venus exists in that context. [124]
This refers to the period of one year after death.
One should avoid the fourteenth lunar day (caturdaśī), the Nandā and Bhadrā tithis, the days of Venus and Saturn,
the inauspicious asterisms such as Tripuṣkara, and asterisms with two or three quarters.
From the latter half of the Vasu asterism (Uttaraphalgunī) through five [asterisms], and in the three-quartered asterism (Pūrvaphalgunī), the two Puṣkaras (Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā),
and in the asterisms of Pūṣan (Revatī) and Brahmā (Rohiṇī), there shall be the destruction of the family from fire.
In the latter half of that day, when the moon and stars are auspicious for the performer,
having first spoken of the cremation, the time for the *śrāddha* is now described.
Or at the end of three fortnights, or three months, or six months, or during the even fortnights;
on these very occasions, these sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites are also performed.

Furthermore, the rite of re-consecration (punar-saṃskāra) must certainly be performed without conflict with the proper time for the *śrāddha* offerings. Moreover: "The rite for the deceased should not be performed under the Kṛttikās, on a Nandā tithi, on a Friday, or during the three births [of Jupiter]; it would cause the destruction of the lineage."

One should consider all of this in the case of a single performance of the Mahālaya rite, a rite for a specific desire, a deficient Śrāddha, rites performed with new grains, and matters concerning the lapse of the prescribed time.
Thus concludes the determination of the time for re-consecration in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the procedure regarding the *pālāśa* [leaves];
on this point, another *smṛti* states:
If the bodies of one who has died in another country cannot be found,
one should fashion a substitute for them using the stalks of Palāśa leaves.
One should place forty-five on the head, ten on the neck,
thirty on the chest, and likewise twenty on the abdomen.
One should pay one hundred for the two arms, ten for the fingers of the arms,
six for the two testicles, and four for the penis alone.
One should give one hundred [beads] on the two thighs, fifty on the knees and shanks, and ten on the toes; one should bind them with a woolen thread.
"Having bathed and adorned him, one should fashion that form and perform its touching;
then a son, or a brother, or even another relative should offer it. Just as the cremation rite is performed, so should it be done by the wise. Thus [it is said].
Hārīta has also shown the number [of days] based on the count of palāśa stalks:
"When a Brahmin who has gone to another country dies due to the passage of time,
it would be as if his body were destroyed— especially in the case of one who maintains the sacred fires."
Then, having spread out a black antelope skin and likewise a human-shaped figure,
one should carefully arrange three hundred and sixty stalks of *palāśa* leaves.
One should give fifty on the head, and ten indeed on the neck;
one should give one hundred on the two arms, and ten indeed on the fingers.
One should strike thirty times on the chest, and likewise twenty on the abdomen;
one should strike eight times on the testicles and place five on the penis.
One should give one hundred [offerings] for the two thighs, thirty for the knees and shanks, and ten for the toes; this is the ritual procedure for the deceased.
The determination of the vessels, such as the *camasa* cups and others, is now being described.
Indeed, one employs all the vessels in their natural order.
One should cause the *dhruvā* ladle to be placed in the right hand, and the *sphya* and *juhū* to be set down;
one should throw the *upabhṛt* into the left hand, and place the *sruk*, *sruva*, and *araṇi* upon the chest.
One should place the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle in the mouth, the two *sruva* spoons in the nostrils,
two pieces of gold in the eyes, or one should place the two *sruk* ladles in the ears.
The *prāśitra* [portion] is [in the mouth]; the mortar is between the two jaws;
and likewise, the pestle is in the teeth—if there should be pressing-stones (*grāvan*) at that time.
Having set aside the skull-bowls, one should place a single bowl upon the forehead;
however, one should place the mortar for grinding flour upon the belly.
One should place the vessel for clarified butter at the navel, and having cut away the winnowing basket, place it on both sides;
and if one is performing the Sānnāyya offering, one should place the two Sānnāyya jars upon the two wings.
Then he should place a stone on the penis, and two grinding stones (dṛṣad-upala) on the testicles;
he should set a yoke-pin (śamyā) behind [the penis] from the position of the right foot.
"Having placed the vessel for the *agnihotra* and indeed that for the *anvāhārya* offering in the northern direction, one should place a *kūrca* (bundle of grass) upon the head;
this is the procedure to be performed again when the cremation and the funeral rites (*śavasamskāra*) are to be carried out."

The mention of the death of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for one who has not maintained them; and it has been stated by Kātyāyana:
"One who has maintained the sacred fires should be cremated according to rule with the three fires;
likewise, even one who has not maintained them [should be cremated] with his own domestic fire."

"One should place the oblation vessel at the site where the vessels are piled. [127] Thus it is said. Regarding the options for fewer or more [vessels] as stated by Parāśara, Gautama, and others, an option should be understood to apply to those who have maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and so forth, because there is no reason to establish a fixed number of *palāśa* stalks for them.
Thus ends the section on the *pālāśa* rite in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Regarding the subject matter of improper deaths for those who maintain the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*),
Pāraskara states the specific rule for one who has died an untimely death while maintaining the fires:
If a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires is killed by a Caṇḍāla, a Śvapāka, by cows,
or by other Brahmins, or even if he is drawn in by poison;
A Brahmin should burn that [deceased] Brahmin in the *lokāgni* fire, devoid of mantras.
Having taken the bones after they have been burnt, he should then wash them with milk.
He should burn them again according to the prescribed rule, using his own fire and independently.
According to the independent procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch, Hārīta states:
"When the death penalty has been incurred by a Brāhmaṇa, whether by the hand of a Caṇḍāla or by striking him with a weapon himself,
one should burn that twice-born man like a Śūdra."
Having taken the burnt bone again at the instruction of the Brahmins,
and having washed it with milk, one should cremate that bone as if it were that of a deceased person.
One should again perform the cremation with mantras according to the prescribed rule;
in this very same manner, one should carry out the rite for the death of one who is censured.
The son or other heir should perform three *prājāpatya* penances for the purification of the deceased;
having washed and bathed the body, he should cremate it according to the rites for the dead.
Having bound him with *kuśa* grass and *palāśa* leaves, and having covered him with a cloth,
one should carry him to the cremation ground and perform the collection of the vessels and other rites.
"According to the rule, the collection [of bones] is prescribed for relatives on the second day;

on the third, having offered water, one should perform the *śrāddha* on the fourth. This triad of *kṛcchra* penances refers to the case of a son who is utterly incapable [to perform the rites] due to the death occurring through negligence (*pramāda*). However, for one who is capable:
[Death] caused by a Brahmin, water, a snake, cattle, wild animals and the like,
by hanging, water, poison, snakes and so forth, or by [accidents involving] stones, weapons, or lightning;
In the case of death through negligence, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and three Taptakṛcchras;
alternatively, one may perform six Kṛcchras for six months, or give ten or five cows as a gift.

"One should perform the cremation according to rule, as well as the water-libation and the *śrāddha*. The ellipsis here is "the son or other [heir] having performed [these]. Because there would otherwise arise a contradiction with many statements concerning penance for such an untimely death, there is an option (*vikalpa*). For one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the period of impurity (*āśauca*) should be observed starting from the commencement of the funeral rites; for one who does not maintain the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), it starts from the moment of death. As it has been said: "For one without the sacred fires, [impurity lasts] until the departure [of the soul]; for one with the sacred fires, until the rite of consecration (*saṃskāra-karman*)."
"Purification [occurs] through collection [of the bones] after cremation, according to the rule from the day of death.

Because of the scriptural statement, "Of the sacramental rite for one who possesses the sacred fires," when a father who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) dies in another land, as long as the sacramental rite is performed according to the rule, there is absolutely no lapse of the *saṃdhyā* and other duties for the sons and others. By this statement, it should be understood that in the absence of cremation according to the rule for one who has maintained the sacred fires, there is no taking on of impurity (*āśauca*), because of the expression "starting from the cremation."
[129] For among the twice-born, impurity lasts until the departure of the breath for one who does not maintain a sacred fire;
however, for one who maintains a sacred fire, one should know it begins from the cremation when he has died in a foreign land.
Likewise: "As long as the funeral rites have not been performed according to the rules for one who has died while residing in a foreign land,
there is no lapse of the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) and other duties for the sons and others."
But for one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), if the cremation according to rule does not take place, there is no taking up of impurity;
rather, impurity is prescribed starting from the cremation.
Pāraskara also says:
"For one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), impurity is prescribed for ten days starting from the cremation;
however, when cremation occurs after death for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni), [the impurity is calculated] from the time of death."
If [the cremation] takes place while the period of impurity is still ongoing, one is purified by the remainder of that period;
but when the day of impurity has passed and the cremation occurs again, [one must observe the full period].
Purification after three nights is prescribed for one who has taken up [the Vedic study] when death occurs;
however, for a son who has not taken it up, the full period of impurity indeed applies.

"For twice-born men who have died an untimely death, whether within ten days or outside that period, there is neither impurity nor ritual defilement; having attained purity, one should cremate them. From that time forward, the water libation, the rice-ball offering (piṇḍa), the period of defilement, and the ancestral rite (śrāddha) [are to be performed]. Thus it is said.
Bṛhaspati:

If the cremation rite is performed again while a period of impurity is still ongoing, purification shall occur by means of the remainder of that very period; if [the rite] has already passed, there shall be *sūtaka* (birth-impurity).

[130] One should observe the period of impurity for parents according to their respective castes for ten days and so forth; it should be understood that the same applies mutually among co-wives and between husband and wife.
"Prajāpati has declared that for sapindas, the period of impurity shall be three nights. Thus says Vasiṣṭha:
"A son whose father has died should perform the funeral rites (aurdhvadehika)."
If one is unable to perform it, one should remain observant of the rules regarding ritual impurity.
Whether within ten days or after that period, when he is capable of performing the rite,
he should perform the *śrāddha* according to the rules after three nights have elapsed.

"This impurity belongs to the cremator; it does not exist for others. In the case of a lapse of time, even if it occurs earlier, it is equal [to the full period]. The meaning is that "earlier" refers to a time prior to the *sūtaka* (birth-impurity), and it is equal in duration to the remaining period of impurity. It should be understood that what was stated regarding co-wives and the mutual relationship between husband and wife applies specifically to cases where there are no sons. Thus says Parāśara.
One who has consumed food left over from above, food left over from below, or food from the intermediate space during a period of impurity,
as well as one who has participated in a funeral impurity, should perform three *kṛcchra* penances.
"When two causes [for suicide] have occurred, one should perform half of the *prājāpatya* penance;
and in all other such causes, one should perform even fifteen [such penances]. All else will be explained under the section on penances for self-destruction.
Thus, in the Smṛticandrikā,
[section 131]:
rules concerning the death of one who maintains the sacred fires when the date of death is unknown, and so forth.

Parāśara states what must be done when the date of death and so forth of one who has died in another country is unknown: "If a Brahmin who has gone to another country meets his death during his journey abroad, and his condition [the time of death] is not known..."
"On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, on the new moon day, and on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight—
one should perform the water libation, the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), and the śrāddha ceremony there."

It is understood that even the acceptance of impurity (*āśauca*) due to cremation is intended there, because on the three days beginning with the eighth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*), the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and water is impossible without such impurity. For one who has died in another country is of two kinds: one for whom the funeral rites have been performed (*kṛtasaṃskāra*) and one for whom they have not (*akṛtasaṃskāra*). The case of one for whom the rites have been performed will be discussed at the end of the section on impurity. One for whom the rites have not been performed is also of two kinds, distinguished by whether the day of death is known or unknown. For one whose day of death is known, the annual (*pratyābdika*) and other Śrāddha rites must be performed on that very day; however, on any other day, the cremation and the assumption of impurity take place. As for the offering of funeral cakes, water, and so forth, it should be performed after considering an unprohibited day, lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), weekday (*vāra*), and so on, because the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) proceed in this manner. Thus, it is stated in another Smṛti:
But upon the death of a great guru, one who observes a fast while wearing wet clothes must perform the funeral rites according to the rules, even if a year has passed.
Having undertaken the rules of impurity and the shaving of hair and beard,
one becomes pure through water according to the prescribed rite every day until the end of the ten-day period.
When the eleventh day has arrived, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite should take place;
for others, such as those preceded by brothers, there shall be water with sesame seeds at every Śrāddha.
[132] This [procedure] has been stated for one who has undergone the purificatory rites; now that for one who has not is being described.
The funeral rite (pretakarma) is recorded as being of two kinds: for one who is near and for one who is far away.
If the consecration (saṃskāra) takes place while one is nearby, one should not purify the day at all.
However, if the consecration is performed again during the period of impurity (āśauca), then the day must be purified;
for if the deceased is consecrated again, that day requires purification.

If one performs the rites for the deceased after a year has passed, the day must be selected only after careful purification; in that case, the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) is auspicious, as is the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), while one should avoid the three lunar stations (*tripada-ṛkṣaka*). Thus it is said.
Kātyāyana says: When the cremation of a corpse takes place in one's presence, one should not observe the period of impurity at all;
for if one were to wait for the prescribed time, the corpse would become putrid.
If one has been abandoned by sons, friends, or kinsmen, or if they have become estranged,
one should not even attempt to purify the lunar days (tithis) and other such factors for them, as it would bring great danger upon them.
Whether by day or by night, if the corpse remains anywhere, they say that it is "stale"; what is the procedure for its cremation?
Having established [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance;
likewise, having bathed it with cow-dung water when it is soaked or emits a foul odor.
Permitted by the Brahmins, he whose body is infested with worms or has been defiled by outcaste dog-cookers (śvapākas) should perform the Taptakṛcchra penance.
Having performed the bath as before with ghee and honey,
one should then sprinkle it with holy waters and subsequently drench it with fragrant water.
"Having given a cow to a preeminent brahmin, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
All of this will be explained in the section on penances for an untimely death (*durmaraṇa-prāyaścitta*).
Thus ends the section on the procedure for cases where the date of death and so forth are unknown, within the *Smṛticandrikā*.

Now follows the procedure for the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) at the conclusion of the period of impurity (*āśauca*). After the period of impurity has passed, the declaration of an auspicious day must be performed. Saṃvarta states:
Once the period of impurity has passed, one should perform the sweeping and plastering of the house;
having immersed oneself in water along with one's clothes, one becomes pure through the recitation of the *puṇyāha* formulas.
Vasiṣṭha also says:
"At the end of the period of impurity, the consecration of the Brāhmaṇa must be performed with the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, the water-mantras, and the Pāvamānī hymns."
"And having accepted the benedictions, one should then perform the śrāddha rite. Vyāsa also says:
"Having honored the Brāhmaṇas with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should cause them to pronounce the word 'svasti' (well-being)."
In a righteous act, in a resolve, in battle, or in the sight of a marvel.
"And for the sake of sacrifice, at the installation [of images], and in all purificatory rites,
one who desires purity, one who desires satisfaction, and one who constantly desires the highest good [should perform them]. Thus says Yama as well.
The recitation for the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) is prescribed in this manner for a Brāhmaṇa;
for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, one should perform this very same rite preceded by the syllable Oṃ three times.

[134] However, for Śūdras, one should perform the rite excluding the mantras, saying: "May it be an auspicious day (puṇyāha). For a Brāhmaṇa, there is an increase [in the ritual] through the utterance of the formula three times: "May there be prosperity (vṛddhi). Thus say Kāśyapa and Āpastamba: "In worldly rites for prosperity, at that time the formulas should be: 'An auspicious day!', 'Well-being!', and 'May there be success! All of this has been clearly set forth in the Gṛhyasūtra.
Thus ends the procedure for the recitation of the *puṇyāha* at the conclusion of the period of impurity (*āśauca*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite; regarding this, Marīci says:
"At the end of the period of impurity, one should then properly complete the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*);
there, the *śrāddha* must be offered—this is the rule for all castes.

Thus, after the period of impurity has passed, on the eleventh day, a Brāhmaṇa should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. The meaning is that this rule—"one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* on the eleventh day"—is the same for the Kṣatriya and other castes as well.

Now, one might ask: why should the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite not be performed for all castes immediately after the completion of the period of impurity (*āśauca*), since those such as Kṣatriyas and others who observe longer periods of impurity would lack purity on the eleventh day? For it is ordained that "a rite must be performed by one who is pure," thus establishing purity as an essential constituent of the ritual. If this is argued, [the answer is:
"When the impurity has departed, he should perform the sweeping and smearing of the house";
thus, the purification of the house occurs immediately after the period of impurity.

This is not so; for after introducing the topic generally with "At the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka), the declaration of a holy day (puṇyāhavācana) [should be performed]," Viṣṇu has specifically prescribed the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on the eleventh day. Likewise:
"Even one who is impure should perform the first *śrāddha* on the eleventh day;
for the performer there is temporary purity, yet he remains impure thereafter."
Thus, because of the statement of Śaṅkha and because of the prescription for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite on the eleventh day during the period of impurity (*āśauca*), [one might object]:
"But this is inconsistent;
for that *śrāddha* which is performed on the eleventh day is declared to be the general [rite]."
For all four castes, however, the period of birth-impurity is distinct for each.

This is its meaning: the *śrāddha* prescribed for the day immediately following the period of impurity (*āśauca*) is common to all four castes (*varṇas*), not to the Brāhmaṇa alone. If it is asked how, then, the term "eleventh day" (*ekādaśāha*) is applicable, [the answer is] that it is possible through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to refer to the day immediately following the period of impurity.

To this it is replied: The *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha qualified by the time of the eleventh day is prescribed for all four castes (*varṇas*). According to the maxim "in an injunction, the primary meaning of a word is not to be set aside," it is untenable to take the word "eleventh day" (*ekādaśāha*) figuratively as referring to the day immediately following the period of impurity (*āśauca*), because when the primary sense is possible, it is improper to assume an alternative mode of operation. Therefore, the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha must be performed on the eleventh day itself even by Kṣatriyas and the other castes.

If it is argued that on the eleventh day there is no entitlement to perform the *śrāddha* for Kṣatriyas and others because they lack purity, we say no; for there exists a temporary purity, according to the rule: "The performer has temporary purity. As for the claim that the intent of Śaṅkha’s statement—that one may perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* on the eleventh day even while impure when another period of impurity occurs during an existing one—refers to a specific case, that is not so; for the objection remains the same, namely that there is still an absence of purity even in that instance. Furthermore, there is no reason to restrict Śaṅkha’s general statement to a specific scope. And as for what was said—that since Viṣṇu prescribes the *ekoddiṣṭa* by beginning generally with the phrase "now, upon the cessation of impurity," the *ekoddiṣṭa* must be performed by everyone immediately after the period of impurity—that is not correct, because Viṣṇu’s statement is appropriately understood as referring specifically to Brāhmaṇas subject to the ten-day period of impurity. Therefore, it is well said that on the eleventh day, the *ekoddiṣṭa-śrāddha* must be performed even by Kṣatriyas and others. Vyāsa says:

"A wise man should perform two *ekoddiṣṭa* rites immediately after the period of impurity (*sūtaka*). Even if the impurity has already fallen away, he should not excessively delay the independent rite. Here, "independent" means other than the *navaśrāddha*; and the *navaśrāddha* consists of the two mixed with the new [rice]. And Gautama says:
One should feed a Brahmin at the first [offering], or otherwise, one should offer oblations into the fire;
then one should feed the Brahmin again, for it is said that there should be a double repetition.

The independent *ekoddiṣṭa* must indeed be performed even during a period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*). As for the statement, "In all *śrāddha* rites, however, the father comes first for both parents," that refers to all *śrāddhas* other than the independent *ekoddiṣṭa*, such as the *navamiśra* and others. Regarding the rule "on the eleventh day," any *navamiśra* and so forth other than the eleventh-day rite should be performed immediately after the obstacle is removed if an impediment of impurity occurs. Bṛhaspati has shown that there is a fault in neglecting the independent *ekoddiṣṭa* on the eleventh day.
"One should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha on the eleventh day;
if one does not perform it, one must undergo the rite again.
[137] Thus, since the first of the sixteen rites is prescribed for a different time on the eleventh day, it should not be performed if there is an interruption due to ritual impurity (*āśauca*).
"But if there should be an obstacle on the eleventh day for the first [rite],
it should be performed on the twelfth day or even on the twenty-third day."

On this eleventh day, the feeding of eleven Brahmins must be performed for the sake of the deceased. Regarding this, Satyavrata says: "On the eleventh day, having invited eleven Brahmins for the sake of the deceased and having fed them according to rule with various kinds of food, snacks, and savory dishes, one should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and give as sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) clothing, gold, a bronze vessel, sandals, an umbrella, and a water-pot to a virtuous Brahmin. In the absence of Brahmins, the rite should be performed in the fire. Thus says Kāśyapa: "When the *ekoddiṣṭa* ceremony has arrived and there is an absence of Brahmins, how should it be done?"
Having performed worship, one should offer milk-rice as an oblation into a well-kindled fire.
"With the *Pauruṣa* hymn, [the offering] is measured by thirty-two mouthfuls. Thus [it is said]. Vyāsa also says:
"On the eleventh day, one should give to eleven Brahmins."
"For that which is to be performed with reference to Rudra is indeed for the purpose of pleasing Rudra. Thus [it is said]. Its application is determined by local custom. And Śātātapa says:
"One should feed eleven Brahmins, intending them for Rudra."
"For the sake of the liberation of the state of a preta, [one should perform this] with those who consume honey, milk, and ghee.
Regarding another scope for this, Pracetas says:
"And when the ritual release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga) has been prescribed, but it cannot be obtained or the capacity is lacking..."
"For the sake of liberating the state of being a preta, one should feed eleven Rudras. Thus it is said.
Thus ends the procedure for the Ekoddiṣṭa rite in the Smṛticandrikā;
[138] now follows the procedure for the release of a bull (vṛṣotsarga).
On the eleventh day, the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) should be performed. Regarding this, the Purāṇa states:
"One should release a bull that is blue, red, or even black, provided it is available;
one who performs this does not see hell after death, whether he be a killer of cows or even a slayer of a Brahmin."
On the eleventh day after the death of a deceased person, his son or his brother’s son should release a dark-blue bull, or one of whatever color is available.
"Men who have committed great sins are liberated from the state of being a preta. Thus says Vyāsa:
"When the eleventh day has arrived, it is the means for the deceased to attain heaven."
"Having released one bull, one should feed the Brahmins at the *śrāddha*. Thus says Kāśyapa:
"Either a blue or a black [bull] on the eleventh day after the death [of the deceased]."
For the sake of purifying his sin, he [offered] a bull according to the instruction of the Rudras.
Whether he be a Brahmin, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or likewise a Śūdra, one should abandon that which is joined with fire-offerings (homa) and causes displeasure to Rudra.
One who dies without a bull goes to the Raurava hell, which is shrouded in darkness;
likewise, a woman who has sons and a husband goes there if she dies while her husband is still living.
By virtue of her devotion to her husband, she does not go to that world even if she is deprived of her husband;
[she destroys] the sin committed during seven lifetimes, whether in childhood or in old age.
[139] At the very moment of the release of the bull for the sake of his father, the impurity perishes;
once the period of impurity has passed, the son [should release] a decorated blue bull.
"Intending it for the ancestors, one should perform the rite of oblation (homa) dedicated to Rudra;
then, by relinquishing [the merit], the human being goes to the world of Rudra.
As for that statement:
If a woman who has sons dies before her two [husbands], one should not release a bull for her; rather, one should release a single cow.

Thus, the injunction "he should release a bull and a cow" applies to one who is capable. One who is incapable, or one whose husband and sons are living, should perform only the rite of releasing the bull (*vṛṣotsarga*). Vyāsa states:

"A devoted wife (*pativratā*), one who has male relatives (*bandhumatī*), one who has a daughter (*putrikī*), or one who is fortunate (*subhagā*)—if she dies, she shall not release a single bull; rather, she should release a bull together with a cow."
Vasiṣṭha says: "If the bull is not released when the eleventh day has arrived,
his state as a piśāca remains fixed, even by hundreds of performed śrāddhas."
Lokākṣi says:
On the eleventh day, one should diligently perform the rite of releasing a bull,
even if a woman who has sons and a husband should die before both [the husband and son].
"That one should not release a bull for her" is improper;
a husband should never perform the rite of releasing a bull on behalf of his wife.
If the performer himself is present, or if she is childless,
another person may perform the cremation and other rites, such as the *śrāddha*, by his authorization.
If, out of delusion, one should perform [the śrāddha] excluding Vṛṣa, the Rudras, and the Vasus until the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite,
it would cause the destruction of the lineage.

"If the one who performs the consecration (*saṃskartā*) should be the son, he shall release a dark-blue bull. Now, the mention of "the son" refers to the son of a brother. The characteristics of the dark-blue bull have been stated by Śātātapa:
"He who is red in color, but white in the face and the tail..."
That bull which is white in its hooves and horns is called "blue" (nīla).
One should have a trident, a discus, or another such mark made for him;
whichever deity a person is devoted to, he should have that deity's emblem made.
One who desires heaven should perform the release of a bull according to the Nāndīmukha rite for the sake of liberation from the state of a preta, or worship Rudra in the form of a Vṛddhi ceremony.
"One should feed eight Brahmins with gold or water"—
this refers to the occasion of performing the *vṛṣotsarga* (the rite of releasing a bull) again at a later time for the sake of pleasing the ancestors.
Thus ends the procedure for the release of a bull in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Herein is the exposition of the sixteen *śrāddhas*:
the twelve monthly rites, as well as the *ūnaṣāṇmāsika* (the six-monthly rite performed before the completion of six months).
The three-pakṣika, the less-than-yearly, and likewise the less-than-monthly.
And likewise the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa; thus are the sixteen śrāddhas:
on the eleventh day, at one month, at the "deficient" (ūna) [fortnight], at the first [sixth], and similarly at the last.
[141] For men who have abandoned their bodies, one should offer sixteen *śrāddhas*: one each month for a year, and those belonging to the three-fortnight period.
In the fourth, the fifth, as well as the ninth and the eleventh months—
there, with twelve months having elapsed, one should perform the Śrāddha twelve times.
This must be done according to the sacred tradition; therein, one should also gratify the Brahmins with libations.
Gālava says: An *ūna-ṣāṇmāsika* [śrāddha] is performed in the sixth month even if it is deficient; an *ūna-māsika* is performed when one month is deficient;
a *traipakṣika* occurs at the end of three fortnights, provided an odd-numbered day has passed.
"Every month on the anniversary of death, and also the *nyūnābdika* (the deficient annual rite)—thus [there are] sixteen. Bhṛgu also says:
"The first [śrāddha] should be on the eleventh day; the *nyūnamāsika* (monthly deficient rite) on the twelfth day."
It may occur after one, two, or three days, or even when a third part remains.
"Likewise, there should be the *ūnābdika* (the annual rite performed before a year has passed), as well as the *ūnaṣāṇmāsika* (the six-month rite performed before six months have passed).

The *traipakṣika* (three-fortnightly rite) should be performed at the end of three fortnights; however, the others [the monthly rites] are to be performed on the anniversary of the day of death. Thus says Aṅgiras.
In the eleventh month, the first [monthly rite] should be performed; if the month is deficient, it is the *ūnamāsika*.
The *traipakṣika* (three-fortnightly rite) occurs at the third fortnight, and on an odd day thereafter.
"Likewise, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed on the anniversary of death when less than five years have passed; however, the others [the sixteen *śrāddhas*] must be performed.

When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed before the completion of a year—on the twelfth day or other such occasions—it must be done only after having offered the sixteen *śrāddhas* on the eleventh day and so forth. Regarding this, Dakṣa says:
"Having performed the sixteen *śrāddhas*, one should perform the *sapiṇḍana*."
Paiṭhīnasi says:
One should perform the sixteen Śrāddhas prior to the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa;
without having offered the sixteen Śrāddhas, one must not perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa at all.

"When the son performs the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the twelfth day, he should perform all sixteen *śrāddhas* at midday. When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed after having offered the *śrāddhas* on the third fortnight (*tripakṣa*) and so forth, there is no re-performance of those monthly rites that occurred prior to it, because they were already performed at their proper time. However, there is a re-performance only of those monthly rites occurring subsequent to it. Thus said Gālava:
If one desires to perform the *sāpiṇḍya* rite at times such as three fortnights and so forth,
there must be a repetition of the monthly rites for the learned (*śiṣṭas*) according to their proper time.
"In the eleventh [year], however, there is a re-performance of those rites performed [previously] according to the proper time;
one should perform those very same rites again at their respective times according to the rule.
Regarding this very point, Gālava states a specific detail:
"Before the three fortnights for one who maintains the sacred fires, it should be on the day of the funeral rites;
after that, for one without fires, all [rites] are performed from the day of death. Thus says Jātūkarṇya.
"Whatever *śrāddha* is performed after three fortnights should take place on the anniversary of the day of death;
however, for a twice-born who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), one should perform it before the cremation.
Thus Prajāpati states the rule for the monthly *śrāddhas* occurring after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.

Starting from the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, one should perform the monthly *navaśrāddha* (the "new" offerings) on the tenth or eleventh day, or even on the third day if it is deficient; indeed, the monthly rites must be performed.
In the three fortnights— the twelfth, the twenty-fourth,
and having made the fifteen [fortnights]— one should proceed in order through the end, middle, and beginning.
If [the period] is deficient by one month, it is indeed "deficient-monthly" (ūnamāsika);
some say that if a third part of the month remains, one should perform [the rite].
Regarding the three-pakṣa rite: when the three pakṣas have elapsed, on the odd day—the eleventh—it shall be the first; such is the determination for the monthly rites.
The meaning is "after ten days.
One should perform the first [Śrāddha] on the eleventh day after the end of the period of impurity,
or on the twenty-third day, or even on the twenty-seventh day.
If it should be deficient by three fortnights, one should perform the rite at the end of the fortnight on an odd day;
likewise, if it is deficient by six months or a year, one should act according to the analogy.
"Indeed, on the anniversary days of death each month, the monthly rites (māsika) are performed subsequently.
Gautama states that after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, there is an abridgment (*apakarṣa*) of the monthly rites:
"The rites for the consecration of the deceased consist of sixteen *śrāddhas*."
But when actions are performed at the proper time, one is not released from their consequences otherwise.
Due to irregularities in place, time, and other factors, or out of fear of death, disease, and the like,
the sixteen rites should indeed be performed on the eleventh day, even if they have been postponed.

"Furthermore, one may perform even those sixteen *śrāddhas* whose times and duties have been specified, having postponed them during a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, on the anniversary of the deceased's death. Thus says Śāṭyāyani.
"Even those [rites] performed by anticipation prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* are again brought forward,
because of the prohibition against performing them after a *vṛddhi* [rite]. Thus says Viṣṇu.
A twice-born performer of the rite may even perform all the śrāddhas for deceased ancestors after the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa by drawing them forward into the nāndīmukha ceremony.
But the performer who conducts the ancestral rites for the deceased without the prescribed increase [of offerings] sinks into a terrible hell together with his ancestors.
He who performs the monthly rites after having completed the Vṛddhi-tantra will undoubtedly meet with untimely death.
"But he who, being devoid of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* and other [auspicious rites], brings forward the *śrāddhas*, that performer of *śrāddhas* sinks into a terrible hell along with his ancestors.
The meaning is that one should not bring forward the *preta-śrāddha* when the *vṛddhi* has not yet arrived. Thus says Pracetas.
One should perform the sixteen śrāddhas here on the eleventh day;
however, one should diligently perform the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa on the twelfth day.
One should perform all the monthly rites at their proper times;
or, when the Vṛddhi-śrāddha is imminent, one may even perform them prematurely.

"One should not perform it on one's birth-star (janmarkṣa), nor on the Nandā tithis, nor on a day belonging to Venus; nor on a Sunday or a Tuesday; however, there is no fault if it is performed on the day of death. Thus says Śātātapa.
Even by drawing forward the monthly rites, one should perform them on the anniversary of that person's death,
as well as during the Tripuṣkara yoga, on the Nandā tithis, on the new moon day, and on the day of Venus.

"One should not perform [the rite] on the fourteenth day, nor during the three deficient [periods], nor under the asterism of Agni (Kṛttikā). Thus says Dakṣa: "Nor on the Tripuṣkara days, nor on the Nandās, nor on Sinīvālī, nor on the day of Bhṛgu (Saturday)."
"And on the fourteenth day, they are not deficient during Kṛttikā and Tripuṣkara. Thus says Viṣṇu:
"And on the Sinīvālī day, they are not deficient during Kṛttikā and Puṣkara."

Before the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, one should perform the monthly (*māsika*) offerings according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure. After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, for the wives of brothers and others, the monthly rites are performed solely by the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure; however, for the mother, father, and elder brothers, they are performed solely by the *pārvaṇa* procedure. As Dakṣa has said: "For wives, brothers, and paternal uncles, after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the performance of the monthly rites is again according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure."
"The rite for fathers, mothers, elder brothers, and others is performed again by means of the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha]. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
"Those sixteen śrāddhas which take place prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*..."
For one should perform those śrāddhas according to the procedure for the ekoddiṣṭa.
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, whenever one performs [the annual rites], one should perform them again;
whatever manner one performed [the rites] for each year, in that same manner one should perform even those already completed."

Just as a son or other descendant should perform the annual *pārvaṇa* rite for his father and others, so too should he perform the monthly rites (*māsika*) after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Just as one should perform the annual rite for younger brothers, sons, wives, teachers, and others according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure, so too should he perform the monthly rites after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*; this is the meaning. It was stated previously that the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha is to be performed in the afternoon. Regarding the three types of *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, Manu states that when there is a conflict of lunar dates (*tithi-dvaidha*), it should be performed at midday.
One should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite at midday, as well as the *navaśrāddha* and other such rites;
however, it must never be performed during the twilight (*saṃdhyā*) nor at night.

According to such statements, for one who has died here, the *navaśrāddha* and the covering of the naked (*nagnapracchādana*) should not be performed immediately after cremation; rather, they should be performed on the following day at midday.

"The *tilodaka*, the *piṇḍa*, and likewise the ninth [rite], the covering of the naked—one should not perform these at night, nor if one performs them during the twilight (*saṃdhyā*), it is fruitless."

And from the words of Jātūkarṇi: "In the case of the sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites known as 'mixed with nine' (*navamiśra*), when there is doubt regarding the lunar day (*tithi*)—as to whether it should be one that extends into the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) or one that extends into the evening (*sāyāhna*)—generally, the lunar day extending into the evening is to be accepted; however, for the sake of the ancestors (*pitṛ-artha*), it should be one belonging to the afternoon. "The lunar days belonging to the afternoon bring auspiciousness for the sake of the ancestors;
for the ancestors, the afternoon is [their time], so [the rite] should follow that which extends into the afternoon."
"She should be accepted for the ancestral rites (pitṛkārya), but not one that follows after the forenoon. Thus says Vṛddhamanu:
"The ancestors wait upon that [day] in which the sun sets."

"For the lunar days (tithis) were assigned to them by the Self-Existent One as the afternoon. [147] Thus, the general scripture is also considered "general" because it functions by depending solely upon the basic rule (*vidhi*). The afternoon consists of three *muhūrtas* and extends until sunset. The triad of alternatives does not concern the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite specifically, as it functions by depending upon the general rules for ancestral rites (*pitryakarman*). Regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa* Śrāddha, the alternative of that which extends through midday is based on a specific scriptural injunction (*vācanika*). As stated in the *Śivarāghava-saṃvāda*: "That lunar day which extends through midday shall be the one used for the *ekoddiṣṭa*."
"In the case of the *pārvaṇa* [rite], that lunar day (*tithi*) which extends through the afternoon shall be the one used. Thus say Hārīta and Śātātapa. Furthermore:
"The *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with raw food) is performed in the forenoon, while the *ekoddiṣṭa* (rite for a single ancestor) is performed at midday."
The Pārvaṇa rite should take place in the afternoon, while the rite occasioned by prosperity (vṛddhi) should be performed in the morning.

"That śrāddha which is prescribed for a single person and is devoid of the rite for the gods (daiva) is called ekoddiṣṭa; it is proclaimed to be performed at midday. This midday, known as the *gāndharva*, *kutapa*, and *rohiṇa* periods, consists of three muhūrtas. At its commencement, the preceding and succeeding portions of the *kutapa* are optionally chosen according to one's preference. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"One who is self-restrained should commence the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite during the first part of the *kūṭapa*, or near the time of sunset, at that very same time.
Regarding the time of completion, Gautama says:
A wise man, knowing the rule, should perform the *śrāddha* beginning at the *kutapa* hour and extending to the *rauhiṇa*; having established the ritual procedure, he must not let the *rauhiṇa* pass.

When the time overlaps with the *gāndharva* muhūrta in both cases, the one overlapping the preceding [muhūrta] is to be taken, for it is the former because it extends through the evening until sunset. By the force of the general rule, when it occupies three muhūrtas in both cases, the former alone is to be taken, just as in the determination regarding the general afternoon (*aparāhṇa*).
Thus concludes the determination of the sixteen *śrāddhas* and other rites in the *Smṛticandrikā*.

Now, the times for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*: Regarding this, Āśvalāyana states: "Now, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed when a year has elapsed, or on the twelfth day. Kātyāyana states: "Now, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed when a year has elapsed, or on the twelfth day, or in the third fortnight. Baudhāyana states: "Now, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed when a year has elapsed, or in the third fortnight, or in the third month, or on the twelfth day, or on the eleventh day. Vyāsa [states as follows].
One must not perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite without having first offered the sixteen *śrāddhas*;
for as long as the deceased has not been made a *sapiṇḍa*, the status of being an ancestor (*pitṛtva*) does not arise.

For a son who has not been formally adopted, no auspicious merit whatsoever exists; nor does he possess any incidental merit, nor that resulting from optional rites, nor the fruits of sacrifices (iṣṭa) or charitable works (pūrta), and so forth.
The *śrāddha* for parents and others is not performed until after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been completed;
it may be performed on the eleventh, the twelfth, or even the twenty-third day.
"Or after three fortnights, or after three months, or on the sixth or even the eleventh day. Thus says Gautama:
"On the eleventh or twelfth day, or after three fortnights, or after three months."
In the sixth or eleventh year, or when the [year] is complete and an auspicious occasion has arrived.
"These eight times for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite have been proclaimed:
when the performer possesses the sacred fires (*sāgni*), both the first [times] apply; when the deceased possesses the sacred fires, the one immediately following [the first];
but for one without sacred fires (*anagni*), the seven times beginning with the second have been declared. Thus it is said.
Regarding this, Hārīta states the purpose of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the eleventh day:
"If the new moon preceding the day of death should fall on the tenth day,
the son who maintains the sacred fires must indeed perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on that [new moon]."
The meaning is: when, counting from the day after the death onwards, the eleventh day falls on the new moon (amāvāsyā), it is on that day [the rite should be performed]. Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
"The first [such] new moon should be on the tenth day from the day of death;
on that occasion, a son who maintains the sacred fires must certainly perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa."
The ablative case in "mṛtāhāt" is used in the sense of a limit (maryādā); the meaning is "starting from the day after the anniversary of death. Kārṣṇāgni also says:
"A son who maintains the sacred fires should perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite as before, provided it is after ten nights have passed, on the new moon day, or at another time within the year."

If the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed on the eleventh day, then having offered the nine *śrāddhas* and other rites that precede the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* in the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* at midday (*madhyāhna*) and perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). Regarding this, Satyavrata says:
"One performing [the rite] on the eleventh day should perform everything in the forenoon;
and one should perform the *sāpiṇḍya* at midday—so said Śāṇḍila. [150] Thus.
Bhṛgu says: But if the new moon that precedes the anniversary of death falls on the tenth day,
the son who maintains the sacred fires should certainly perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on that occasion.
"Furthermore, without *sāpiṇḍya*, a son may not perform the *pitṛyajña*;
nor does one who performs neither the *pārvaṇa* nor the *abhyudaya* [śrāddha] obtain the fruit thereof. Thus says Devala.

"Once the deceased has reached the status of a paternal ancestor (*paitṛka-pada*) through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the *pitṛyajña* for one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) proceeds on the day of the *sinīvālī* (the new moon). Thus, when the new moon occurs on the twelfth day from the anniversary of the death of the father who was consecrated for a sacrifice (*dīkṣita*), one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the eleventh day and then perform the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* on the afternoon of that new moon day. So says Jābāli.
In the case of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rites performed at times such as the twelfth day,
these rules regarding the presence or absence of the sacred fire shall indeed act as restrictive injunctions.

"One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the eleventh day; if the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurs on the twelfth, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and then undertake the *pitṛyajña*. Thus, in cases other than the eleventh or twelfth day or the new moon, whether one possesses the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) or does not (*anagnika*), one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* during the seven periods beginning with the twelfth day. And so says Pracetas:
On the eleventh day, one who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite;
on the twelfth day or other such occasions, it may be performed by one who maintains the fires or even by one who does not.
"Having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, one should perform the rites of the new moon (*dārśika*).
[151] Regarding this, a specific rule is shown in the *Mahābhārata*:
"O hero, when a householder has no sacred fire (*anagni*), he should then perform it [the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*]."
If the deceased is a *preta* who possesses fire, the *sapiṇḍana* rite should be performed on the twelfth day.
O King, the sacrificer shall possess the sacred fires, while the deceased shall be without them;
this occurs on the eleventh or twelfth day, or after three fortnights, or after three months.
