If that [rite] has been omitted through negligence on the twenty-third day, or even after six months or a year,
it should be performed on the twelfth or eleventh day.
"One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the father on the twenty-third day,
provided that the *sapiṇḍana* has not already been performed on the twelfth or eleventh day;
however, one should perform it at a later time as circumstances permit."

The householder is the performer of the *śrāddha*. Garga says: "Furthermore, if the *sapiṇḍana* is not performed during the twelfth day due to an emergency, one should perform it on the thirteenth day or even on the twenty-third day."
Bṛhaspati: When the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite is to be performed at times such as the twelfth day and so forth,
one should carry it out after having carefully determined an auspicious lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
Regarding the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, the great seers have declared three constellations:
Prājāpatya, Raudra, and that which has Saumya as its deity.
"Or even without the *tripādārka* asterism, excluding the Sun, Mars, and Saturn;
or the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* may take place on the day following the monthly anniversary. Thus says Aṅgiras.
"Regarding the *sapiṇḍana* for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras,
a period of twelve days is recommended, because it serves as the cause for the performer's own infinite [merit]. Thus says Vyāsa.
"Because family customs are infinite, because the lifespan of men is subject to decay,
and because the body is unstable, the twelve-day period is recommended. Thus says Vṛddha-Manu.
"On the twelfth day for Brahmins, at the end of the period of impurity for kings,
or after three fortnights for Vaiśyas— then the *sapiṇḍana* rite should take place. Thus says Prajāpati.
The Sapiṇḍana ceremony for Brahmins should take place on the eleventh day or the twelfth day;
for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, it should take place at the end of the period of impurity.
"For Śūdras, purification for the performer occurs at the twelfth day itself. Thus says Saṃvarta:
"For Brahmins, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite should take place on the twelfth day."
For Śūdras, it should take place on the twelfth day, or it may occur at the end of the period of impurity.
One may perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite for virtuous Śūdras even during a period of impurity;
for the performer there is temporary purity, yet impurity indeed persists thereafter.
For Śūdras who have fallen away from their own dharma,
the Sapiṇḍana rite may take place in the sixth month, at the end of the year, or after three fortnights, and so forth.
"Delighting in his wife, pure, a supporter of his dependents, and devoted to the performance of *śrāddha* rites—
one should perform the *sapiṇḍana* on the twelfth day at the end of the period of impurity.
Thus says Āpastamba.
For Śūdras and those of low birth, the Sapiṇḍana rite should not be performed with cooked food at the end of the period of impurity;
rather, one should perform the Śrāddha with uncooked food.
Or, being composed, he should perform the *sāpiṇḍya* offering with meat, barley, wheat, or rice, using cooked food alone, beginning with the ancestors.
"One should join the *piṇḍa* for the deceased by name to the three ancestors, beginning with the father.
Thus [ends the section] on the times for *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the time for the re-performance of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
In this regard, Kāśyapa says: "For those who have died out of the natural order [of seniority], the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is prescribed;
if one dies later after [the others] have already passed away, one should perform the *sapiṇḍana* again."
Dakṣa says: When a son performs the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite while bypassing his living grandfather,
or even when bypassing both, [he incurs a fault].
"When both of them have passed away, one should perform the *sapiṇḍana* again at the proper time. Thus says Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:
"Even if the order is inverted, the *sāpiṇḍya* must be performed; this is the consensus of the sages."
Even in that case, once the sapinda-relationship for the elder has been established, one should perform it again for this [younger] person.
Whether it be a legitimate son of the body or one born of the wife, such is the eternal law:
one should not have the funeral rites performed by others while a living son is available.
A brother, or a brother’s son, a sapinda, or even a disciple,
should always perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for one who is childless.
"Alternatively, the wife of the deceased may perform [the rite] without mantras;
or she may have it performed by a priest, or even perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* again. Thus says Prajāpati.
The son alone should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his parents;
or alternatively, it may be performed by a disciple, a fellow student, a servant, or a family priest.
"One should perform [the rites] for up to ten days, excluding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*," so says Gālava:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha must be performed by the sons, and not by others."
"One should have the cremation and other rites performed by secondary sons until the end of the tenth day.
Regarding this, a specific rule has been shown by Gautama:
"Whether it be an elder brother, a younger brother, a *sapiṇḍa*, or even a *sodaka*..."
The son should perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, or [the father himself] when an occasion for prosperity has arisen.
If one should undertake a *vṛddhi-śrāddha* while omitting the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*,
there is no doubt that his death will occur before its time has passed.

"He who is devoid of the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, though he has sons, sinks into a terrible hell along with his ancestors after performing the *sapiṇḍana*. (155) Thus, when a *vṛddhi* occasion has arisen, the son should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* separately again, even if it has already been performed by the brothers, *sapiṇḍas*, *sodakas*, and others. Likewise:

"Whether he be the elder brother or the younger brother, even if he has not inherited the property, the nine *śrāddhas* and the sixteen [monthly *śrāddhas*] shall be considered as performed by all [the brothers] together. Thus says Viṣṇu.
Whether he be the eldest or the youngest, a sapinda or even a sodaka—
whosoever is present has the right to perform the sapindikarana rite.

"Furthermore, they may perform [the rites] as before for the sake of establishing his entitlement to the ancestral offerings (lepabhāktva), or for the sake of establishing his eligibility for the Śrāddha; thus he is even released from the state of being a preta. Thus says Āpastamba.
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a father may at any time be performed by his relatives;
once he is liberated from the state of being a *preta*, they should perform the *sapiṇḍana* again.
As for that which Yama says:
A son residing in another country, upon hearing of his father’s demise,
shall immediately perform the shaving of the head and offer water with sesame seeds until the end of the ten-day period.
One should perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha on the eleventh day.
Thus [it is said]; that refers to the case of an elder brother. Śātātapa says:

Whether it be an elder or a younger brother, upon hearing of the death of his parents in another land, he should have his hair and other [body hair] shaved and then immerse himself in water along with his clothes.
Upon hearing [of the death], one should not take food nor engage in sexual intercourse;
at the end of ten days, the younger brother should respectfully perform the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha.
"The eldest son shall perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* again, even if it has already been performed. Thus says Vṛddha-Śātātapa:
"Whether the elder or the younger brother, [should encounter] the death of the parents in another country..."
Having heard [the news] and having shaved his hair, he should perform a bath with his clothes on.
"For ten days, however, one should remain celibate and offer water with sesame seeds;
and one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, provided it has not already been performed by another," so says Gautama.
If the elder brother is residing in another country when the younger brother performs the Śrāddha,
the son must perform the Śrāddha again and carry out the Sāpiṇḍya ceremony as before.
One should announce, "I shall perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha. In place of the word "upatiṣṭhatu" (may it attend), one should employ the word "svadhā.
This is done with reference to the deceased father, following the procedure of a portion of the *pārvaṇa* rite. Thus it is said.
Śātātapa says: "When the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha has not been performed by the eldest brother,
that eldest brother must perform it again once the joining of the rice-balls (piṇḍasaṃyojana) has been completed."
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha states:
When the Śrāddha has been performed by a younger brother, the elder brother must perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa again, omitting the word "preta."
One should perform the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa Śrāddha preceded by the rites for the gods;
there, one should feed the ancestors alone, yet designate the deceased once again.
Even the youngest son, though residing in a foreign land, upon hearing of his father's demise,
should perform the Pārvaṇa Śrāddha after ten days have elapsed.
The Śrāddha rite called Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa should be performed like the Pārvaṇa; one should perform the joining of the arghya water as well as the joining of the piṇḍas.
"But once he is liberated from the state of a *preta*, one should no longer designate him as a *preta*.
Gautama says that all [other] rites should be performed without the word 'preta'. Thus says Gālava.
The *navaśrāddha*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and the sixteen other *śrāddhas* should be performed by only one person, even among those who have divided their wealth.
"After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, every year on the anniversary of death, the sons must perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* separately for their mother and father. Thus says Gautama.
"Whatever has been done by the eldest alone, with the consent of all,
or with undivided wealth, shall be considered as done by all.
A specific detail regarding this matter has been shown by Bṛhaspati:
All sons, if the eldest son does not perform it, should separately perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for their parents according to the ritual procedure of the *pitṛyajña*.
"The rite performed by the elder brother cannot be performed again by the younger brother"—
so says Lokākṣi.
Whether the estate is divided or undivided, the *sapiṇḍana* for the mother and father [is to be performed].
If the younger brother should act in some way, the elder brother should act even more so.
"The established rule is that among the piṇḍas for the father, grandfather, and so forth, the mother's piṇḍa is included.
Thus ends the section on the time for the *punaḥ-sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.

Now follows the procedure for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. Regarding this, Pracetas states: "For one's own father who has become a *preta*, [the rite] is performed according to the rules of the *ekoddiṣṭa*."
For these ancestors, beginning with the grandfather, one should perform the rite according to the pārvaṇa procedure.
"For two *śrāddhas* must indeed be performed; that [second] is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Thus says Viṣṇu:
"One should perform [the rite] on the twelfth day starting from the father's death."
This is indeed the gateway for the liberation of the deceased father from the state of being a preta.
In order to establish the sapinda relationship with the grandfather and others,
and for the sake of establishing the status of being a *samānodaka* (distant kinsman), the son [performs the rite] for his father.

For these ancestors, beginning with the grandfather, one should perform the rite according to the *pārvaṇa* method; however, for one's own father who has become a *preta*, it should be done according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure.
Thus, the *sapiṇḍana* rite possesses the dual nature of both the *pārvaṇa* and the *ekoddiṣṭa*; indeed, *kāma* and *kāla* are specified for the *vaiśvadeva* portion.

Having indicated the grandfather and the others, one should then utter the name of the father; thereafter, one should proclaim the relationship, the lineage, the personal names, and the Vasus and other deities.
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha is declared to begin with the ancestors (*pitṛ*);
some say it begins with the deceased (*preta*), but that which has been stated is incorrect.
Having performed the worship of the Viśvedevas, the worship of the deceased (preta-pūjana) follows immediately;
for within the ritual procedure (tantra) of the Pārvaṇa rite, there occurs another intermediate ritual procedure.
Alternatively, one may construct three pits or three mandalas;
those for the deities are in the north, while those for the ancestors are in the middle.
[159] On the right side, however, follows the sequence for washing the feet:
first, having worshipped the gods facing east, one then worships the ancestors facing north.
Recalling the prescribed ritual, one should prepare four vessels containing sesame seeds, perfumes, and other offerings, for the deceased who is seated facing west.
One should place [the offerings] there first for the father, then for the grandfather,
then for the great-grandfather as the deity, and finally the highest one for the sake of the deceased.
One should offer water from a portion of the vessel to them in due order,
as well as perfumes, flowers, incense, a lamp, clothing, and so forth.
Having given according to the extent of his wealth, he should feed the Brahmins;
even at the occasion of an Ekoddiṣṭa rite, whatever [is prescribed], such as the invocation (āvāhana) and so forth, [should be performed].
One should employ the word *svadhā*, incense, lamps, and the word *namaḥ*.
In the *piṇḍa* rite (*sapiṇḍana*), one should employ the invocation (*āvāhana*), the word *svadhā*, incense, and lamps.
One should certainly not perform it in the place of prostration;
rather, this [rite] should take place after offering two oblations of *caru* either into the hand of a Brahmin or into the fire.
Having removed the embers from the fire, one should offer food with the mantra "Svāhā" to the deceased and to Yama, having uttered his lineage name and personal name.
Or else, having offered into the hand of the preta at the end of the meal, one should announce the names of the ancestors and so forth in due order, saying, "This [is for] such-and-such."
Finally, saying, "O Yajñaśarman, may this *piṇḍa* attend you," he should offer the fourth *piṇḍa* for the deceased with his right hand.
Then, one should bring the water contained in the vessel for the *preta*s for the sake of the ancestors and others,
using these two verses beginning with "samānaḥ" and "mantraḥ" in their respective order.
Having taken the preta-piṇḍa with the Madhu-mantra and divided it into three parts,
one should join them to the piṇḍas of the ancestors with the two verses beginning with "saṃgacchadhvam."
The offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) is prescribed with the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," following the joining of the rice-balls, due to the cessation of the state of being a preta.
In all instances such as the *mārjana* and others, the fourth [paternal ancestor] is excluded;
the word "father" (*pitṛ*) alone, however, denotes the paternal ancestors in general.
"One should infer the relationship with the grandfather and others from the mantras, the *sūtras*, and so forth.

When the elder brother resides in another country and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, one should perform the *sapiṇḍana* in this very manner, omitting the word 'preta' (the deceased). Thus it is said.
As for the statement of Kātyāyana:
"Once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, separate status is no longer possible;
but if separation has already been effected, then [after death] there is again *sapiṇḍatā* with the ancestors."
Thus, as for the statement:
"He who should offer a separate rice-ball to a deceased person for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed,
he becomes a destroyer of the ritual injunction and is regarded as a slayer of his father."

Thus, this [text] is intended to prohibit a separate *ekoddiṣṭa* rite performed by a younger brother for the sake of performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* that has already been performed by the elder brother, and it is also intended to prohibit the *ekoddiṣṭa* on the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*) for parents.
Thus concludes the procedure for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* in the case of following the deceased in death (*anugamana*).

In the case of following [the husband in death], the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite must be performed together with the husband. Regarding this, Yama states: "The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of a woman must be performed by her husband alone;
for even though she is dead, she has attained oneness with him through mantras, oblations, and vows."
Śātātapa also says:
"A woman who has followed her deceased lord is entitled to share the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) with him,
even while dwelling in heaven, until the dissolution of all beings."
Vasiṣṭha says:
"In the funeral procession, however, the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite is performed together with the husband;
even for the husband and the father-in-law, one should place a blade of grass between them."
Some say that there is *sāpiṇḍya* with the husband and others; as Śaṅkha says:
"A woman who, having followed her deceased husband, has gone to the fire—for her, indeed, at the conclusion of the collection of bones, [the lineage] is that of the husband alone."
"The *navaśrāddha* (the nine funeral rites) ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed according to the time of death, even if it occurs at different times;

the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha is performed together with the husband and the other three [ancestors]. Regarding this, some say that in the case of following the husband in death, ascending the same funeral pyre, or dying on the same day, there is no separate *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the woman; rather, by performing it for the husband, the *sāpiṇḍya* for the woman is also accomplished. Viṣṇu says:

"When the father has already performed the *sapiṇḍana* for his mother, he should perform it together with her; by the father’s own *sapiṇḍana*, hers too shall be accomplished. Thus says Sumantu as well.
If both husband and wife die at the same time, or if it is the time for the wife’s ascension to the funeral pyre, then the rites up to the sixteenth day should be performed separately for each.

"If her *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not been performed [along with] that of her husband," and so forth—such statements should be understood as referring to those women who are unable to perform a separate *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* when ascending the same funeral pyre (*ekacityārohaṇa*), because the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled by the fact that what is done for the husband is also done for the wife. However, one who is capable should perform it separately. Regarding this, another *smṛti* states:
"The devoted wife who performs the ascension to the husband's funeral pyre..."
When the twelfth day has arrived, one should offer a separate funeral ball (piṇḍa).
"A husband and wife who have ascended the same funeral pyre both meet their end;
for them, the monthly śrāddhas, the *navaśrāddha*, and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* are performed separately. Thus says Śaṅkha.
"When the father has died, the wife should perform the rites for both;
they declare that these [rites] continue even in the case of simultaneous death. Thus says Gautama.

"But a woman who is devoted to her husband and follows him [in death] shall perform the *śrāddha* rites, such as the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* separately. Thus says Vyāghrapāda.
"Once, the death of both husband and wife shall consume both from the *aupāsana* fire;
however, the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and the water-rites must be performed separately by the son.

[163] Thus, when the rites such as the *śrāddha* and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* are to be performed separately—whether in the case of *sahagamana* (following the husband in death) on the day following the husband's death, or in the case of *anugamana* (ascension to the funeral pyre) on the subsequent day—the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed on the twelfth day. This has been stated in another *smṛti*:

"In the case of the simultaneous death of both parents, or on a day other than that of the mother's [death], or upon following [the husband] in death during her period, one should perform the Śrāddha at the appropriate time. Thus, in the event of the simultaneous death of both parents, or when the mother dies on a day subsequent to the father's death, or when she dies while following him in death on the following day, one should perform the sixteen Śrāddhas, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, and so forth, for the mother at their respective times, such as the eleventh day and so on. Devala also says:
Whether she follows her husband on that very day or on the following day,
the Navaśrāddha, the Ṣoḍaśa-śrāddha, and the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa should be performed according to the rules.
"But it should be performed at the proper time, as is done every year," so says Vasiṣṭha:
"The woman who follows her husband while he is being cremated..."

"The śrāddha for death and so forth should be performed; however, the cremation and other rites for those two [the husband and wife] shall not be done together. Thus it is stated. Also in the Vahni Purāṇa:
"The virtuous woman who follows her husband as he is being cremated..."
For her, the śrāddha rite, the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa), and the water libation are performed separately.
"But one should complete the *sapiṇḍana* on the twelfth day after death.

From such statements as these, it is stated that having offered the nine *navaśrāddhas* for the mother on an odd-numbered day, and having drawn forward and offered the nine mixed (*navamiśra*) offerings on the eleventh day for the mother, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa-śrāddha* for the mother must be performed on the twelfth day. Others, however, say that the *śrāddha* for the mother should be performed at the time of the *śrāddha* for the father. As Śātātapa says:
"If she follows her husband on that very day or on the following day..."
"Purity shall be attained together with the husband, and the *śrāddha* ceremony should take place on the same day.
Thus says Pracetas as well:
"When [a wife] has died along with her husband, [the purification occurs] on the day of his death or on the following day."

"Impurity (āśauca) regarding death and so forth shall apply [to the relatives], but not to the cremation and so forth of those two. This means that the impurity resulting from the husband's death and so forth applies to the wife. Also, in the Viśvādarśa:
"But a devoted wife (pativratā) who follows her husband on another day by ascending the funeral pyre..."
"Purification from the impurity of the husband's death occurs after ten days; there shall be two separate *śrāddha* rites at one and the same time. Thus it is said. Also in another *Smṛti*:
"If a wife, being in her menses, follows her husband [in death]..."
Having cast her deceased husband into a vat of oil or into salt, [she should proceed].
"Relatives should perform the cremation together with her after three nights;
they should perform the *śrāddha* on a single day—this indeed is the settled rule for both. Thus says Gālava.
A husband and wife who have met their death by ascending the same funeral pyre should have the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite performed for the husband on the eleventh day,
as well as the sixteenth-day rite.
"When the twelfth day has arrived, one should cast a single *piṇḍa* for both;
one should then join that [piṇḍa] of the father into the *piṇḍas* of the grandfather and the others."

Regarding this, there is one view that one should perform the *śrāddha* on the day following the husband’s death if they die on the same day and are cremated on the same funeral pyre, or even if she dies on a subsequent day, at the time appropriate for her own specific relationship. Another view is that one should perform the mother’s *śrāddha* at the time prescribed for the husband’s *śrāddha*. In that very context, regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, there is yet another view that one should cast a single *piṇḍa* for the couple together and then join that *piṇḍa* with the *piṇḍas* of the grandfather and the other ancestors. Since the *smṛtis* are of equal authority in these matters, an option should be understood as permissible according to one’s preference. A specific detail in this regard has been shown by Pracetas:

"At one time, death may come to both husband and wife by ascending the funeral pyre together; otherwise, the *śrāddha* for the mother should be performed separately from that of the father, and likewise for the mother as for the father. Thus says Atri.
If the husband and wife arrive at the same time,
then the ancestral śrāddha ceremony must be performed again with separate cooking.
But seeing her husband being cremated, a woman devoted to her husband should follow him; their Śrāddha ceremony shall be performed separately on the eleventh day.
"When the twelfth day has arrived, one should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the father;
having prepared the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for the mother, one should then join it with the rice-ball of the father.
Likewise:
But if a mother dies at the time of her son's father's death,
having performed the *sapiṇḍana* separately on the twelfth day, [the period of impurity] lasts until the end of the sixteenth day.
But once he is liberated from the state of a preta, the sapindikarana rite should be performed for him together with his mother.
The word "should perform" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Others say that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite should be performed in a combined manner (*tantra*) on the anniversary of death. As Kāśyapa says:
"Having invited ten, eight, or twelve Brahmins on the twelfth day, and having honored them with all ritual services according to the extent of one's wealth," [166]
Having spread the *kuśa* grass with their tips pointing south in two layers as before,
[one places] for the ancestors and others on the eastern blades of *darbha*, but for the sake of the deceased (*preta*) on the western ones.
Having designated the grandfather and the other three ancestors as in the rite for the ancestors (pitṛyajña), [he offers] the balls of rice;
then, at the western [ball], he says: "O Yajñaśarman, may this ball of rice attend upon you."
Upon the two-fold spread of darbha grass, one should prepare the arghya vessels:
first for the father and others, and immediately thereafter for the mother.
One should gradually pour water from the *arghya* vessel of the father into those of the grandfather and the others,
using the two mantras beginning with "ye samānāḥ" in their respective order.
One should offer the *arghya* for the mother with two *ṛc*-verses among the three beginning with the mother;
likewise, one should join the *piṇḍa* thus divided into three parts to the three *piṇḍas*.
"In the case of the simultaneous death of both parents, however, the rule for following [the procedure] is prescribed;

otherwise, one should perform them separately—so said Pitāmaha. Here, regarding the position of eight Brahmins: one each for the sake of the deceased mother and father, three for the ancestors beginning with the father, two for the Vaiśvadeva, and one for Viṣṇu. According to the position of Dakṣa, the Vaiśvadeva rite is performed by a single ritual procedure (*tantra*); everything else is clear. The meaning is that, having honored [the guests] with the services following the meal, one should perform the joining of the *piṇḍas* and the *arghya* offerings by a single ritual procedure, in accordance with one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. The worship of Viṣṇu has been mentioned in the context of the *Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* Śrāddha.
"One should perform the worship of the deity at the beginning and the end, as well as during the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite.
Thus [says the tradition]. Śāṇḍila also says: "In the same manner, one should worship Viṣṇu during the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Thus [ends the citation].

Regarding this, the performance of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha for both parents simultaneously (*tantreṇa*) as mentioned in the Tantra should be applied to cases of incapacity, based on a careful consideration of the plural statements previously cited. It is stated in the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*: "If the death of the husband and wife occurs at the same time, [the fire] shall consume both from the *aupāsana* fire;
thereafter, the son must perform the rites of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water separately."
A single twice-born man, acting separately for the Ekoddiṣṭa and the Sapinda rites,
should offer water and the rice-ball (piṇḍa) intended for the father into the fire and into the [offerings] for the grandfather and others.

"One should place water in the *mātrargha* vessel and offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to the three ancestors beginning with the father; having fed the Brahmins, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability.
Regarding this, Pulastya states a specific detail:
If the father has died an ill death or a good death while remaining uncremated,
then when the mother dies at a later time, the rites such as cremation and so forth must be performed for her.
"But one should burn both [the husband and wife] together on a single funeral mound using the *aupāsana* fire," so says Saṃvarta.
"O Lord of the Earth, if a father remains uncremated for a long time..."
If indeed the mother has died, then the cremation and other rites for those two [the father and mother] are performed together.
"The offering of water, the gift of funeral cakes, the *navaśrāddha*, and the *sapiṇḍana*—
these must be performed for one's parents by the son; this is the eternal law," so says Yama.
If the wife dies before the collection of the husband's bones,
she should be offered in that very same fire, provided the fire does not go out.

"When the fire has been extinguished, one should again have a separate funeral pyre and so forth prepared for her; however, the rites beginning with the water libation and ending with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed for both of them together. Thus it is stated in another *Smṛti*.
The husband shall perform the sapindikarana for a childless wife together with his mother and other ancestors;
however, in the case of a son, he performs it together with his own father.
The son of women married through the Brāhma form of marriage belongs to the paternal grandfather's side and so forth;
whereas the son born of women married through the Āsura and other forms belongs to either the father’s side or the mother’s side.
That lineage is established through the distinction between marriage and offspring;
even for one who has no son, his lawful wife shall perform the sapinda-rite.
One should not perform the *pārvaṇa* rite for those who have renounced the world on the twelfth day.

The meaning of this is as follows: the husband of a childless wife shall perform her *sapiṇḍana* with his mother and the others—namely, with his mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother. Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi says:
"But when a childless woman has died, the husband shall perform the *sapiṇḍana*."
"Along with her mother-in-law and the others, on the day she dies together with them.

Thus, the son of a woman married through the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, or Prājāpatya forms of marriage should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for her together with his grandmother (*pitāmahī*) and the other female ancestors. Regarding this, Satyavrata says:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of a mother is prescribed as being performed with the grandmother and the other [female ancestors]."
But when she dies without a son, the husband shall perform the sapindikarana rite.

"If her mother-in-law and the others died previously, she becomes one with them; if the husband has died, she has attained oneness with him alone. [169] Thus it is said. For a woman married according to the Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, or Paiśāca rites, her son should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite together with his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, or with his paternal grandmother and the others (or maternal grandfather and the others). Yama says:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the mother is performed with one or three [male ancestors] of the father;
however, a son born of an *āsura* or other such marriage performs it together with the grandmother and the others.
Regarding this very subject, Śātātapa says:
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a mother is prescribed with the maternal grandmother and others;
or women may perform it with the paternal grandmother and others, or with the father and others.

"Or even by the maternal grandfather and others, for a son born of an Āsura or other [marriage]... Thus it is said. The same applies to the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). The exclusion and inclusion of the *gotra* will be explained in the section on marriage.
Thus, in the *Smṛticandrikā*, [the section on] the time for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* following [the death of a relative].
Now, some statements regarding the prohibition of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* are recorded; [says] Śātātapa:
One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for eunuchs, outcasts, and indeed for wicked women; one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for them.
For lifelong ascetics (naiṣṭhika) and wandering mendicants (yati), the Śrāddha rite is dedicated to Nārāyaṇa;
they know that the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite applies only to the student (upakurvāṇaka).
"But the perpetual celibate (naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī), having abandoned the body, shall go to the supreme state;
for him, no Śrāddha should be performed, nor the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite," so says Vṛddhavasiṣṭha.
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is never performed for those who died while observing celibacy (*brahmacārin*);
rather, after performing the rites beginning with cremation up until the sixteenth day according to the Smṛtis, [the period of impurity ends].
When the twelfth day has arrived, having performed the pārvaṇa rite,
one should feed eight Brahmins, dedicating the offering to Nārāyaṇa.
"Or the twice-born may perform the *śrāddha* according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*.

In this regard, for both the *upakurvāṇa* (the student) and the *naiṣṭhika* (the lifelong celibate), the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is optional—either performed or not. Regarding the ascetic (*yati*), Pulastya states:
"The *kuṭīcaka*, the *bahūdaka*, the *haṃsa*, and the *paramahaṃsa*..."
Of the four kinds of mendicants, namely the Ekadaṇḍins and the Tridaṇḍins.
"The sixteen [śrāddhas], the nine śrāddhas, and the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa are not [performed]. Thus says Uśanas:
"The Kuṭīcaka, the Bahūdaka, the Haṃsa, and the Paramahaṃsaka..."
The sapindikarana rite for them must not be performed by the son.
Merely by the taking up of the staff, the state of a preta does not cease;
for the sake of liberation from the state of a preta, there is the procedure of the sixteen śrāddhas.
The offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water for those who have recently died serves to alleviate their hunger, thirst, and other such needs;
the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha rite is the prescribed method for attaining the status of an ancestor (*pitṛ*).
On the twelfth day, a son should perform the Pārvaṇa rite for ascetics who have transcended the three stages of life,
in order to establish their eligibility for the Śrāddha ceremony.
"Regarding the four types of monks, on the twelfth day, a *pārvaṇa* *śrāddha* must be performed for them by their kinsmen, relatives, sons, and others. Thus says Yama.
The legitimate son of the body shall never perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite;
nor shall he ever perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for ascetics.
"When the eleventh day has arrived, one should perform the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha. Thus says Prajāpati:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is never to be performed for ascetics (*yatis*)."
"When the eleventh day has arrived, the *pārvaṇa* rite is prescribed. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
"For an ascetic (*yati*), there shall be neither the *navaśrāddha* nor the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."
"When the eleventh day has arrived, one should indeed perform for him the pārvaṇa rite. Thus says Vasiṣṭha:
"The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, water, the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), the period of impurity (*āśauca*), and the funeral rites (*pretakarma*)."
One should not perform any rite other than the pārvaṇa for a mendicant who has become one with Brahman.

Having become Brahman, the practitioner meditates: "I am Brahman. Pulastya said: If one should renounce the cycle of worldly existence, being devoted to the knowledge of Brahman, he may become either a *kuṭīcaka* or a *bahūdaka*.
Then one becomes a *haṃsa*; beyond that, a *parahaṃsa*.
Whether holding a single staff or a triple staff, one must always be a master of the staff of the mind.
One should burn the *kuṭīcaka*, fill the *bahūdaka*,
cast the *haṃsa* into the water, and dissolve the *paramahaṃsa*.
The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is not performed for all [deceased relatives] according to the injunctions of the Smṛtis;
rather, when the eleventh day has arrived, one should perform the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha.
A son should perform the piṇḍayajña and the darśa-śrāddha on the anniversary of the father's death;
for an ascetic (yati), it should be performed during the mahālaya period, at the new moon, or on the day of his passing.
"For others, it should be the pārvaṇa rite, or it may be the ekoddiṣṭa. Thus says Sumantu:
"The legitimate son (aurasa), or the son born of the wife (kṣetraja), or a brother, or even his son..."
But the disciples, resident pupils, and kings should perform the pārvaṇa śrāddha.
One who follows the *kuṭīcaka* mode should perform the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* on occasions such as the new moon;
likewise, one who follows the *bahūdaka* mode should perform the *nārāyaṇabali* and the *pārvaṇa*.
If a Haṃsa dies, his son should perform the Pārvaṇa rite according to the rules for the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña);
likewise, he should perform the Nārāyaṇabali for one who is a Paramahaṃsa.
Having worshipped Viṣṇu according to the rules, having offered the arghya and the supreme bali,
and having offered the caru-oblation sixteen times with the Puruṣasūkta;
"Having fed twelve Brahmins under names such as Keśava and others,
or else one should feed Brahmins alone at all times. Thus it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa as well.
Devoted to the knowledge of Brahman, he should enter the fourth stage of life,
either as a bearer of a single staff or a triple staff, completely free from all attachments.
When the eleventh day has arrived, or indeed on the twelfth day,
the legitimate son should perform the Śrāddha rite according to the Pārvaṇa procedure.
"In the annual śrāddha performed on the new moon day, at sacred fords (tīrthas), and also during the Mahālaya,
one should always state the relationship along with the name and lineage (gotra) at the times of the śrāddha. Thus it is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa.
If a Kṣatriya becomes king and should honor [the twice-born] contrary to the dharma of Brahmins,
he becomes a Śūdra king who is to be honored by the twice-born like a Vaiśya.
A lifelong celibate is more venerable than one who has not entered the stages of life;
however, the householder is more venerable than both of those two, and the teacher of the earth is more venerable than all three.
Among these four, the kuṭīcaka and the bahūdaka [are distinguished];
however, all ascetics (yatis) have the authority to perform the funeral rites for the deceased.
The entitlement to perform the *śrāddha* for ascetics does not exist at all except for a biological son;
however, when the eleventh day has arrived, one should diligently worship Viṣṇu.
"One should feed Brāhmaṇas according to one's ability, while recollecting Viṣṇu as their form.
Thus it is said in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa:
"In that very manner, having been initiated, he entered the stage of the householder."
Among those two, the one who observes vows is superior; among them, he who has taken recourse to renunciation is the best.

Even for those belonging to the three castes who have performed the purificatory rites, as well as for those in the various stages of life (āśramas), if one performs the funeral rites for ascetics (yatins), he goes to hell; it is not otherwise.
"No water should be offered here, nor the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* *śrāddha*;
one should perform the *nārāyaṇabali* for him on the eleventh day.
Thus are some statements regarding the prohibition of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
[174] Now, regarding the *navamiśraikoddiṣṭa* (the single-offering rite mixed with nine),
Yājñavalkya says:
The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is devoid of the deities; it has a single offering (*argha*) and a single purifier (*pavitraka*);
indeed, it is without the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), and is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*).

"At the place for the inexhaustible [offering] (*akṣayya*), when dismissing the Brahmins, one should say, 'May you rise,' and they should reply, 'We have been delighted. This [instruction] pertains to the *navaśrāddha* and the *navamiśra* by virtue of the context. Regarding this as well, Bodhāyana has shown a specific rule for the *ekoddiṣṭa* performed for the purpose of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
Even though the invocation and other rites are prohibited in an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite,
one should nevertheless perform them all when that *ekoddiṣṭa* has become a *sapiṇḍana*.
Bodhāyana has stated that for one who has died, there should be the invocation and the utterance of the word *svadhā*.
Incense is not said to be a product of wheat cooked in oil.
"One should not offer all of this at an *ekoddiṣṭa* [śrāddha]; rather, all of this is offered at the *sapiṇḍana*.
At all *ekoddiṣṭas*, there is no prior invitation;
however, for the purpose of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the invitation should take place on the preceding day."
Regarding this, Vyāsa states the specific rule:

"Having performed the nine *śrāddhas*, the mixed *śrāddhas*, and likewise the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* according to the prescribed rite, one should bathe; however, one must not bathe on the anniversary of the death."
Thus concludes the determination of the *navamiśra-ekoddiṣṭa* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, the *navaśrāddhas*.

In this regard, Āśvalāyana—introducing the designation "nine *śrāddhas*" for those performed during the nine-day period following death—considers the *navaśrāddha* to extend up to the end of the tenth day. Śivasvāmin states: "The followers of the Āśvalāyana branch say there are five *navaśrāddhas*;
the Āpastambas say six; and the Aitareyins state that there is an option (*vibhāṣā*)."
Prajāpati says:
"The *navaśrāddha* lasts until the end of the tenth day; that which is mixed occurs after a year.
Beginning from the eleventh day, one should perform [the śrāddhas] for the sake of liberation from the state of being a *preta*."
Vasiṣṭha says:
"At the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka), one who is pure should perform the *navaśrāddha* on the eleventh day;
the *navaśrāddha* lasts for ten days, while that which is mixed with the new [impurity] lasts for six days, performed daily."
Regarding this, some say there is a "six-ninth śrāddha" (ṣaṇṇavaśrāddha). Aṅgiras states:
"On the first day, the third day, the fifth, the seventh, as well as the ninth and the eleventh—this is called the six-ninth śrāddha."
Vyāsa says: "One should perform the nine *navasrāddhas* according to the rules for the *ekoddhiṣṭa* rite, on uneven days up to twelve days after death."
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"In the fifth, the seventh, likewise in the third and the first,
and in the ninth and the eleventh— these indeed are the nine Śrāddhas."
"A preta who has reached the Vaitaraṇī river shall obtain satisfaction.
Regarding this, Kāśyapa states the settled rule:
"The followers of the Āśvalāyana Śākhā say there are nine *navaśrāddhas*."
The followers of Āpastamba say there are six; others belonging to different recensions say there are either six or five.
"Some authorities maintain that there should be exactly five [days], provided the ninth is omitted; they, the authors of the Smṛtis, know that one should perform it on the eleventh day.
Regarding this, a specific detail is stated in the Nāgara-khaṇḍa:
"Nine, seven, and six [funeral rites] for kings, with nine *śrāddhas* in sequence;
however, for the first and last of the castes, the great seers say there are six. Thus it is stated in another *Smṛti*.

Regarding the statement, "At the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka), they prescribe the Ekoddiṣṭa Śrāddha at home," because of the specific mention here of "at home at the end of sūtaka," the nine Navaśrāddhas should be performed at the place of death— either in the cremation ground (śmaśāna) or at the site where the funeral water offering (piṇḍodaka) was made.
Thus concludes the description of the *navaśrāddha* in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the *nagnapracchādanaśrāddha*; regarding this, Gobhila says:
On the anniversary of the day of death, at the conclusion of the ritual bath, one should perform the Śrāddha rite for the covering of the naked.
Or in a jar filled with rice and wrapped in a cloth.
Having covered it with a bronze vessel, one should pour clarified butter into it;
having placed gold therein according to the extent of one's wealth,
[one should give it] to a man of noble birth who is poor, learned in the Vedas, and a householder.
"Then, remembering Viṣṇu in his mind with devotion, he should give [the gift],
having honored a Brāhmaṇa on behalf of the deceased, and then dismiss him. Thus says Vyāsa.
"One should offer clothing, rice, an earthen vessel, a lamp, and a bronze bowl after the cremation; for that is indeed for the covering of the naked.
Thus it is stated that another *śrāddha* is a constituent part of the collection of the bones (*saṃcayana*).
"A twice-born man should perform [the rite] on the third day from the day of the cremation of the deceased. Thus it is said.
A specific detail is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"And for the sake of the deceased, one should feed the twice-born at the door of the house on the fourth day."
And on the second day, the shaving of the hair should be performed by the relatives.
On the fourth day, all the kinsmen should perform the collection of the bones;
they should devoutly engage an even number of pure Brahmins who are well-versed in the Vedas.
On the fifth, the ninth, and likewise on the eleventh day, one should feed an even number of Brahmins; thereafter, they know that as the *navaśrāddha*.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"On the fourth day for Brāhmaṇas, on the fifth day for kings,
on the ninth day for Vaiśyas, and on the tenth day for Śūdras."

"At the end of the period of impurity, one should feed ten Brahmins for the sake of the deceased; however, for the purpose of the *navaśrāddha*, one should feed one on the eleventh day. Thus ends the section on the *nagnapracchādana-śrāddha* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
[178] Now, the Nārāyaṇabali according to the Brahmapurāṇa.
I shall describe the Nārāyaṇa-bali as it was spoken by Vyāsa in the past;
[it concerns those who have died] from outcasts, water, serpents, and the like, or from lightning, flames, poisons, and so forth.
[The same applies] for those who die by means of mountains, trees, stones, weapons, or beasts with fangs, claws, or beaks,
as well as for lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika), ascetics (yati), and practitioners of austerities (tapasvin).
Especially for Vaiṣṇavas and others who desire liberation,
as well as for those such as lifelong celibates (naiṣṭhika) who have died, one should perform [the rite] on the twelfth day.
One may perform it after a year has passed for one killed by Caṇḍālas and the like,
or in the event of a calamity, a crisis, illness, or a change of country.
When there is doubt regarding the agent, the substance, and so forth, or when a doubt concerning life is observed—
even on whatever day it may be, provided it is outside the year.
When the sun is in its northern course, during the equinoxes or the solstices,
under the asterisms of Śroṇā or Rohiṇī, or on the eleventh day of either fortnight;
On the day before, having invited six or even twelve Brahmins,
he should choose one as the preceptor (ācārya), who is endowed with noble lineage, good conduct, and virtuous qualities.

One should perform the ritual bath there with earth and water according to the prescribed rules, [visualizing the deity] as complete in all limbs and one who has reached the further shore of the meaning of the Vedas and Shastras.
Wearing white garments and properly donning the upper robe,
the performer, having restrained his senses, shall formally resolve upon the fast.
Having washed one's feet, sipped water for purification (ācamana), and sat upon an auspicious seat,
one should smear an area the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung and water.

Having prepared a sacrificial pit or a leveled altar, and having smeared it with red-colored clay and other materials according to the previously mentioned procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch,
one should invite the Brahmins, worship them, and perform the recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*).
Adorned with primary and secondary ornaments, most captivating and supreme,
one should place within its center a water-pot [representing] Viṣṇu and Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
One should place there an image made of gold, silver, or other materials,
and worship it with two garments, gold and silver, and auspicious fragrances, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata).
One should first perform the purification of oneself and then fashion the five-fingered [mudrā] in sequence;
having procured the ritual substances, vessels, and so forth, one should thereafter perform the ritual depositions (nyāsa) and other rites.
Taking perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and so forth, one should invoke the Lord;
"Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" is proclaimed as the root mantra.
And salutations to Vaivasvata, and likewise salutations to Yama;
having worshipped him with all ritual offerings, including fragrant perfumes and captivating garlands.
Having praised Hari with the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as with his specific deities,
and with dance, song, instrumental music, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas;
Having praised Viṣṇu with the Thousand Names and through hymns, narratives, and so forth,
and having worshipped him properly three times, one should keep a vigil during the night.
In this manner, one should worship Keśava and the others in the petals starting from the east;
with a concentrated mind, one should offer rice-balls mixed with my ghee and sesame seeds.
[180] With the sacred thread over the right shoulder and the left hand facing downward, one should offer five rice-balls upon *kuśa* grass while facing south, for Brahmā and for Śiva.
Mentally recollecting Yama, Viṣṇu, and the deceased, one should not give [the offering] to the wife and others; rather, having bathed, one should proceed toward home.
The teacher, having risen in the morning, bathed, and performed his daily obligatory rites such as the twilight prayers,
should then, during the forenoon, worship Viṣṇu and Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
Having worshipped Keśava and the others, as well as Brahmā and Śaṅkara,
one should subsequently perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the rules of one's own domestic ritual manual (svagṛhya).
Having offered oblations from the cooked food with these two verses, "viṣṇor nu kaṃ" and "paromātā," [one should offer] to Nārāyaṇa, Yama, Brahmā, and Śiva with the mantra:
"Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāyaiva yamāya brahmaṇe śive."
One should offer sixteen oblations with the Puruṣasūkta alone;
one should conclude the rite with fuel-sticks and clarified butter while reciting the names beginning with Keśava.
Then, having summoned the Brahmins, one should seat them for the sake of the deity;
first for the sake of Viṣṇu, and then Yama Vaivasvata.
The rite for Rudra is for the purpose of injunction, while another is prescribed for the sake of the deceased;
those for the sake of the gods are performed facing east, and that for the sake of the deceased facing north.
One should perform the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) as previously prescribed, starting with the deities;
one should offer rings, garments, and other articles according to one's capacity.
Having requested permission with the words, "I shall perform [the offering] in the fire," and being thus prompted,
he should prepare the food according to the ritual rules for the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) and cause the twice-born to eat.
Then, having ascertained that the Brahmins are satisfied and having asked them about their satisfaction according to the prescribed rule,
one should offer rice-balls mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds upon the sacrificial grass.
One should first offer to Viṣṇu, and then to Brahmā and Śiva;
one should offer the fifth pinda to Yama, the son of Vivasvat.
But for the sixth [offering], recollecting the name and lineage of the deceased preta,
one should release them at the edge of the water while uttering the name of Viṣṇu.

At the conclusion of the *homa*, according to the twelve-fold division, one should worship Viṣṇu and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, with three Brahmins, and the ancestors beginning with the father with another three Brahmins.
One should offer [oblations] to the maternal grandfather and others, as well as to the preceptor, who has taken the form of a deceased ancestor,
according to the Pārvaṇa rite and by names beginning with Keśava.
Having honored and fed them, one should offer the *bali* at the conclusion of the *piṇḍa* rite with the mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa and likewise to the father; *svadhā*, obeisance!"
Having thus offered the bali-oblation for the maternal grandfather and others by their names,
and having fed those Brahmins, he should give them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should properly honor the preceptor with garments, perfumes, unbroken grains, and flowers;
and [one should also give] a bull, a cow, two oxen, gold, or even bell-metal.
One should give a garment or a sacrificial fee according to one's ability, even if [the recipient] has the form of a deceased person;
having received their blessing, one should prostrate and ask for forgiveness from them.
Having performed this rite beginning with the [offering for] a son, one shall indeed obtain sons;
moreover, one is liberated from the fault of untimely death—of this there is no doubt.

"This rite, performed with devotion out of a desire to conquer the world of Viṣṇu, brings one all desires in this life and he goes to the world of Viṣṇu. (182) Thus it is said. However, regarding one killed by a snake, this specific rule is shown in the Tvaṣṭṛ-purāṇa.
"Having fashioned a Naga [image] out of a bhāra of gold and likewise a cow,
and having given them to a Brahmin according to the prescribed rite, one attains freedom from debt to one's father.
An exception to this is shown in the *Ādityapurāṇa*:
Even through negligence, death occurs suddenly and unexpectedly by means of horned animals,
fanged beasts, venomous serpents, poison, lightning, water, and other such causes.
"Whether he has been killed by Caṇḍālas or by thieves anywhere at all,
the cremation and other rites must be performed for him, because he has not fallen [from his caste]," so says Aṅgiras.

"If someone dies through negligence by means of fire, water, or the like, for him the period of impurity (aśauca) must be observed, and one should perform the offerings of rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water-libations. Even in that case, it is only after the performance of the penance (prāyaścitta). Gautama states: "But he for whom the penance ends with death—once dead, he becomes pure; all [his relatives] should perform the water-libations and the funeral rites (pretakārya). Śātātapa says:
An old man who has ceased his ritual purification, who has rejected medical treatment,
and who kills himself by means of a precipice, fire, fasting, or water;
"For him, the period of impurity lasts three nights; on the second day, the collection of bones takes place;
on the third, having offered water, one should perform the *śrāddha* on the fourth.
Furthermore, there is a rule regarding such acts as leaping from a cliff (*bhṛgupatana*), and likewise the *Purāṇa*:
If a man is afflicted by great diseases that are difficult to cure,
he may enter a blazing fire or likewise practice fasting unto death.
[183] Or like a mass of water that is unfathomable...
And so forth will be stated [later]:
"In the case of those who die unintentionally from a Brahmin, fire, water, a *caṇḍāla*, a horned animal, a snake, or one accused of a crime, one should cause two *aindava* fasts to be performed."

Thus ends the procedure for the *nārāyaṇabali* in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now, regarding the subject of funeral rites (*saṃskāra*) in the event of the death of a woman in her menses (*rajasvalā*), [the following applies] to the death of one who is menstruating.
Having silently carried out that deceased woman, who was adorned with rustic ornaments,
and having bathed her according to the prescribed rite with mantras and the five products of the cow;
The bath with water from golden jars should be performed ten or twelve times;
having thus removed all impurities, one should likewise put on other ornaments.
Having covered her with another garment, one should likewise cremate a woman in her menses.
The sacramental rite for a pregnant woman who has died:
if a pregnant woman dies,
her sacramental rite is prescribed as declared by Bodhāyana, Bharadvāja, Śaunaka, and others.
Having resolved upon the Pitṛmedha rite and performed the ritual for the wooden pyre,
one should subsequently place the deceased to the south or west of the wooden pyre according to the prescribed rule.
Having set aside the Gṛhya-tantras and having performed the wiping with the *adarvī* ladle,
one should scrape the interior of the vessel with the *Hiraṇyagarbha* mantra.
If he dies on the left side before the fetus is seen, one should cast him into a pit;
but having seen him alive, one should consecrate him with the mantra: "Now you are my son."
Having hidden gold and consecrated that infant with water,
one should go to the village and give the breast to the child, saying, "That which is yours, O breast."
Having ensured that the prince was well-protected, he went to the side of the corpse and applied clarified butter to the belly with five verses beginning with "śatāyudhāya syonā."
And with the *yajus* formulas, one offers twelve oblations with "To Prāṇa, svāhā!
and so forth; five with "To Prāṇa," etc., and five with "To the eye," etc.
"Bodhāyana and others say [it should be done] with the *vyāhṛtis*, but Śaunaka says with the mantras; having sprinkled [the disciple] again and obtained the permission of the twice-born."
Having made the belly free of wounds, one should gradually place [the body] upon the funeral pyre,
sprinkling it three times with earth, with *kuśa* grass and cow’s urine, and with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
"Having bathed [the deceased] and clothed him with garments, one should cremate him according to the rites for the dead"—
thus Śaunaka has declared, while Bodhāyana and others have said this.
On the eighth day, one should give cows, land, and so forth to a brahmin according to one's capacity; such is the compendium of the Smṛtis, O Bharadvāja.

Regarding death during childbirth: when the woman who has given birth has died, how do the performers of the sacrifice proceed? Having taken water in a jar, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), [they perform the rites].
Then, having been consecrated with meritorious verses, one shall thereafter obtain purity through speech by means of the Puruṣasūkta and those very verses spoken in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
[185] And with the Vāmana-sūkta and water from a vessel of gold, one should perform the purification by reciting it at least three times; otherwise, it is impure.
Then, having washed [the image] with water from a golden vessel using *darbha*, *udumbara*, *padma*, *palāśa*, and *aśvattha*— the fifth— as the fifth, one should clothe it in new garments.

Having covered [the body] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having adorned it according to the instruction of the twice-born, one should cremate it according to the rules for the dead; thus say the Vājasaneyins.
Thus concludes the section on the subject of funeral rites (*saṃskāra*) regarding the death of a woman in her menses and others in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now follows the determination of expiations (*prāyaścitta*) and other matters concerning defects such as food that has been kept overnight (*paryuṣita*).
[Section: Expiation for defects such as food kept overnight.
Whether by day or by night, if a corpse remains anywhere, they say that it is "stale"; what then is the procedure for its cremation?
Having bathed [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
if it is soaked, broken, or emits an excessively foul odor, it should be bathed with cow-dung water.
Having performed the *taptakṛcchra* penance, the twice-born should bathe with meritorious waters;
wherever a worm has appeared, he should bathe that spot with cow-dung water.
Having washed it repeatedly with earth, ashes, kuśa grass, and cow urine,
and having attained purification through three *taptakṛcchra* penances, one should burn what has been burnt again.
If one is touched by someone afflicted with *daṇḍāla* (a skin disease), or if he dies after being so touched,
the twice-born, having performed the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance and having bathed him with the previously mentioned mantras, [should proceed].
Having adorned [the body] with garments and other ornaments, one should cremate it according to the rites for the deceased.
[186] If one touches a menstruating woman, a woman who has recently given birth, an outcaste, or a child,
or if one touches a corpse or someone dying, a Cāndrāyaṇa penance is the purifier in all such cases.

But according to the rule, a sage should not purify with dogs, pigs, deer, and the like that which has been touched by one who has fallen from Bhṛgu’s lineage or by one who does not observe vows, even if it is ancient.

An aged man abandoned by physicians, one incapable of performing rites of purification and proper conduct, a killer of a Brahmin with his own hand, a thief, a drinker of liquor, and one who violates the teacher’s bed;
One may burn one's body in a fire of dried cow-dung or by leaping from a precipice;
one should destroy one's lifespan at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Or one may enter a great river; there is no fault in such a death.
In the Ādipurāṇa:
"If a man is afflicted by great diseases that are difficult to cure,
he should enter a blazing fire or likewise practice fasting unto death."
One might go to a bottomless mass of water, or even to a fall from a precipice,
or one might diligently travel upon the great path to the Snowy Mountain.
Or one who casts off the body at the branch of the banyan tree at Prayāga,
or joyfully enters the Sarasvatī while situated between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.

One who dies in Vārāṇasī, having rejected medical treatment and being situated amidst wood and stones while standing in the midst of the waters of the Jāhnavī, shall attain the highest worlds; such a person, though a self-killer, shall never suffer [the consequences] anywhere.
Remaining unliberated, Hara went to the root of his ear.
"He declares the *praṇava* to be the savior; it is not otherwise for anyone, anywhere. Thus says the *Brahmagarbha*:
"Even one who is unable to perform [the rites], being afflicted by a great disease..."
"One who undertakes a great voyage upon the waters of the ocean does not incur sin [for eating such food] in the next world.

Thus ends the determination of expiations and related matters regarding defects such as stale food in the *Smṛticandrikā*. Now follows the procedure for the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*) of an ascetic (*yati*).
In this regard, Yama says:
"For one who has desisted from all attachments and is devoted to the yoga of meditation,
no cremation should be performed, nor any period of impurity, nor any water-libation rites."
Then, in a clean place, having washed his body with water while reciting the Gāyatrī,
and having anointed it with honey and clarified butter, he should wash it again with fragrant substances.
With these verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," with the three beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," with the Pavamāna-anuvāka, with the Śuddhavatī verses, and with the Taratsamandī verses;
With the three verses beginning "O pure ones, Agni is pure," "Proclaim with hymns the Knower of Beings," and "Thy purifier and thy course are pure," he should recite them.
Having consecrated [it] with the tips of kusha grass, or having obtained the permission of the twice-born,
and having adorned it on all sides with perfumes and garlands while reciting the Gayatri;
Then, having placed [the body] in a sturdy litter, the Brahmins should carry it firmly;
for while they are carrying it, immediate purification is prescribed.
"Having slowly dug into the earth, one should place only the head within it;
by merely bathing, Svāyambhuva declared that purification is attained. Thus says Bodhāyana.
Now, the dharma of renunciants and the procedure for those who have died is declared:
having gone from the village toward the east, the north, or some other direction.
Either beneath a Brahma-tree, an Aśvattha, or a Śamī tree,
or having dug [the pit] at the base of a sacrificial tree, or on a riverbank in a pure place.
Having sprinkled the pit, which has been dug with the seven vyāhṛtis, with water using the [seven] vyāhṛtis,
one should then spread kuśa grass over it and consecrate it with water while reciting the syllable Om (praṇava).
Having bathed the corpse with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the Puruṣasūkta,
and having adorned it with perfumes and garlands, the righteous man should take it up in a basket.
He places the corpse in a pit, facing either eastward or northward, with the mantra:
"O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation! and "This Viṣṇu strode across."
Having placed the staff in his right hand,
he should then cause the sling to be set down in the sacrificial pit with the verse, "That which is beyond this dust."

With the *pavitramantra* used by the gods, one should place the water-purifier (*jalapavitraka*) in the mouth; with the *Sāvitrī* and the *praṇava*, one should place the vessel of Brahman (*brahmabhājana*) in the stomach.
With the verse, "The earth has gone to the earth, O Mother," he should place the water-pot in the middle.
One should cause the ten Hotṛ priests to recite the consecratory formulas beginning with "cittiḥ śruk."
Having filled the pit with sand and dust so that it cannot be broken by wild beasts and the like, one should then sweep and smear it.
"Having adorned [the body] with perfumes and other substances, then, in the case of death in great waters, purification occurs by mere bathing; there is no ritual procedure nor the offering of water.
In this regard, even the kinsmen should perform only a bath with their clothes on. And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
A son, a brother, a daughter’s son, a sapinda relative, or even a disciple,
by touching an ascetic— even after carrying him— becomes pure immediately through bathing.
But when the father has renounced the world and passed away, his sons who are nearby must perform the cremation and whatever other rites are required according to their ability.
One should cremate [the body] according to the ritual for the Pitṛmedha, using the Uttapana fire;
or even according to the ritual for the Hotṛ priest, with the Gāyatrī or the Praṇava.
By merely immersing themselves in water and touching [the deceased], the kinsmen become pure;
having performed the cremation, the twice-born relatives attain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
When the eleventh day arrives, the pārvaṇa rite is prescribed;
however, the son must not perform the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa for them.
For by the mere taking up of the triple staff (tridaṇḍa), the deceased has already attained [the state of liberation], so says the sage Uśanas.
"One should strike the *kuṭīcaka* and fill the *bahūdaka*;
the *haṃsa* should be cast into water, and one should pierce the supreme *haṃsa*.
Thus ends the section on the ritual for the consecration of ascetics (*yati-saṃskāra-vidhi*) in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
[190] Now, regarding the casting of bones into the waters of the Gaṅgā,
on this point Śāṇḍilya says:
"Whoever casts their bones at Dvāravatī, Setubandha, the Godāvarī, or Puṣkara, shall attain liberation upon death. Thus say Śaṅkha and Likhita.

"Having duly cast the bones at the Gaṅgā, at Prayāga, at Kedāra, and at the excellent Puṣkara, one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at Gayā; thus one is liberated from the debt to one's parents, and they both eternally attain liberation. Thus it is said.
Yogayājñavalkya states: "A son should especially cast the bones into the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Kāverī, the Śutudrī, or the Sarasvatī."
Śālaṅkāyana says: Having performed the collection of the bones according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Gṛhya-sūtra,
and having placed the bones in a jar, one should deposit the jar in the ground.
Having touched that and performed the purification of the bones, the rite succeeds for one reciting the remaining mantras at the top of a tree or on an auspicious spot.
The wise man, having placed it there, should maintain protection until the completion of the journey;
he should deposit it on the ground to the east and not look back for six months.
Or [the removal] of the earth for three fortnights or three months is not required,
because the body is impermanent and [the rite] occurs when the proper time, materials, and other factors are available.
[191] When one month and so forth have elapsed, if he desires to extract the bones,
he shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for three years, two years, and one year, respectively, according to the sequence of months and so on.
The word "having done" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Then there shall be the pacification of that fault; otherwise, one would go to hell.
[This applies] in the case of a son who dies an untimely death at a great pilgrimage site within ten days [of birth].
Having performed the purification by collecting the bones, one should cast them into the water;
for one whose death occurred in half-water, having cremated him outside according to the prescribed rite.
Preceded by the recitation of the mantras intended for the collection of the bones,
[one should perform the rite] with sesame seeds, clarified butter, honey, fragments of gold, and water.
"Having extinguished the fire with milk, one should cast it into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Āpastamba also says: "On the fourth day, there is the collection of the bones; their casting into the waters of the Gaṅgā [follows]. Jayanta describes the method for extracting the bones:
"The performer should avoid three births, the Bhadrā [nakṣatra], and the constellations of the three quarters (tripād)."
And the days of Mars, Venus, and the Sun, as well as the lunar phase known as Bhadra and the Karaṇa called Bava.
Having gone to that place with his kinsmen for the purpose of extracting the vertebrae,
he paid homage there, preceded by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Having formed this intention and touched water while reciting this mantra:
"O Earth, endowed with wealth, everything has gone to dissolution within you;
O Purifier, grant me the bones of my father and ancestors, which have been protected as an embryo."
Having thus prayed to the Goddess of the Earth, one should slowly recite the *bhūmir bhūmiṃ* mantra.
Having dug with a wooden tool and taken the bones from the jar,
one should take care that the jar does not move.
One should fill the pitcher with fragrant substances, flowers, fruits, and earth;
one should level the ground and cast the sacrificial offering (bali) there.
Once she has attained satisfaction with abundant food, drink, edibles, and so forth,
he should then consecrate her with the three-verse hymn beginning with "balittha."
Then, having taken the bone and placed it on the riverbank,
the son washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the ritual procedure for the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
This other purification is declared to be complete by means of water from a golden vessel,
after having repeatedly touched those bones a hundred times with clay and other substances.
Those Brahmins who know the ritual procedures and who contemplate all beings should perform the ablution;
they shall turn a non-divine object into a divinity, and a divinity into a supreme divinity.
And he should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to those highly fortunate brahmins;
the performer of the rite should perform a bath for his own purification, or have it performed.
According to their own capacity, they should perform the consecration with thirty or twenty-five [verses] known as the "Earth" (mṛttikā),
and thereafter perform the consecration with the water from the jars (kumbha) in hundreds and so forth.
With the hymns of the Śrīsūkta, Rudrasūkta, and Pavamānasūkta, as well as those known as the Viṣṇusūkta and others,
one should meditate upon the Vasus, Rudras, Ādityas, and the ancestral deities within them.

One should worship Śiva, Viṣṇu, as well as Indra and all other chosen deities, according to the prescribed ritual, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings ending with the food offering (naivedya).
Having paid homage to the one who knows the ritual procedure, one should satisfy him with sacrificial fees.
"Having bound it firmly with the skins of female sheep, with silken garments, with linen, with silk-cloth, or with a rope of *kuśa* grass, one should cast it into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Thus it is said in the *Ādipurāṇa*.
Furthermore, wherever the Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī makes her presence,
the casting of bones into those waters conduces to the world of Brahmā.
Those who occasionally carry the bones of their parents or ancestors to the waters of the Gaṅgā—
being overcome by compassion for those relatives as well— their sacred bathing places (tīrthas) yield fruit.
Then, having bathed, having sprinkled [the bones] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and having scattered gold, honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds,
he should place the bones in a vessel made of a lump of clay and look toward the direction presided over by the King of the Ancestors (Yama).
Having entered the water with the words "Homage be to the Dharma," he should cast [the offering] while saying "May He be pleased with me.
Then, having risen and gazed at the radiant sun, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a preeminent Brahmin.
"When this is done, for one residing in the city of the departed (Pretapura), there shall be a transition to heaven equal to that of Mahendra.
Thus it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "As long as a human's bone remains in the waters of the Gaṅgā..."
"For that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "If a man places the bones of his mother, father, or ancestors in the sky at the Daśāśvamedha [tirtha]..."
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, having sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and having scattered gold, honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds;

Having placed it in a meritorious clay vessel and saying, "Homage be to Dharma," one should cast it into the water with the *pitṛ-tīrtha* out of devotion; then, having bowed, one should gaze at the sun with self-restraint.
Having also given a sacrificial fee according to his ability, he shall lead all the ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
[194] On the eighth day of the latter fortnight of the month of Nabhas, when the sun is at the meridian, one should,
with the permission of Brahmins, cast the bones into the waters of the Gaṅgā on that eighth day while the sun is at its zenith.

"When this is done, even a great sinner—a drinker of liquor or one who has violated the teacher's bed—even if joined by all [other] sins, shall be liberated; there is no doubt in this matter. Thus it is stated in the *Padmapurāṇa*.
Having performed the purification of the bones with the names beginning with Keśava and others,
one should place them in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and worship them thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings.
Having obtained the permission of the twice-born, being well-composed, disciplined in his resolve, he should pronounce the names of his lineage and personal name while at the Ganges.

"By means of the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta, [one should say] 'Salutation indeed to Dharma,' and then one should dismiss the bones; one should mutter that [mantra] as long as there are bones. Thus ends the section on the method of depositing the bones in the Smṛticandrikā.
Now, the procedure for the Gayā-śrāddha.
Regarding this, the Ādi-purāṇa states:
"One who is prepared to go to Gayā in order to perform the śrāddha according to the prescribed rite..."
Having assumed the guise of a rag-robe wearer, he performed a circumambulation of the village as well.
Then, having gone to another village and partaken of food remaining from a śrāddha ceremony,
he should proceed after performing a circumambulation, avoiding the acceptance of gifts.

The meaning is as follows: having performed a *śrāddha* for nine deities at his own home, primarily consisting of ghee, and taking the remaining ghee from that *śrāddha*, he should circumambulate the village, go to another village, eat there, and then, after circumambulating that village as well, he should depart while avoiding the acceptance of gifts and other such things. Furthermore, the renunciation of accepting gifts lasts until the completion of the *Agastya-śrāddha*.
Having gone to the Uttaramānasa lake by this very procedure, and having sipped water (*ācamana*) with *kuśa* grass in hand, he should sprinkle water upon his head.
If they do not speak, one should go to the place known as Kanaka.
"Abbruvann" (not speaking) is a prohibition against the useless employment of speech.
In that regard, having sipped water and sprinkled his head, he should look at the sun;
and having bathed in the middle of the lake at Gayā, he attains the supreme state of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Having seen [the site] and entered it, one should then perform the śrāddha according to the rules,
as well as the ekoddiṣṭa for paternal uncles, maternal uncles, and others.
On the following day, one should perform the bath of Mataṅga at Vāpī and at Dharmapṛṣṭha;
thereafter, at midday, the Śrāddha and the Piṇḍas should be offered at the well and the sacrificial post.
The separate mention of the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍadāna*) is for the purpose of highlighting its preeminence at Gayā.
Having bathed in the lake of Brahmā and performed the circumambulation of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*),
one should perform the *śrāddha* and the pouring of water over the funeral cakes on the third day.
Having touched the waters of a great river, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the deities;
thus one attains imperishable worlds and uplifts one's entire lineage.
One should perform that [rite] at Gayāśiras on the fourth day, including the śrāddha and the offering of piṇḍas;
on the fifth day, one should go to the banyan tree known as Akṣaya.
At Gayā and at Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, one is liberated from all sins;
