and when one performs a śrāddha at Gayāśīrṣa, offering it by name for those [ancestors], they are likewise freed.
Those dwelling in hell go to heaven, and those dwelling in heaven attain liberation. Between heaven and the netherworld (pātāla), there is no sacred site equal to Gayā.
When a funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) is offered at Gayāśiras, the ancestors attain the state of gods.
The wise Mahādeva set foot upon Muṇḍapṛṣṭha after performing very difficult austerities for many thousands of years.
Even by a short time here, a person devoted to dharma quickly liberates himself from evil, just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
Having bathed at Gayākūpa and performed the libations,
a man should then perform the śrāddha ceremony according to the prescribed rules beneath the banyan tree.
There is the place known as Akṣayavaṭa, renowned throughout the three worlds;
whatever is given there to the ancestors shall certainly become inexhaustible.
By taking refuge at the foot of a banyan tree, even with only vegetables or water,
a single meal offered to a Brahmin becomes equivalent to ten million meals fed.
Gayā is the most excellent of all sacred fords, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having offered the funeral cakes and water there, and having beheld one's great-grandfather.
One obtains inexhaustible worlds and uplifts one's entire lineage;
all ancestors are thereby delivered through this dharma—what could be greater than this?
O great sage, it is heard that even the ancestors sang this verse:
"May there arise in our lineage those who walk upon the path of the righteous."
Those who, having gone to Gayā, shall offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) for us with devotion;
and the man who dwells at Gayā during both the bright and dark fortnights—he purifies his lineage even unto the seventh generation; there is no doubt in this matter.
Seeing his son arrive at Gayā, there would be a festival for the ancestors;
having touched even the water with his feet, will he not give it to us?
For one who has merely set out from home toward Gayā,
every step is indeed a staircase for the ancestors' ascent to heaven.
The sin of one who kills a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a killer of a child,
or a betrayer of his teacher is indeed destroyed for him who goes to Gayā.
The killer of a Brahmin, the ungrateful person, and the slayer of a cow— these five types of sinners—
all attain purification by offering the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) at Gayā.
When an eclipse of the moon or the sun occurs during the Makara transit,
the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā— which is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds— is accomplished.
At Gayā, the Śrāddha rite is inexhaustible, as are recitations, burnt offerings, and austerities;
for that merit indeed dwells in the abode of the ancestors, and therefore it becomes inexhaustible there.
In Bharata’s holy hermitage, which is surrounded by the most meritorious beings,
the sacred footprint of Mataṅga is seen by all men.
Then, O Bhārata, by resorting to Gayā while remaining celibate and having conquered his senses, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice simply by going there.
One should understand that celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is required except during the period favorable for conception.
From there, O Indra among kings, one should go to Dhenuka, which is world-renowned;
there, O great king, a most wonderful sign remains even today.
O joy of the Kurus, O best of kings, the footprints of a tawny cow with her calf were seen as she was walking through the mud.
O Indra among kings, O bull of the Bharatas, by touching those footprints,
whatever inauspiciousness men possess is destroyed, O Bhārata.
From there, one should go to Gṛdhravaṭa, the abode of the wise deity;
having bathed there with ashes, one should approach Nṛpadhvaja.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the twelve-year vow shall have been performed;
for the other castes, however, there shall be the destruction of all sins.
From there, one should go to that world-renowned mountain, Udayanta;
there, O bull of the Bharatas, the footprints of Sāvitrī are seen.
There, a Brahmin who has undertaken his vows should perform the twilight devotions;
by doing so, he becomes one who has performed the twilight devotions for twelve years.
O bull among sages, the gateway to the womb is located right there;
having gone there, men are liberated from the perils of the womb.
Then, O King, by visiting the sacred fords in due order,
one who has not yet reached perfection shall obtain abundant success in wealth as well as great spiritual accomplishment.
From there, O king of kings, one should proceed with a concentrated mind to Dharmapṛṣṭha;
there, O great king Yudhiṣṭhira, Dharma dwells eternally.
Having reached that place, O Indra among kings, a man obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice;
thereafter, he reaches Viśalya, which is renowned throughout the three worlds.
He obtains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world;
likewise, a pure man, having reached the abode of Maheśvara,
obtains the Pitṛmedha sacrifice and uplifts his entire lineage.
Having reached the [river] that causes darkness for the dwellers of heaven, one who has conquered the senses does not fall into an evil rebirth and obtains the merit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Then, a student of sacred knowledge firm in his vows should go to Māṣapada;
having bathed there at Māṣapada, he shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
There, O bull of the Bharatas, is the world-renowned confluence of ten million sacred fords;
one who has undertaken a vow should perform an ablution there at that confluence of ten million fords.
One obtains the Puṇḍarīka reward and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
By the word *puṇḍarīka*, the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice is designated.
[The regions of] *gopracāra* ... were established by Brahmā.
When they are merely touched, the ancestors shall attain liberation.
For there was a certain preeminent and foremost seer who offered water among the mango trees;
thus the mangoes were watered and the ancestors were satisfied—a single action that accomplished two purposes.
That river known as Vaitaraṇī, famous throughout the three worlds,
was filled with water by that illustrious lady for the sake of delivering the ancestors.
Having gone there and bathed, the man who performs the gift of a cow shall undoubtedly deliver twenty-one generations of his lineage.
The Mahānadī, the Brahma-lake, the inexhaustible banyan tree, Prabhāsa, Udyanta, Gayāśiras,
the Sarasvatī, Dhenuka, and Dharmapṛṣṭha— these in Gayā are equal to Kurukṣetra.
If, at some point through the passage of time, a son should go to Gayā,
he should feed those very Brahmins who were designated by Brahmā.
Those Brahmins whose station is the assembly of Brahmā, who likewise drink the Soma,
and whose consecrations were performed by Brahmā himself, are remembered as being equal to Brahmā.
The abandonment of the body at Gayā is prescribed as a meritorious act;
likewise, the performance of śrāddha, the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa), and the libation of water are highly extolled at Gayā.
He who performs the rite of releasing a bull in the unsurpassed sacred field of Gayā obtains merit equal to that of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
One should place the funeral ball (piṇḍa) on the ground between that well and the sacrificial post;
by performing this with water from the well, what is given to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
In the assembly hall, the holy sacrificial post (yūpa) was established by Brahmā;
by circumambulating that post, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
To the north of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is a most sacred pilgrimage site named Kanakanandā, frequented by hosts of Brahmanical sages;
having bathed there, human beings go to heaven in their own physical bodies.
Furthermore, whatever śrāddha is offered there is declared to be eternally inexhaustible;
there is a beautiful lotus pond there known by the name Supuṇyā.
Having bathed there, one whose impurities are exhausted is liberated from the three debts;
furthermore, a śrāddha performed there becomes infinite and yields great prosperity.
One who performs the *śrāddha* rite there shall always deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants.
Having bathed in the Mānasa lake, one should then perform the *śrāddha*.
On the shore of that lake, however, is the great temple of the God.
Having ascended the celestial chariot, a man immediately goes to heaven;
having gone to Uttaramānasa, he attains the highest perfection.
One should perform the śrāddha for him with devotion according to one's means;
thus one obtains divine desires and finds the means to liberation.
A great marvel is seen in the excellent Mānasa lake,
and the celestial sounds of the constellations and planets are heard.
Having offered a śrāddha at Gṛdhravaṭa in Gayā, one obtains great fruit;
where the head of Gogayā is located, there flows the meritorious Mahānadī.
The sacred bathing place of Brahmasaras is always frequented by sages and gods;
whatever fruit is said to be obtained at Sannihati when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu,
that entire fruit is declared to be gained day after day at Gayā.
His ancestors rejoice like farmers at a bountiful rain;
he who goes to Gayā and offers food makes his ancestors truly possessed of a son.
Whatever one who stays at Gayā gives, all that attains infinity;
likewise on the thirteenth day of the month and under the Maghā asterism, there is no doubt.
Thus concludes the determination of the procedure for the *gayā-śrāddha* in the *Smṛticandrikā*.
Now, those entitled to perform the *gayā-śrāddha*.
In this regard, sons and others should be understood as the qualified performers [of the rites]. However, a specific exception is stated:
"While sons exist, one should certainly not have another perform the *svadhā* [offering].
This is an exception (*apavāda*) to the statement of Ṛśyaśṛṅga.
"Whether one's own son or the son of another, whenever one might cast a funeral cake (piṇḍa) into the Gayā-kūpa under someone's name, that person shall be led to eternal Brahman.
Thus, there is also another distinction.
O one of great intelligence, for one's own self at Gayā, one should perform the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) even without sesame seeds; likewise, so too for other members of one's lineage.

The word "anyā" (others) is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). From this very statement, it is understood that in other cases, the offering of a funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) for oneself should not be performed. Likewise:
"Caste-fellows, kinsmen, friends, relatives, and well-wishers—for them as well, the husband should give [the cake] to his wife; this is the eternal law (*sanātana-dharma*)."
Regarding this, Gobhila states an exception concerning Gayā:
"A father may offer to his sons, and an elder brother may offer even to his younger brothers; at Gayā, however, one should offer the funeral cake with effort and a concentrated mind. [203]
By the use of the word "api" (also), the husband should offer the *piṇḍa* for his wife as well. Likewise:
"But while one's parents are living, one should offer the *piṇḍa* at Gayā;
and that should be offered with a jujube fruit, or with barley-food, or with a fruit."
One should perform that rite while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (upavītī), using sesame seeds mixed with curd;
for thus, according to the Śruti, all go to heaven by means of the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
"Therefore, one should diligently offer the rice-ball (piṇḍa) to them as well, according to the prescribed rite. Thus says Vṛddha-Śātātapa:
"Out of affection, one should offer rice-balls at Gayā for all [deceased] persons, regardless of their caste (varṇa) or sectarian mark (liṅga)."
"A man who performs [the rites] himself correctly shall attain great prosperity. Thus says Marīci:
"A Brahmin must certainly not perform the funeral rites for Śūdras."
"Even by a Śūdra, [the Śrāddha] for a Brāhmaṇa may sometimes be performed, except when under the influence of sin.
Thus concludes the determination of those entitled to perform the Gayā-Śrāddha.
Thus [ends the work of] the son of the venerable Keśavāditya Bhaṭṭopādhyāya, who is proficient in all branches of learning...
The section on impurity (āśaucakāṇḍa) in the Smṛticandrikā composed by Yājñikadevaṇabhaṭṭopādhyāya Somayājī is completed.
